en: Preface:
As for the *Suishan Suwen Lu* (Record of Water Repentance Heard Along the Way), it is a commentary by Master Zhuzhong. Formerly, National Teacher Wudao suffered from a human-faced ulcer;
had he not been moved by the appearance of Lord Nāgārjuna and the water of the mountain stream, how could he have avoided [this calamity]?

Furthermore, one becomes an enemy to oneself. Only now do I realize that when causes and conditions converge, karmic retribution is difficult to escape; that the entanglements of past lives remain unresolved, and the ripening of fruits never errs.

As the ancient masters have said: "If you wish to exit the wheel of suffering, nothing precedes the upholding of the precepts. If you wish to purify the root of the precepts, nothing precedes repentance.
Therefore, to harbor flaws and blemishes is not permitted by the Buddha, whereas confessing prior transgressions is what the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* esteems. From this...
This wondrous composition of sacred texts is divided into three fascicles and is titled the *Water Repentance*. I humbly reflect that this Dharma-gate of the repentance scriptures is lofty and vast;

its principles of cause and effect are distinct, its language concise yet its meaning comprehensive, and its depth is unfathomable. Were it not for a detailed analysis and systematic classification, those who are ordinary and ignorant would find it difficult to attain awakening.
This is especially so as the human spirit no longer conforms to antiquity and the social mores of the age decline daily. As for viewing...
The scriptures and repentance manuals of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have been dismissed as迂談 (迂谈) and 腐論 (腐论)—迂闊 and 陳腐 discourse—that cannot be trusted or followed.
Therefore, Master Zhuzhong’s commentary on the *Suiwen yilu* is elegant without being boastful and analytical without being contentious.

It compiles a wealth of material with extreme thoroughness and completeness; its illumination of the principles of good and evil, fortune and calamity, leaves nothing unilluminated, revealing the One [Reality].

It is the most subtle of all gateways; it is ultimate, indeed it is ultimate. It serves not only to provide for the merit of the unseen realm, but also acts as a precious raft for those lost at the ford of delusion—nothing surpasses this.
Furthermore, Master Zhudong was a dragon-elephant within the Buddha-dharma.

There were no teachings expounded in the Chan palace that he did not consult, and among the three teachings and the hundred schools, there was nothing he had not mastered through comprehensive study. Therefore, students ought to investigate this deeply.
This is my earnest intention. It is not merely for my own self-exhortation, but also intended to serve as a medicinal cauterization for those who have yet to attain or realize [the truth].
Alas! Amidst the destruction of war and fire, nothing remains; even among my fellow practitioners, there is regret that they have never been able to see this book.
I suspect that at the time it was printed, the copies were few, and thus its circulation has been extremely limited. I myself have harbored a deep longing for it for over twenty years.
Previously, while at the residence of my fellow practitioner, I first obtained one fascicle; however, it was incomplete and missing portions.

Later, upon meeting the lay devotee Shen of Qingyuan, I finally acquired the complete work. It seems there must have been some invisible forces silently assisting me. I have respectfully read through it once.
I am eager to have this work published so that it may be circulated. At that time, however, the monastery’s construction was underway and my resources were utterly depleted;
thus, I hesitated and the project remained unmanifested. Now, having received the generous assistance of my fellow practitioners, my wish has indeed been fulfilled.
I hope that those who share my aspirations will study it together.
Preface respectfully composed by the śramaṇa Rui-bin, a descendant of the lineage of the Tiantai teachings and contemplations, incumbent of Yiwu Temple on Mount Lingjiu in Hangzhou,
on the day of the Buddha’s Bathing Festival in the fourth month of the year of Yiwei, the twenty-first year of the Guangxu era.
Preface to the *Suiwen lu* (Record of What Was Heard):

My merit is meager and my virtue is cool; I can only tie my bundle of coarse grass and withdraw my feet. Because my conditions for wisdom are stingy and my intellect dull, it is especially fitting that I shut my door and bury my head.

I repent for the early transgressions of my past extravagance and restrain the fish-like mind that flutters and drags about. I shall wash away my faults with the water of the *Bimí*, drying up [the stream of delusion].
I have spent the year sitting upon a meditation cushion; yet I fear I may deeply辜负 (betray) the Buddha’s compassion and have entered the gates of Chan in vain.

Furthermore, as the city of the repentance society is besieged, I have not escaped errors such as confusing "wu" for "an" or "hai" for "shi. The sword of wisdom remains sheathed in its scabbard, making it difficult to pierce the lacquer bucket or the oil lamp.

Now, National Teacher Wudao, whose learning encompasses both the inner and outer paths and whose insight penetrates past and present, has composed the *Zuoyuan Chanyan* (Repentance for Eradicating Vengeful Spirits), much like the Minister of Works [Du Fu].

In these poems, the words are near at hand yet the meaning is far-reaching; the events are humble yet the principles are vast. They cannot be fathomed by the narrow vision of a mere pipe, nor can they be fully reflected upon by the limited mind of a wild beast.
I fear that were I to cast my wild eyes about with contempt and ply my stubborn tongue to discourse from my breast, I would surely err regarding the Sage’s intent and profane the profound verses.
Upon hearing this, the wise would feel their hearts chill; upon seeing it, the discerning would have their hair stand on end.
Therefore, I first verified the original texts of the two Piṭakas, followed by a critical examination of the commentaries and exegeses of various worthies.

Having selected those that were most accurate and appropriate, I have compiled them to perpetuate their fragrance. I cite the sublime words of both mundane and supramundane teachings to encourage my own friends and those yet to be converted.

I, Wang, have thus discarded my robes and bowl to carve this onto woodblocks. Relying upon the generosity of donors (*dāna*) to assist in the engraving, I seek to manifest the noble intent of the virtuous—the love of good for good—and to clarify the refined sentiments of the beginner—the reverence for the worthy.
Together we shall glorify the sublime legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and exhaustively purify the accumulated karmic evils of ourselves.
Although this is but the power of aspiration of one individual at a single moment, I still hope that those of wisdom and sagacity throughout the four quarters will [support it].
Having weighed these matters, I venture to carve this woodblock so that it may be widely disseminated to distant lands.

This is the preface to the *Re-engraved Record of the Water Repentance as Heard*, composed by the Way-man Zheng on a midsummer day at Jingming Hermitage atop Mount Gaosheng in the ancient city of Shaozhou. Recorded with reverence.
The source of the mind is fundamentally clear and still; the essence of its nature is originally devoid of purity or defilement.

It is only due to the slightest discrepancy of a single thought that thousands of lifetimes of error and perversity are brought about. Wandering through the three realms and appearing and disappearing within the four modes of birth—to reflect on this in silence is truly to be lamented.
Therefore, when the Venerable Nāgārjuna observed the delusion and confusion of sentient beings, he consequently revealed the Kāmaloka [realm] to them.

I am ill. Desiring to compose the preface and origin narrative for the text of repentance, I reported that the facial sores upon my knees would soon be healed, and that the ten lifetimes of karmic enmity with Yuan Chao would be eliminated from this point forward.
The three-fascicle text of repentance for the Shu Ridge was thus completed.

I have gathered the profound writings of the Flower Treasury (Avataṃsaka) to create a confession for the present life; yet, alas, those whose faculties are dull and stubborn not only fail to comprehend its principles, but moreover—

Furthermore, if one does not understand its text, how can one penetrate the subtle and merge with the vast? Zen Master Zhongchan’s compassionate concern was profound and his intent to rescue and deliver others was earnest;

he annotated the *Suiwen yilu* (Record of What Was Heard) so that those performing repentance rituals would be struck with clarity regarding the unfailing nature of karmic retribution, and would resolutely reform themselves.
Yet, its circulation has not been widespread, and no woodblocks have yet been carved.

I have searched extensively for famous monasteries, yet these records are rarely seen. What remains is only that of Master Noh of the Fazangyuan; though one volume has been transmitted, how can it endure forever?
Therefore, I have exhorted others to raise funds for a new printing so that it may be shared with all who share our affinity, ensuring that the Buddha-dharma shall remain imperishable.
Recorded on the Dragon Boat Festival of the Jiwei year, the ninth year of the Great Qing Xianfeng era,
by Hai-men Yan-jing, a junior student of the Tiantai teachings and contemplations.
Proofread by Chan-zong, a junior student of Wulin.
Master Zhizhou’s Explanation of the Water Repentance: Preface.
As for the true nature, which is suchness (*tathatā*), how could there be any necessity regarding sin or merit? To single out sins and single out merits is like placing a speck of dust in one's eye.
"Dust settled upon a mirror"—how profound are the words of Vipaśyin Buddha! "Sin and merit are both empty," said Viśvabhū.
"Sin and merit are like illusions," said Krakucchanda. "One who can know that the nature of sin is empty [attains liberation]," said Kanakamuni.
Contemplating these verses of the Seven Buddhas is truly the progenitor of the true method of repentance. Yet, why was the *Water Repentance* (Shui-chan) composed by Master Wù?
When the Duke was in Han, he was fearful of Yuan Shao. Later, when the seven kingdoms raised their arms in rebellion, he proposed the execution of Chao Cuo.
Although Cuo repeatedly sought revenge, because the Duke’s family had long been associated with eminent monks, there was no opening through which to strike back.

Now that the Duke has become the National Preceptor and enjoys excessive honor, Cuo has finally gained access by manifesting as a facial ulcer on the Duke’s knee, its agony piercing to the very marrow. Neither Lu Ban nor Bian Que can cure it. Thus it is shown.

"One should not greedily cling to fame and profit; let this serve as a warning for those who come after. Master Wù recalled the words of the extraordinary monk and soon arrived at the place of the twin pines on Chá-lǒng.
He ordered that [the patient] be washed with rock spring water, and he was healed immediately. Later, because of this, he composed the *Water Repentance* (Shuǐchàn).
This is recorded in detail in his own biography. If one establishes a grand plan for the empire, one must inevitably encounter great difficulties;
if one eliminates the great calamities of the world, one must inevitably endure great suspicion from the world. Both Daoyang and Xiao Cuo could have been free from regret;
why, then, did he seek further retribution? When Xiao Cuo was deliberating on the reduction of the seven kingdoms, his father had already grown anxious.
It is said that while the House of Liu was at peace, what of the Rhao clan? Did their father truly harbor the intent to kill Zuo?
When the Wus and Chus rose in rebellion, Zou Ang did not begrudge a single person to appease the seven kingdoms; he acted solely out of loyalty to the House of Liu.
How could he have had leisure to plan for the Rhao clan? Alas, this matter is worthy of reflection. I once held the Classics as a student and observed this.
To say that a transgression cannot be repented of is to treat a sin that *can* be repented as a talisman for rebels and traitors.
To now claim that such is the meaning of entering the Buddha-vehicle is incorrect. If sins could not be repented of, it would cut off the path for the world to reform itself;
there would be no hope for seeing one's nature, and the very mandate of the Buddha would nearly perish. It is like the stains on clothing: they must necessarily rely on cleansing agents.
"Wash! When the clothes have been washed away and remain, where can the grime still be? Master Wugong composed this repentance ritual; it is truly beneficial for future generations.

Now, Master Zhigong’s commentary on this repentance ritual is of great merit for people of the present day. It is only fitting that he should diligently propagate and translate it, expediting its dissemination."

Regarding the *Qijue* [commentary]: if one understands that what the Buddha speaks of as "seeing and hearing" is not truly seeing and hearing, then all knots of doubt will be swept away and no residual conceptual meaning will remain.
Thus, one knows that transgression originally has no form and repentance fundamentally has no abiding place. This commentary, too, is not a definitive exposition.
I wish that those who read the *Suixunlu* (Record of Following What is Heard) would contemplate it in this way.
Written by the Buddha-disciple Dae-jin of Geumsa Temple, this is the Preface to the *Compassionate Water Repentance Ritual* (*Jibjae suisang*).

(A "preface" [seo] signifies a beginning; it is like a cocoon finding its thread: once the thread is found, the entire silk of the cocoon is revealed. Once the preface to a repentance ritual is found, the full purport of that ritual is understood. The name of the author of the preface cannot be verified.)

I venture to submit that regarding the holy teachings—the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma Piṭakas—apart from those translated at the seats of the translators, among the works composed by the various sages thereafter, has there ever been one produced without being moved by some inspiration?

(The word "venture" [qiè] means to do so privately; it refers to what is first thought in the private mind before being made manifest in speech. The teachings of the Great Sage are divided into the three Piṭakas of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma:

the Sūtras elucidate wisdom and principle, while the Vinaya elucidates precepts and conduct. Beyond these, the compositions of the wise are for the most part largely the result of their minds being moved by specific events. This statement was made immediately upon my birth. If one were to set them forth item by item...
If one were to enumerate them by category, they would be difficult to record in their entirety. As for this sacred text being called the *Water Repentance*, I shall ask you to explain its origins.

(To describe it item by item and cite each matter, with categories opened up separately, would be impossible to exhaust; I shall merely attempt to state the general circumstances of this efficacious repentance. In the past, during the reign of Emperor Yizong of the Tang dynasty, there was the National Preceptor Wudala, whose name was Zhixuan.
(Tang is the dynastic name; he was a descendant of Li Yuan’s younger brother, Li Shide. This was the time when the repentance was composed. Yizong was one who could truly believe in the Triple Gem.)

The title of National Preceptor (Guoshi) arose from this, as he was honored by the Emperor and served as a teacher to those who had attained enlightenment through the rites. "Wuda" (Awakened Attainment) was his style name; "Zhixuan" (Knowing the Mysterious) was his given name.

Before he became prominent, he once encountered a monk in the capital at a lodging whose location he has forgotten (when serving as a participant in the summer retreat, he once met an extraordinary monk in the royal capital;
they met unexpectedly, though he forgot the address of the residence). This monk suffered from *kāmalā* disease, and everyone loathed him, yet Zhixuan associated with him.
He lived as a neighbor, frequently looking after him with no sign of weariness. (The *kāmalā* disease is a malignant illness; it is great leprosy, and for this reason all people loathe it.

This holy monk manifested a malignant disease for two purposes: first, to test the heart of Master Da; second, to manifest a portent of impending calamity. As a neighbor—meaning they shared a single room—he became increasingly diligent over time. He sought the means to alleviate the suffering, and Xuan alone took pity on him, occasionally attending to his needs.

When they parted ways, the monk was moved by his sense of integrity and righteousness, and he blessed him, saying: "In the future, if you encounter difficulties, you may go to Pengcheng in Western Shu."

They sought one another at Chaluṅg Mountain in the prefecture. On that mountain were two pine trees serving as markers. (The term "jie zhi" refers to the conclusion of the summer retreat; each departed separately. A sick monk, moved by their lofty character and commitment to the Way, knew that Master Da would surely face hardships later.

Thus he prayed: "In the future, should you encounter difficulties, there will certainly be honorable fortune on another day; your past karmic obstructions shall naturally be cleared. Xishu is the name of a province, present-day Sichuan. Pengzhou is the name of a prefecture. Chaluṅg Mountain is also called Jiulǒng Mountain.

This was where a transcendent being manifested in the body of a bhikṣu to deliver sentient beings, and the place from which the Elder Da emerged to escape suffering. "Mutually seeking" means visiting one another. "Illness must be treated. The two tall pines rose up beyond the clouds. "Zhi" means to visit. Hereafter...

National Teacher Wudao resided at Anguo Temple. His virtue and conduct were preeminent. (Anguo Temple in Chang’an: his learning and knowledge were abundant; he extensively opened the dharma assembly, and his reputation and virtue shone brightly.

This [first sentence] explains the cause of his attainment of honor, while the following [sentence] records the reality of his manifest excellence). Emperor Yizong personally attended his dharma seat and bestowed sandalwood for his dharma throne; the favor was exceedingly generous.

(In the twelfth year of the Xiantong era, the Emperor visited Anguo Temple and provided a dharma throne made of sandalwood and various precious materials. He appointed him as National Teacher; hence it is said that the favor was exceedingly generous). From then on, suddenly...

A human-faced ulcer grew upon his knee, complete with eyebrows, eyes, a mouth, and teeth. Whenever he was fed with food and drink, it would open its mouth and swallow it, no different from a human being.
He summoned famous physicians everywhere, yet they all stood with hands folded, remaining silent. (The phrase "疊恩渥甚厚" [the favors were exceedingly profound] is a general statement;

"human face," "eyebrows," "eyes," "mouth," and "teeth" are specified individually. Since it possessed a mouth and teeth, it naturally partook of food and drink. "餧" means to feed; "啖" means to eat. Having produced this ulcer, he must have suffered great agony. Though he summoned renowned physicians everywhere, none could treat it.)

He stood with hands clasped, speechless; his eyes were fixed and his mouth was silent. At that time, beneath the words "there was originally no difference," there are seven characters stating: "His suffering was such that it cannot be described.

He then recalled the words of a fellow monk from days past and went deep into the mountains to search for him. Finding that evening had already fallen, he wandered about looking in all directions until he saw two pines amidst the mist and clouds.

He believed that the appointment they had made was not in vain. (The term *ji* means to recall or reflect upon. Because the master physician had folded his hands and could offer no remedy, he then reflected back upon the illness before it had become manifest.)

The monk’s words were: "Go far to Mount Chalung in Chengdu. It will be at the very height of evening; look in all four directions and there will be nothing else to see but tall pines, lush and verdant, rising far above the mists and clouds. The long-cherished hope and the promise made from a thousand li away shall surely not prove false.

Although his words accorded with the scene, he had not yet met the one who shared his realization. He immediately hurried to that place, where lofty towers and vast halls gleamed with intermingled gold and azure. The monk stood at the entrance of the gate and received him with great joy.
He invited him to stay the night, and when [the traveler] informed him of his ailment, the monk said, "It is no cause for concern."

...Furthermore, there is a spring beneath the cliff. If one washes in it at dawn, one will be cured immediately. (The character *qù* means "to enter quickly. The visiting monk entered in haste; the resident monk waited at the gate, looking back to receive him, and they were both filled with great joy. Consequently, he stayed the night.

When asked the reason for his visit, he explained that he suffered from a malignant disease and had come to pray to the Holy Monk. Kāśyapa said, "It shall do no harm. Beneath this cliff there is a small pool where the spring water is so clear and limpid it reflects the heart.

Wash in it tomorrow morning and you will be swiftly healed. *Zhuó* means "to wash. The spring is, in fact, the water of samādhi). At daybreak, the youth led him to the site of the spring. Just as he was cupping the water in his hands, the sores on the man's face suddenly—
He cried out, "It must not be washed yet! Your discernment is profound and far-reaching; you have investigated the past and present.

Have you ever read the biographies of Yuan Ang and Chao Cuo in the *Book of the Western Han*? [The other] replied, "I have read them. "If you have indeed read them, do you not know that Yuan Ang caused Chao Cuo to be executed?
You are Yuan Ang, and I am Chao Cuo. When Cuo was led to the Eastern Market to be beheaded, how great was his grievance!"

"Alas! (The character *jù* means to cup water with both hands. The ulcer then cried out loudly, speaking human words. 'Do not wash me yet; I wish to recount the origins of my wound. During the reign of Emperor Jing of the Han, the seven states of Wu, Chu, and others rebelled because Emperor Jing had confiscated their territories.

Wan [the ulcer] did not know that he was rebelling because of the execution of Chao Cuo; even if he had not been executed, he would have rebelled anyway. Yet Yuan Ang and Cuo served as ministers together. Ang envied Cuo and said to Emperor Jing: 'Please withdraw your attendants; Cuo shall then hasten to take refuge in the eastern corridor.

It was already evident that people of the time called Cuo a 'sack of wisdom' (*zhináng*) upon hearing Ang’s proposal. Later, Cuo was indeed decapitated in the Eastern Market. This was the grievance of being killed by a sword of the tongue. Because the grievance was heavy and the resentment deep, it could not be forgotten; hence there is the following sequence of events."

(Regarding the passage beginning with "For generations he has sought retribution from you," etc.): For many lifetimes he has sought retribution from you, yet for ten generations you have been a high monk whose precepts were pure and strict; thus, the retribution could find no opportunity.
Now, you have received the sovereign’s favor to an excessive degree, and the mind of fame and profit has arisen, thereby causing a decline in your virtue.

This is why it was able to harm you. (Regarding the phrase "For many lives he sought retribution for past grievances": because enmity cannot be revived when one maintains the pure precepts through successive lifetimes, the retribution could find no opportunity. The deity of the precepts protected and shielded him.)

Therefore, the following passage explains the cause for receiving retribution. "To encounter" (*yu*) means to await one another. When the Sovereign showed favor and treated me with hospitality—specifically, when he personally attended the Dharma assembly and bestowed upon me a seat of fragrant sandalwood, appointing me as National Preceptor—I became excessively extravagant.

Once bound by the snares of fame and the shackles of profit, my refined and solemn moral virtue was impaired; only then could [the retribution] be added. Thus it is said, "to harm. One should know that enjoying blessings is the chief cause for the loss of virtue, and creating evil is the root of suffering. If you wish to seek transcendence from the world, you must refine your observance of the precepts. Not only should resentment not be harbored, but one should especially cherish one's merit in daily life).
Now, I have been cleansed by the Venerable Kāṇadeva through the Dharma-water of samādhi. From this point forward...

"Go; we shall no longer be enemies with you. (Kanakamuni was the name of the Venerable One, which originated from his ulcerous mouth; he was what is known as an extraordinary monk. "Samādhi-water" refers to the water of samādhi within a mind of compassion.

Because of this water, the defiled minds harboring resentment accumulated over many lifetimes were washed away. Thereafter, the two Śākyas were free of grievance. It can be understood that the monk suffering from the ailment appeared for the sake of Master Da, and the kāmalā disease was manifested for the sake of Master Da.)

"If this action had not been taken, how could the grievance of Master Da have been released? How could the Water Repentance (Shuichan) have been established? One must know that every event has its cause.

Upon hearing this, Wuda was struck with such awe that his soul left his body; he hurriedly cupped water in his hands and washed [the wound], yet the pain pierced to the very marrow, and he fainted before reviving.

Upon waking, the ulcer was no longer visible. (He had fainted and revived; he had died and returned to life. The resentment that had pierced his bones and clung to his body was dispelled by the fierce power of the Buddha-dharma, resulting in ultimate liberation.

Having attained rebirth, his knee was restored to its former state. He then realized that the traces of sages and worthies are intermingled with the mundane and cannot be fathomed by ordinary sentiments. When he wished to gaze upon and pay respects once more, he looked back toward the monastery, but it could not be seen again.

(From the time he himself drew water as a youth until his desire to worship again and look back at the temple, he was unable to see it a second time. One should know that this applies not only to Kāṇadeva, but also to the Elder Dà.)

Yet he blends his tracks within the mundane world. Master Da merely manifested suffering for the sake of sentient beings. In the past, manifesting in the body of a high official, he created the causes of evil; today, manifesting in the form of a bhikṣu, he repays the retribution for killing. Although ten lifetimes have passed, the retribution occurs in a single instant.

This demonstrates that cause and effect are never obscured. As for its liberation [from worldly concerns], there were the "Sore" (Chang), "Noga," the "Boy" (Dongzi), and the "Temple Buildings" (Si Yu); all these can no longer be seen, having collectively become like dreams and illusions. Yet, the sacred precincts have never truly ceased to exist; though what was manifest has vanished, new structures have arisen in succession.

Because he established a hermitage at that site, it eventually became a monastery (zhao ti). Reaching our Song Dynasty—(verifying from the preface that the master was a person of the Song era)—during the Zhidao era, it was granted the name Zhide Chan Temple.
There was the eminent monk Master Xingu who composed a record chronicling these events in great detail.

Detailed Account. (He went to the mountain tree-stūpa. Although that which had manifested as magnificent and vast had vanished, the Zhaoti [招提] stūpa emerged once more in splendid newness. "Dai" (迨) means "reaching. "Zhidao" (至道) is a reign title. In this year, by imperial decree, the nameplate for Zhaoti was bestowed, naming it Zhide Chan Temple (至德禪寺).
[The note says: "Xin followed the ancients; this has not yet been verified. At that time, Wuda was moved by its extraordinary nature and reflected deeply on his grievances spanning many lifetimes.

He thought: "Were I not to encounter a sage, by what means could these be released? Consequently, he composed a *chánfǎ* (repentance ritual), which he recited morning and evening. (The character "yù" [遇] should correspond to the preceding "gùjié" [顧接]. He cleared away the brush and established [the site])."*)

Master An composed this liturgy for repentance and recitation to forget fame and profit, to melt away the distinction between self and others, and to bring his remaining life to completion while deeply cultivating the seeds of the Way. The author [of this preface] has extracted the essential points of the Great Canon to form this text for the repentance that purifies transgressions.

Later, it was propagated throughout the world; the current three-volume *Sūtra of Repentance* is precisely this work. It takes the meaning of using the water of samādhi to wash away karmic resentment as its principle, and thus it is titled the *Water Repentance*.
This is the true title of the work that records the extraordinary response of Master Wuda’s encounter with Kāṇadeva.

Establishing the Thesis: This is merely a report on the origins [of this practice], spoken for its sake. (Because the *chánwén* [text of repentance] is concise and rigorous, its phrasing and characters are refined and solemn;

its words can awaken the mind and its matters are sufficient to alert the ear, it has thus been disseminated throughout the world and through successive generations. The following section explains the reasons for establishing its name and serves as the preface to the *Shuǐchán*.

Now, I shall briefly recount these historical facts and highlight the legacy of our predecessors, so that those who open this volume—whether performing the ritual or reciting it—may know that the deeds of former sages have their own origins and precedents. Throughout...

The fruits and causes of the kalpa are not obscure. (The Master himself speaks: I venture to recount the actual events of former times and clarify the noble teachings of past generations, so that those with the karmic affinity in this final age who encounter this repentance may chant the names [of the Buddhas], gaze upon them in reverence, kneel and recite the text of repentance, thereby diminishing their sins and increasing their merit.

Furthermore, one may gain a rough understanding of the Tang-era worthy, the Elder Daolao—how his integrity first moved people, how he was subsequently favored by the sovereign, and how, when his long-standing grievances found an opportunity, he even escaped from suffering.

His establishment of the hermitage and his composition of the repentance ritual each have their origins and precedents. Since cause and effect are not obscure, let this serve as a warning to future generations regarding those who are envious of the virtuous and jealous of talent; that a sword-like tongue used to wound others will inevitably receive its fixed retribution. Beware!)

Verses in Praise of the Buddha (One must offer praise upon seeing the Buddha to express the sincerity of one's refuge and reverence. This serves as a cause for attaining Buddhahood; it is silently held within the mind and clearly articulated by the mouth, enabling those with whom one has a karmic affinity to hear it.

This awakens their past causes, such that both body and mind take refuge. Thus, there is mutual benefit: virtues increase daily on the Path, good friends multiply, and evils diminish. How could these verses in praise of the Buddha be omitted? One should explain them.)

Great Compassion and Great Mercy, pitying all sentient beings. (Two lines. Praising the causes for attaining Buddhahood. *Maitrī* [loving-kindness], *karuṇā* [compassion], *muditā* [sympathetic joy], and *upekṣā* [equanimity] are the four immeasurable minds possessed by Bodhisattvas. Because these four are immeasurable, they are each called "great.

Furthermore, while the practice of the Śrāvakas’ fourfold equanimity cannot truly benefit sentient beings, the Bodhisattva’s practice of the fourfold equanimity can truly and universally benefit them. Loving-kindness is able to bestow happiness, not merely for a single time, in a single place, or toward a single sentient being;

rather, even as it passes through immeasurable times, immeasurable places, and delivers immeasurable sentient beings, it bestows immeasurable happiness. According to the desires of sentient beings, it is like the sun casting its shadow or a mother responding to her child. Yet this mind that bestows happiness never ceases nor rests, until it causes sentient beings to attain the Great [Nirvāṇa].)

Because there are four kinds of bliss within *nirvāṇa*, it is called "Great Compassion" (*mahāmaitrī*). The *Mahā-sūtra* says: "In taming the mind, nothing is equal to taming anger. For example, a domestic dog does not fear humans, whereas a wild deer of the mountains and forests flees in terror upon seeing a person. Anger is difficult to remove, like a dog guarding a house; compassion is easily lost, like that wild deer.

Furthermore, it is like drawing on stone, where the pattern remains forever; or like drawing on water, which quickly vanishes and its trace does not endure long. Anger is like drawing on stone; the roots of all virtues are like that drawing on water. Moreover, it is like a great mass of fire."

That light endures for a long time, whereas the light of a flash of lightning cannot remain even for a moment. Anger is like a mass of fire, while loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is like a flash of lightning; therefore, this mind is difficult to subdue.

It is further said that all Buddha-dharmas—such as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the knowledge of others' minds, the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the knowledge of the ultimate limit (*pūrvāntajñāna*), the wisdom of the *śrāvaka*, the wisdom of the *pratyekabuddha*, the wisdom of the *bodhisattva*, and the wisdom of the Buddha—all have loving-kindness as their root. For loving-kindness is itself the Tathāgata, itself the Mahāyāna, itself the path to enlightenment (*bodhimārga*), and itself...

Mahābrahmā is the father and mother of all sentient beings; he is the inconceivable realm of the Buddhas; he is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings. Furthermore, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is itself permanence; permanence is the Dharma; the Dharma is the Saṃgha;

the Saṃgha is loving-kindness; and loving-kindness is the Tathāgata. It is the unsurpassed path of all Bodhisattvas; it is the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*). This is as explained in detail in the sūtras, even to the point where it says: when Daṇḍapāṇi instructed King Ajātaśatru to release a drunken elephant to trample the Buddha and his disciples, the Buddha entered the samādhi of loving-kindness.

From his five fingers, he manifested five lions. Upon seeing them, the elephant was struck with terror and lost control of its bowels; it threw its whole body to the ground and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. This was due to the power of the roots of goodness cultivated through loving-kindness, which caused the elephant to be tamed. As for great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*): compassion is able to uproot suffering. Its salvation...

The mind that seeks to alleviate suffering is, with respect to time, place, and sentient beings, entirely immeasurable. According to the adverse conditions encountered by sentient beings and that which they wish to be liberated from, it uproots them all—like a hand reaching out to pull one from drowning water or like medicine for extracting a malignant tumor—and this is the mind that uproots suffering.

They are always refined and always diligent, pursuing the severance of the suffering of the two kinds of birth-and-death for sentient beings until it is finally ended. As long as the birth-and-death of sentient beings does not cease, their compassionate heart does not rest. Because the ocean of suffering of sentient beings is vast and great, the compassionate hearts of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise great.

Regarding the phrase "extracting through suffering": suffering comes from the seeds of evil delusions from previous lives; the water of karma constantly nourishes it, and the roots of suffering penetrate deeply, reaching the bone and reaching the marrow. It is like oil entering flour, or a nail entering wood;

having been so for a long time and becoming knotted, how could it be extracted and removed without the power of the Great Being’s immeasurable compassion? Parents in the world also possess compassion and cherish their children and grandchildren, yet this is limited to a single lifetime. If a child is unfilial, turning their back on kindness and violating righteousness, the parents will give rise to resentment and anger, and their compassionate heart [will fade].

It is slight; therefore, it is not called "great. The compassionate minds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are not like this. When they see suffering sentient beings, their hearts of compassion become even more profound, such that they enter even the five realms of uninterrupted hell amidst great flaming wheels to undergo immeasurable suffering on behalf of all sentient beings.

Such compassion exceeds that of one's parents by immeasurable and boundless degrees; therefore, it is called "Great [Compassion]. Regarding the phrase "to have pity for sentient beings": "pity" (愍) means to feel sorrowful pity (*karuṇā*) and to cherish them. As for "sentient beings" (*sattva*), in relation to the Buddhas, all within the ten dharma-realms—excluding the Buddha-dharma realm—are called sentient beings, for only the Buddhas do not fall into these numerical categories.

When Bodhisattvas correctly sever the "dust-like sands" of afflictions, they reach the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*Samyak-sambodhi-bhūmi*), yet they still possess the ignorance of the mark of birth (*jāti-avidyā*). Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have not even dreamed of the two characters "ignorance" (*avidyā*).

As for the sentient beings of the six realms, they are called "sentient beings" because they are produced through the harmony of the three conditions of father, mother, and self, and because they arise together with the five aggregates (*skandha*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and various other dharmas. Furthermore, even insentient beings such as earth, wood, stone, and metal are called sentient beings because, due to their cultivation in past lives, they are fixed upon a partial death.

Therefore, they fall into ignorance. When the Buddhas were Bodhisattvas, they also made vows to deliver them, thereby attaining the perfect and precious awakening; hence it is said that "sentient and non-sentient beings alike realize the all-encompassing wisdom."

Great Joy and Great Equanimity rescue all sentient beings. (Regarding "Joy": it is to rejoice for oneself and to rejoice for others, such that all are freed from suffering and attain happiness. Regarding "Equanimity": it is to bestow both internal and external wealth entirely upon others.

Even such mental states as thoughts of love and hatred, perceptions of enemy and kin, the intention to deliver living beings, and the bliss of *nirvāṇa*—not even the slightest shadow of these mental conceptions or pleasant notions exists within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; therefore, both are called "Great. "Rescue" (*ji*) means to ferry across.

It signifies using these four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*) as a great vessel to cross the ocean of suffering, extensively saving all sentient beings so they may together reach the other shore. "Sentient beings" (*han-shik*) refers to those who harbor spirits and possess consciousness—the six destinies and the four modes of birth. As the Great Sūtra says: "The four immeasurable minds can cause [beings to be] without..."

One should measure boundless sentient beings and resolve to attain Bodhicitta; therefore, the Bodhisattva binds his mind to them and draws near. The practitioner realizes that all sentient beings ultimately return to the One Path. As for the "One Path," it is the Mahāyāna. The *Cittabhūmi-darśana-sūtra* states:

"The four dharmas, beginning with Great Compassion, can produce all merit and wisdom, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, so that they may swiftly realize Bodhi. (The two preceding phrases [of the verse] consist of the first four characters, which represent the "one who saves" (*nōdo*), and the final two characters, which represent the "those to be saved" (*shōdo*).
The two characters "pitying and rescuing" (*minji*) encompass both the subject and the object, fully clarifying the causes through which the Buddhas receive their retributive rewards).

He adorns himself with the radiance of the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa* and *anuvyañjana*). (This clarifies that these are fruits attained through causes. The Buddha has three bodies: the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The Dharma-body is formless and thus cannot be seen; it can be fully realized only by a Buddha and a Buddha.

What is praised here are the Reward and Transformation bodies, both of which possess the coarse and subtle thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), and eighty-four thousand rays of light.

"By" refers to the cause. "Self" does not mean the self of self and other, but rather the self of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Because the four causal minds have all attained the immeasurable and have reached ultimate perfection, they result in the marks, characteristics, and radiance of the fruit. These three are all attained spontaneously and naturally, without relying on supernatural power, proceeding effortlessly.)
Adorned [with all virtues] (meaning: bringing about the reverential homage of humans and devas).

The assembly, with sincere resolve, takes refuge and pays homage. (The first three phrases praise the Buddha’s wondrous causes and wondrous fruits, which are worthy of respect and veneration; this phrase clarifies the conclusion made with utmost sincerity. "Assembly" is used in contrast to an individual.)

A single person is called "alone. Three people constitute a "group," and from ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred thousand, they are termed a "great assembly. "Equally" means with equal and single-mindedness, free from dualistic thoughts such as subject and object. By means of this, one brings the great assembly together, all of whom direct their sincere hearts toward it because they deeply dread the suffering of birth and death and long for the bliss of Nirvana.

"Vow" (志) refers to the focused concentration of the mental intention. "Sincere heart" (志心) means directing the single mind toward the Buddha without any other thoughts. The Sanskrit term *namas* is translated here as "taking refuge in life" (歸命), and also as "surrendering the body" (歸身); this is because one turns back [from worldly attachments].

"To take refuge" means that the Buddha is not a Buddha external to one's own mind, but rather the fundamental Buddha of one's own mind. To now seek refuge in the Great Awakened One is to return to the awakened mind that has been inherently present. Because one perceives the Buddha as being identical to one's own mind—endowed with immeasurable kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, universally benefiting all sentient beings—one feels a profound resonance within the heart.

Thus, they collectively sacrifice their bodies and lives, single-mindedly and resolutely seeking refuge. This very body, composed of flesh and blood and characterized by illusion and delusion, upon direct realization, becomes a diamond-like indestructible body;

this very life-force, which is the continuity of the conscious mind, becomes the life-force of the wisdom of the Buddha-fruit. "Prostration" (禮) means reverent salutation. When ordinary beings take the Great Sage as their teacher, they must prostrate themselves with the five limbs touching the ground, showing reverence through ritual salutation. This phrase contains a profound and subtle significance, encompassing everything.

The first three characters correspond to "sentient beings" (zhòngshēng) who possess consciousness. The character "etc. (děng) corresponds to the four immeasurable minds—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—all of which are great. The phrase "with a sincere mind" (zhìxīn) corresponds to "pitying and rescuing. The phrase "take refuge" (guīmìng) corresponds to the "physical marks and radiant light.

The character "pay homage" (lǐ) corresponds to "adorned by these [marks] oneself. Having thus attained the principle and mastered the phrasing, one spontaneously gives rise to wisdom. When one performs prostrations in this manner, how could the resulting merit ever be measured?

The Ritual of Repentance for the Altar of Compassion at the Temple of Enabling Fortune (*Qiyun*). “Enabling” (*qi*) means “opening. Within the Buddha-dharma, the mind, and the three [vehicles], all possess the meaning of opening. Previous masters have bequeathed this ritual of repentance because its texts can be consulted and its principles can be realized;

it causes people to benefit upon opening the scroll and to conceive thoughts of joy and fortune. This is the meaning of “opening” in this dharma. Furthermore, although this repentance consists of written words and language, the original intent of the former sages was to reveal and lead sentient beings to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).

Thus, the words and phrases are the true, pure, and wondrous Dharma. To realize that one's own fundamental mind is originally Buddha is the meaning of “opening. Having understood these two meanings of the Buddha-dharma, one then understands the distinction between ritual repentance (*sī-chān*) and principle repentance (*lǐ-chān*), as well as Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Although the methods of repentance differ, they do not go beyond self-reproach within a single thought-moment.

The truly pure and wondrous mind is the heart-flower that blossoms upon the ground. When this is illuminated, one perceives the fundamental Buddha within one’s own mind, the true essence for delivering sentient beings; this is the meaning of "the mind opening. If one attains these three meanings, what cause for concern is there that the teachings are not clear or that Chan is not penetrating? Therefore, in the past, the Venerable Master Ci’en attained realization of the essence of the mind at the place where he practiced repentance.

He moved silently and transformed [his state], which means he silently transformed his thoughts of compassion to extensively benefit all living beings. Only when both self and others benefit can the Great Vehicle method of repentance be fully realized. As for the two characters "Dōjō" (Place of Practice), there is the phenomenal aspect and the principle aspect.

The phenomenal aspect refers to the *āraṇya* (hermitage), as well as the adornments of incense, flowers, lamps, and candles, along with the names corresponding to what is seen. The principle aspect refers to universally applying compassion from within a pure mind—that is, the Middle Way of emptiness and the provisional. Regarding "chàn" (repentance): the full term is *chàn-mó* (Sanskrit: *kṣamā*), which here means...

*Chankuo* (Repentance). *Chan* (Confession) means to lay bare one’s prior transgressions; *hui* (repentance) means to reform the past and cultivate the future, which is called "severing the mind of continuity. Once severed, one never again commits them. Furthermore, *chan* refers to ceasing and severing future faults—that is, not daring to commit further sins that have not yet been committed.

*Hui* refers to feeling self-reproach for past offenses—that is, praying for the eradication of sins already committed. *Fa* (Dharma) has the meaning of "upholding. *Gui* (Method/Rule) means providing a standard that gives rise to understanding, such as the three meanings of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Mind mentioned above. *Chi* (Holding) means to sustain and maintain oneself.

In essence, this enables one to know that this method of repentance is inherently present within one's own nature and is intrinsically pure; furthermore, it allows one to know that transgressions have no inherent nature and that the nature of sin is fundamentally empty. Since emptiness alone does not lead to liberation, one must rely upon the power of the Buddha. Now, the ritual for repentance is established as a model and set forth below.

Repentance possesses ten factors: (1) clearly understanding cause and effect; (2) giving rise to profound dread; (3) deeply engendering shame and remorse; (4) seeking methods for extinguishing transgressions; (5) confessing prior offenses; (6) severing the continuous mind; (7) engendering the mind that protects the Dharma; (8) making great vows to deliver all sentient beings;

(9) constantly recollecting the Buddhas of the ten directions; (10) contemplating that the nature of transgressions is non-arising. Repentance has three meanings: (1) Establishing the name of repentance:

it involves first subduing both the ordained and the laity, reforming the past and cultivating the future, and includes such terms as shame and remorse. (2) Indicating the locus of repentance: according to the Separate Teaching, the locus is the sequential Threefold Contemplation; according to the Perfect Teaching, the locus is the Wondrous Threefold Contemplation. (3) Performing the method of repentance: through the three doors of body, speech, and mind.
According to the Dharma). Furthermore, one should know that both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles each have three types of repentance (*pāpadeśanā*). Regarding the three types of the Mahāyāna:

first, *vidhi-pūrvaka-pratikramaṇa* (repentance through ritual procedure), which involves the fivefold ritual of body and speech according to the Dharma, such as prostrating with the head to the ground and seeking compassion [consisting of: 1. baring the right shoulder; 2. placing the right knee on the ground; 3. joining the palms with a sincere mind; 4. bowing the head to the feet; 5. confessing the names of one’s offenses].

Second, *nimitta-grahaṇa-pratikramaṇa* (repentance by perceiving signs), which involves visualizing a mental image and taking the arising of that sign as the limit [of the practice]. Third, *anutpāda-pratikramaṇa* (repentance of non-arising), which consists of single-mindedly collecting the mind [realizing that] neither offense nor merit has a master [as taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*].

The Vaipulya and Prajñā [sūtras] each have their own ritual procedures; one must establish a fixed period for them. In the Vaipulya, the *Twelve Dream Kings* serves as the support, while the Bodhisattva precepts—such as "seeing light" and "seeing flowers"—assist in this; sitting upright and contemplating the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) constitutes the primary practice. Regarding the three methods of the Hīnayāna: first, the method of formal ritual (*vidhi-karma*).

According to the Sūtra-piṭaka, both light and heavy offenses are permitted to be confessed, whereas the Vinaya does not permit the confession of pārājika offenses, allowing only the confession of the four lesser categories. Second, the method of perceiving signs (*nimitta-grahaṇa*). In the Āgamas, regarding the offense of sexual desire, one performs the visualization of a snake’s mouth.
[The sins] are immediately extinguished, etc. Third, Non-arising (the contemplation of the emptiness of analyzed phenomena).
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in all Buddhas of the three periods of time. (First, "single-minded" refers to being pure and exclusive; it denotes the intent of the will.

Although repentance primarily relies on the practitioner’s own mind to be single-mindedly sincere and achieve sudden awakening, one must nonetheless rely upon the compassionate salvation and silent protection of the Buddhas; therefore, one must take refuge with a single mind. The past, present, and future constitute the "three periods. This gives rise to the names of the eight Buddhas below. In the Sanskrit language, *buddha*; here it is translated as "Awakened One. *Buddha* is...)

The essence [of Buddhahood] is the provisional construct of the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*). "Awakening" (*bodhi*) is wisdom (*prajñā*); it discerns and severs hindrances, illuminates both the ultimate and conventional truths, awakens oneself and others, and brings the practice of awakening to perfection. These qualities correspond, in order, to ordinary beings, the two vehicles, and Bodhisattvas;

only the Tathāgata alone has reached the other shore. He presides over the ten directions as Lord and holds the five natures as Teacher. Because his three types of awakening are perfectly luminous, he is called a Buddha. The Buddhas of the three periods of time are the primary designation, while those listed below are their titles. If one knows that the three periods are simultaneous, then one will know that the three bodies are one essence.

Homage to the past Buddha Vipaśyin. (Namo: this is translated as "taking refuge with the body," and also as "taking refuge with one's life. It means to take the ordinary body and return it to the holy body;

thus, by means of the conditioned body, one realizes the unconditioned essence, and transforms the life-force of the eight consciousnesses into the life-force of wisdom. The two characters for "past" (*guòqù*) should be applied to Viśvabhū as well, because all three Buddhas were the teachers of the past kalpas.

Vipaśyin is also named Vīkṣin; this is translated as "Victorious Vision. He appeared in the world when the human lifespan was eighty thousand years. Śākyamuni first resolved upon Bodhicitta in the presence of Gaganagañja Buddha, and later, after that Buddha’s appearance in the world, he completed the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Therefore, he stands at the head of the seven Buddhas. His lifespan was eighty thousand kalpas. This...

As for the latter two Buddhas, they were both born into kṣatriya families and both bore the clan name Kauṇḍinya. This Buddha attained unsurpassed bodhi beneath a pāṭala tree and convened three assemblies of śrāvakas; his foremost disciples were named Kiśa and Kaṇṭha.

His attendant was named Aśoka; his son was named Skandha-saṃbhava; his father was named Bandhumat; and his mother was named Bandhumatī. The city was named Bandhumatī. The verse of entrusting the Dharma says: "The body receives birth from within the signless, Just like various forms produced by illusion.

The mind-consciousness of the illusory person is originally non-existent; Both sin and merit are empty, with nothing in which to abide. He was the ninth hundred and ninety-eighth Buddha of the past *Vibhūṣaṇa-kalpa*.

Homage to Śikhin Buddha. (Śikhin means "One with a Topknot. He appeared in the world when the human lifespan was seventy thousand years. He is also called Śikhi; in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he is translated as "Fire-Dependent. His lineage was the same as the previous [Buddha]. He realized the fruit of enlightenment beneath a Puṇḍarīka tree.

He also gathered three assemblies of śrāvaka disciples: the first named Jaya, the second named Vaśavartin, and his attendant was named Bhayāpagata. His son was named Aprameya, his father was named Guṇa, and his mother was named Jaya. The city was named Aruṇavatī. He appeared in the world thirty-one kalpas ago.

In that same kalpa, there was also Viśvabhū Buddha. After that, immeasurable kalpas passed in emptiness without any Buddhas. Then, during the Bhadrakalpa, there were four Buddhas, from Krakucchanda down to Śākyamuni.)

The verse of entrustment says: "The arising of all wholesome dharmas is fundamentally an illusion; the creation of all unwholesome karma is likewise an illusion. The body is like a mass of foam, the mind is like the wind; they are illusory manifestations, rootless and devoid of real nature.
(He was the nine hundred and ninety-ninth Buddha of the past *Vyūha-kalpa*).

Homage to Viśvabhū Buddha. (Viśvabhū means "Pervading All Sovereignty. His lifespan was two thousand kalpas. His clan was the same as the previous one. He attained enlightenment beneath a Śāla tree and again assembled the śrāvakas.)

His first disciple was named Nakṣatra (Star), the second was named Uttara (Superior). His attendant was named Śānta (Tranquil), his son was named Sumati (Good Wisdom), his father was named Aruṇadeva (Sun-Deity), and his mother was named Manoramā (Delightful). The city was named Manojñā (At Will). A verse says: "Relying on the four great elements, the body is formed; The mind is originally unborn, arising only because of objects.

If the external object does not exist, the mind likewise does not exist; Sin and merit are like illusions—arising and then ceasing. He was the one thousandth Buddha of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa* (Adorned Eon).

Homage to Krakucchanda Buddha. *Krakucchanda* means "that which should be severed" or "activity. His lifespan was fourteen minor kalpas. He and the two Buddhas mentioned below were all of the Brahmin caste.

They were all of the Kāśyapa clan. He attained the fruit [of enlightenment] beneath an Udumbara tree. He once assembled the Śrāvakas; his foremost disciples were named Ji (Swift) and Li (Power). His attendant was named Zhi (Wisdom); his son was named Shang (Supreme); his father was named Gongde (Merit); and his mother was named Guang (Vast). A certain devaputra was named Wuwei (Fearless), and the city was likewise named Wuwei.

The verse of entrusting the Dharma says: "To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha-body; To realize that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha-illusion. When one realizes that the nature of body and mind is empty, How can such a person differ from the Buddha? This was the first honored Buddha of the present Bhadrakalpa.
When the human lifespan had first decreased to sixty thousand years, he appeared and attained the Buddha-way, serving as the leader of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Homage to the Buddha Kanakamuni. (Kanakamuni means "Golden Sage" in Chinese; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls him Kāṇakamuni, which in the Qin language means "Golden Sage.

His lifespan was thirty minor kalpas. He attained enlightenment beneath a Śirīṣa tree. He convened one assembly of śrāvakas. His foremost disciples were first named Ājīvaka and second named Vithula. His attendant was named Cunda, his son was named Jaya, his father was named Mahāpuṇya, and his mother was named Duṣprasaha.

The son of a deva was named Alaṃkāra, and the city was also named Alaṃkāra. A verse says: "The Buddha does not perceive a body to know he is the Buddha; If there were truly a knowing, there would be no other Buddha. The wise can know that the nature of sin is empty; Tranquil and composed, they have no fear of birth and death. This...
He is currently the second Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa (the Auspicious Aeon). He appeared and attained Buddhahood when the human lifespan was decreasing to forty thousand years.

*Namo Kāśyapa Buddha*. (*Kāśyapa* means "Drinking Light. His lifespan was twenty intermediate kalpas. He attained the fruit [of enlightenment] beneath a Nyagrodha tree. His foremost śrāvaka disciples were first named Śuna and second named Phalguna.

His attendant was named Kātyāyana. His son was named Vinīta; his father was named Viśvadeva; his mother was named Vasudattā; his grandson was named Vijñātṛ; and the city was also named Vijñātṛ, which is the city of Vārāṇasī). The verse says: "All..."

The nature of sentient beings is pure; from the beginning, they are unborn and there is nothing to be extinguished. This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit.

This is the third honored Buddha of the present Bhadrakalpa, who appeared and attained perfect enlightenment when the human lifespan had decreased to twenty thousand years (during the ninth minor kalpa of the Bhadrakalpa).

Homage to the Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha. (He is born from the transformation of the Dharma-eye; he is called the "Original Teacher" because we take refuge in him in the present age. At the end of the second *kalpa*, he encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha;

at the completion of the third great *kalpa*, he was presiding over the world and was named Śākyamuni. This means "Able Benevolent One" and "Tranquil Silence. Because he is able and benevolent, he does not abide in *nirvāṇa*, but enters universally into the realm of affliction to deliver sentient beings.

Because he is tranquil and silent, he does not sink into birth and death, but dwells eternally in the sovereignty of *nirvāṇa*. His lifespan was one hundred years, and he was born into a Kṣatriya family. His clan name was Gautama. During his time as a prince, his name was Siddhārtha, which means "All Meanings Accomplished," for all worldly and world-transcending meanings were fully realized. Regarding Aśvattha...

He attained enlightenment beneath a tree. He gathered a community of disciples; his foremost disciples were first named Śāriputra and second named Maudgalyāyana. His attendant was named Ānanda. His son was named Rāhula.

His father was King Śuddhodana. His mother was named Mahāmāyā. His city was named Kapilavastu. Furthermore, "The Benevolent One" (Muni) is a title for one who guides others through compassion and benefits them. "The Silent One" (Tūṣṇīmbhūta) is a designation for one who has personally realized the truth with sovereign mastery. The verse of the transmission of the Dharma says: "The Dharma is fundamentally without dharma; there is no dharma..."

The Dharma is also the Dharma. Now, at the time when the non-Dharma is entrusted, how has the Dharma ever been the Dharma? This is the fourth Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa. He appeared in the world when the human lifespan was one hundred years. Those who wish to know of its increase and decrease:

when the human lifespan was eighty-four thousand years, it decreased by one year for every passing century, until it reached ten years. Then, after another century, it increased by one year, continuing until it reached eighty-four thousand years again. One such cycle of increase and decrease constitutes a *kṣudra-kalpa* (small kalpa).

Twenty such cycles of increase and decrease constitute a *madhyama-kalpa* (intermediate kalpa). Eighty small kalpas constitute a *mahā-kalpa* (great kalpa). It should be known that one cycle of increase and decrease calculates to one million six hundred and eighty thousand years. From the beginning of the *sthiti-kalpa* (abiding kalpa) until the ninth period of decrease, when the human lifespan is one hundred years, this comprises ten thousand [years].
Five hundred and eleven million years [remain] until the lifespan decreases to ten years (it can be known that ten thousand years still remain thereafter).

Homage to the future Honored Buddha Maitreya. (The former Buddhas belong to the past and present among the three periods of time; this one belongs to the world to come, hence he is called "the Future. *Maitreya* is one translation for *Candali*, which means "Kindly One" (*Maitrī*);

this is his clan name. *Ajita*, which means "Invincible," is his personal name. He currently preaches the Dharma within the Inner Court of Tuṣita Heaven, and will later descend to be born in the Sahā World, in the city of Ketumatī, into the family of a great Brahmin.)

Those born by entering the womb grow to a height of thirty-two *zhang*; their chests are ten *zhang* wide and their faces five *zhang* long. The lifespan of these people is eighty thousand years, and their stature is sixteen *zhang*. Their features are dignified and handsome; they receive food and clothing through transformational birth (*nirmāṇa*) without the need for toil or hardship.

His storehouses will be filled with the seven treasures, yet no one shall look upon them. There shall be no calamities, nor the afflictions of cold, heat, thieves, or any inauspicious events. Within the Huālín Garden, beneath the Nāgapuṣpa tree, he shall attain perfect enlightenment.

During the tenth minor kalpa of the *sthita-kalpa*, when the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years, he shall appear as the lifespan decreases to eighty thousand years. He shall deliver beings through three assemblies: in the first assembly, he shall deliver ninety-nine billion śrāvakas; in the second assembly, ninety-six billion śrāvakas; and in the third assembly, ninety-three billion śrāvakas.

In performing prostrations and repentance, one must first pay homage to the Seven Buddhas, just as the world establishes seven ancestral temples for its patriarchs. This is because, like worldly disciples, one should be filial and obedient toward parents for seven generations. Whenever worshipping the Buddha, one must engage in visualization, employing the mind to direct the name and the body [to perform the ritual].

This is manifested through contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Contemplation consists of the one mind’s emptiness, provisionality, and the middle; the body consists of the one body’s dharma, reward, and transformation aspects. Regarding the verse for worshipping the Buddha, perform prostrations while maintaining this contemplation. Human faculties differ in being sharp or dull, and the wisdom-mind varies in its depth. The Buddha’s body and virtues are inconceivable;

however, within the practitioner’s mind, one should contemplate them according to one's strength and capacity. Such merit will not be in vain; it is like drinking the ocean, ensuring that each person is fully satiated. Therefore, during the sequence of worshipping the Buddha, one should collect the mind and enter into contemplation, contemplating with clarity.

Success is achieved; one immediately attains the Samādhi of the Manifest Presence of All Buddhas. By employing boundless aspiration through my limited body and mind, I shall surely ensure the dual benefit of self and others, repenting and dedicating [merit] toward Bodhi.
Thus, there will be no path that is not realized and no compassion that is not expanded.

Verses in Praise of the Dharma. (The Buddha is that which realizes; the Dharma is that which is realized. For it is because realization depends upon what is realized that the former attains its dignity, and it is through the condition of the one who realizes that the latter is manifested.
Therefore, next, the Dharma is extolled with verses.)

The unsurpassed, most profound, and subtle Dharma. (He praises the Dharma by means of these three meanings. Regarding the character "Dharma" (*dharma*), it follows upon the preceding three meanings. First, as for the "unsurpassed Dharma": the Buddha-Dharma is supreme; there is not a single dharma that can be added to it.

Therefore, one who realizes this is called an "Unsurpassed One" (*anuttara-puruṣa*). The Dharma realized is called the "Unsurpassed Dharma. Because it transcends the Level of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), those at the level of Equal Enlightenment are called "Surpassed Ones" (*sottara-puruṣa*);

they are like Mount Sumeru standing loftily apart from the steepness of the surrounding peaks. It is, for example, like the great ocean, which cannot be compared to the depths of the hundred rivers.)

The subtle and wondrous Dharma refers to the principles of the Buddha-dharma, which are profound, subtle, perfect, and wondrous, and thus inconceivable. Sentient beings are merely able to follow it, yet they cannot know it.

That which is called "that which sentient beings use daily without knowing" is, in its entirety, the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the sages, though it appears as the coarse and defiled phenomena of ordinary people.

"Difficult to encounter in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. (The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "For immeasurable and innumerable kalpas, time passes in vain without a Buddha. Without a Buddha, there is no one from whom to hear the Dharma; therefore, it is said to be difficult to encounter. Furthermore, regarding the difficulty of meeting:

the Sūtra says, "When Buddhas arise in the world, it is remote and difficult to meet them. Even if they appear in the world, it is further difficult for them to preach this Dharma. This phrase should be read as six distinct clauses: first, difficult to meet in a hundred kalpas; second, difficult to encounter in a thousand kalpas; third, difficult to meet in ten thousand kalpas;

fourth, difficult to encounter in a hundred thousand kalpas; fifth, difficult to meet in a million kalpas; sixth, difficult to encounter in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. These proceed from the few to the many, collectively stating that such an opportunity is difficult to encounter throughout vast eons, thereby causing people to give rise to a sense of rarity.
"Encountering such thoughts, with a rare and longing heart, I merely admire the Buddha-dharma.

Now that I have seen, heard, and am able to receive and uphold it... (This pair of phrases follows from the two preceding lines. The words "I now" follow the second line, meaning that such a Dharma, rarely encountered throughout vast eons, has suddenly and fortunately been met by me, a single ordinary person;

this is the joy of joys. The character "attained" (*de*) follows the word "encountered" (*zāoyù*), for it is through encountering it that one is able to see and hear it. Furthermore, the character "attained" stands in the middle, connecting both ends.)

This means that the eye attains seeing, the ear attains hearing, and the mind attains receiving and maintaining (*dhāraṇa*). "Receiving" (*śruta*) refers to taking it into one's heart, bearing it in every thought-moment without the slightest loss—like a lapis lazuli vessel filled with lion’s milk, from which not even a single drop leaks.

"Maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*) refers to clinging firmly without relinquishing; whether by body or mind, to uphold it with tireless devotion and practice it in accordance with its meaning. These acts of seeing, hearing, receiving, and maintaining, when viewed in light of the opening phrase, possess the dual sense of both the subject and the object.

"I vow to understand the true meaning of the Tathāgata. (The word "vow" [願] is a term of resolve; it follows from the two characters of the preceding sentence. This means that since such an encounter has been rare over many kalpas, having now suddenly met with it, one should give rise to the thought of its rarity and a heart of reverence, and should then make a great vow.

The character "to understand" [解] follows from the five characters beginning with "seeing" [見]. This means that once one has obtained seeing, hearing, receiving, and upholding, one must truly awaken to the root and truly understand the distinctions;

only then will one accord with the World-Honored One’s intent in preaching the Dharma to enlighten sentient beings. The five characters beginning with "Tathāgata" [如來] conclude by returning to the first sentence. For this supreme Dharma is possessed by every person, yet because they are caged by deluded thoughts, they do not personally realize and understand it from within; instead, it seems as though the Tathāgata alone has realized it.)

It is unique; therefore, it is ultimately attributed to the realm of the Tathāgata. In truth, among all categories of sentient and insentient beings, there is none that is not fully endowed with this and has attained its original nature. There are two meanings for "Tathāgata": first, it refers to the Buddhas of the three periods of time; second, it refers to the substance of the nature and the function of its manifestation.

"Tathā" (Thus) means the meaning of quiescent extinction (*śamatha*); "Āgata" (Come) means the meaning of illuminating function. That is, from the substance of quiescent extinction, the function of responsive illumination arises; and within the function of responsive illumination, the substance of quiescent extinction is entirely present. Because substance and function are non-dual, it is named "Tathāgata.

Regarding the meaning of "reality" (*tattva*), there are two aspects: first, viewing it in contrast to the false and delusory. By using the worldly, floating, and conventional expressions of language, one reveals the wondrous meaning of reality. It is not that the words themselves are the true meaning; therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* states that one cannot see the Tathāgata by seeing him in form or seeking him through sound. If, regarding the True...

When the ultimate meaning is penetrated, the entire body of illusory words and phrases becomes the reality itself. Second, when viewed in relation to the aforementioned supreme dharmas, the dharma is universal while the meanings are distinct.

That is to say, it may be relatively easy to understand the general dharma of "supreme," but if one can comprehend the specific distinctions within the threefold supreme dharmas—namely, that which is true rather than false and real rather than illusory—that is truly difficult. As the ancients said: "The mind of nirvāṇa is easy to understand; the wisdom of differentiation is difficult to clarify. Is this not precisely what is meant?

This repentance manual establishes its title by presenting both the general and specific aspects together. "Compassion" (cí) is able to bestow happiness; "pity" (bēi) is able to extract one from suffering.

Because of this water, Varuṇa attained the fruit of Buddhahood; because of this water, Candraprabha realized perfect penetration; and because of this water, Kanakavatsa manifested his spiritual powers.
The water of the samādhi of penetration can repay the earnest devotion of former days and wash away the extreme suffering of the present moment.

Having awakened the Master after his exhaustive search for a skilled physician, he recalled the prior agreement made in the past; thus he obtained the release and reported it at the Miraculous Spring.
From fruit back to cause, there is nothing that is not the water of causes; therefore, this is revealed and highlighted (as the Sūtra says: "Transforming others so they may establish merit").
The Dharma-gate of Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the non-harming of all beings; [it is] the Dharma-gate of Compassion (*karuṇā*). The ancients said:

"Ten billion supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and a hundred thousand meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), if they are divorced from loving-kindness, all revert to the works of Māra. One must know that compassion is the wondrous function of wisdom (*prajñā*);
wisdom is the root of compassion. If there is no wisdom, how can there be compassion? Those who possess compassion certainly possess wisdom.
This is the water of wisdom (*prajñā*). For this reason, when the foolish among the world see others obtain happiness, they still obstruct it;

how then could one expect them to be able to grant happiness? When they see others encounter suffering, they only fear that it is not severe enough; how then could one expect them to be able to extract [others] from it?

(Furthermore, the water of compassion distinguishes itself from the water of karmic retribution, which reaches up to the second *dhyāna*. Second, it distinguishes itself from the water of non-virtuous karma, which pervades all three realms. Third, the water of afflictions pervades both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. This...
The water of compassion exhausts both the mundane and supramundane;

heaven and earth cannot encompass it, the sun and moon cannot rival its brilliance, and the three calamities cannot erode it—this is what makes it unique. Through the water of compassion, one nourishes human goodness;

when goodness reaches its peak, one attains the bliss of *nirvāṇa*. (This refers to the text on generating vows and accomplishing virtue after rebirth. Through the water of pity, one washes away the defilements of human ignorance.

Therefore, one is able to leave behind the suffering of birth and death (referring to various repentance texts following [the description of] birth). *Chàn* (repentance), in its full form, is called *chànmó* (Sanskrit: *kṣamā*).

This is translated here as "requesting forbearance" (meaning to request that another person endure one's confession of transgressions). Regarding the term "Dharma" in the phrase "repentance-dharma": although it is a word for requesting forbearance, it is in fact said to have issued from the Buddha’s own mouth.
The characters derive their meaning from the scriptural text. That which is called the Tathāgata’s vast and compassionate thought opens the gate of repentance.

As for the term "scroll" (*juàn*), it carries the sense of being wrapped up; this is spoken in contrast to what is spread out. (In the Western Regions, scriptures are not bound in the manner of Indian manuscripts nor in the format of Chinese printed volumes, but are instead made solely in the form of rolls;

therefore, they are called "scrolls"). When first viewing this Dharma, that which is rolled must be unrolled; once viewed, it is rolled up again. There is a limit to the time of unrolling, while the time of rolling is far more extensive.

Therefore, it is simply called "rolling up" (*juǎn*). Because both the beginning and the end involve rolling up, and because the axis and the scroll are phenomenal marks (*xiàng*), one speaks of "rolling up" to signify the convergence of marks back into their fundamental nature (*xìng*).
"Rolling up" means to gather; it gathers all phenomena so that they all enter into the self-nature of compassion. This refers to the relationship between the subject (*néng*) and the object (*suǒ*).
The general and specific [meanings] may be understood. This concludes the brief explanation of the title of the repentance ritual.
Following the scripture, it is further divided into three parts. First, the introductory section:
all Buddhas, out of compassion for sentient beings, expounded this Water Repentance, which contains the general rules for the ritual site (*maṇḍala*).

The dual titles indicate both the subject and the object of salvation, as well as the speaker and the spoken. This can be understood through the Water Repentance Ritual (*Shuilu Chanfa*) altar arrangement.

Speaking generally in contrast to the specific: for instance, the Liang dynasty ritual is divided into forty chapters, each with a distinct title; these are the specifics. Now, we shall state the total number.
