Nevertheless, according to the "Life Span" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, these accounts are merely expedient means (*upāya*). In reality, since the World-Honored One attained Buddhahood, an inconceivable number of kalpas have passed; hence it is said, "as many as those sands."
Yet we ourselves have become immersed in the six sense-objects and revolve through birth and death with no end in sight;
this is truly something for which we should feel ashamed, abashed, disgraced, and humiliated before the world.

The character "while" (而) implies a sense of shame and disgrace. "Together with" (相與) refers to being entangled by evil friends. "Addicted and immersed" (躭染) means being submerged in and clinging to defilement.
Because one is stained by the dust of the world, the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction open. Thus, one is born and dies again and again.

Having died, one is born again; like the revolving of a wheel, it is therefore called "wheeling" (*saṃsāra*). Regarding birth and death: when the three conditions harmonize, there is birth in each moment.
Until the "fundamental existence" (*mūlabhava*) is exhausted, all of this is termed "birth.

This is that which was non-existent and suddenly comes into being, arising through the convergence of conditions. If form and mind do not support one another, there is death in each moment. From [this point...]
When that which is originally possessed reaches its end, it is called death; this is the sudden absence of what was present, for death occurs when conditions disperse.

That there is no appointed time for escaping birth and death is entirely due to being addicted to and craving the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). Compared to the long-enlightened Śākyamuni Buddha, such people are truly enough to put the whole world to shame.

(One must know that the six sense objects are the realm of the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*); they can give rise to the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākāra-jñatā*), yet their ruin lies in attachment. "I" refers to the six sense faculties.)

The "addictions" (*dāna*) are the six consciousnesses; together with their objects, they constitute the eighteen realms (*dhātu*). Yet, fundamentally, these are the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "It is like a person scorched by fire who, out of a sense of shame and modesty, covers his body with a garment.

Because of this wholesome mind, he is reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, or becomes a Brahmā King or a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning Sage King, never falling into the evil destinies and constantly experiencing peace and bliss. How much more so for one who takes the Tathāgata as their ideal and gives rise to the mind of enlightenment? This may be said four times over.

This is the height of urgency. Reflecting thus, one must sincerely repent, reform the past and cultivate the future, and with courageous diligence, achieve enlightenment in this very life so as to be no different from the Buddha; only then can one set aside all shame.
The power of repentance is fulfilled. The general meaning of the following six chapters may be understood by analogy with this.
Second, regarding "terror": since one is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the actions of body, speech, and mind are constantly associated with transgressions.

"Second, fearing the three miserable realms. 'Fearing' refers to internal anxiety; 'fear' refers to external dread. Since these form a phrase, it follows from the preceding [text] as a statement concerning ordinary beings.
The actions of body, speech, and mind are precisely what cause one to become addicted to the six sensory objects. In the previous chapter, the word 'I' was used as a general reference;
here, 'body, speech, and mind' is the specific elaboration. 'Corresponding' means being in accord; that is, there will never be an escape."

Regarding the underlying intent: when the six faculties grasp the six objects, if they are apprehended individually, one receives individual retribution; if they are mutually attached, one receives combined retribution.
There is not even a hair’s breadth of error [this principle originates from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*].
By reason of these causes and conditions, after the end of life, one should fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts, and undergo immeasurable suffering.
This is truly something to be amazed at and alarmed by; it is something to be terrified of and fearful of.

With greed and ignorance as the causes and the ten non-virtuous actions as the conditions, once one's life has ended, one immediately receives the retribution in places of terror—the three miserable realms.
(Since there is fear, one should seek a place of refuge: first, *svabhāva-nirvāṇa*; second, *anuttara-nirvāṇa*.

Hell is the Path of Fire (so named because of its heat). The animal realm is the Path of Blood (so named because of mutual devouring). The hungry ghost realm is the Path of Blades (blades and staves...)

It is by being driven and coerced that one receives this name. An ancient saying states: "A single retribution in the three miserable realms lasts five thousand kalpas; when will one ever emerge from it? Hearing of these three miserable realms is truly enough to startle the ear;

thus it is said they are "startling. Contemplating them is truly enough to chill the heart; thus it is said they are "terrifying. Imagining them should truly give rise to dread; thus it is said they are "frightful.
Seeing them would certainly cause the soul to dissolve; thus it is said they are "dreadful. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "It is like a person who..."

Suppose one has an only son; whether he is walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the father’s mind constantly dwells upon him. If the son commits a transgression, the father uses kind words to guide and admonish him, never treating him with harshness. A bodhisattva is likewise: seeing sentient beings, whether they have fallen into the three miserable realms or are among humans and devas, the bodhisattva’s mind does not abandon them, nor does he give rise to anger.
Third, regarding renunciation: one constantly contemplates that within birth and death there is only impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, impurity, and falsity;
it is like bubbles upon water, arising and ceasing swiftly, revolving and wandering like a wheel.

(This refers to the revulsion toward the defiled body. The Great Sūtra says: "The root of revulsion is right knowledge and vision (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*). The root of right vision is samādhi. The root of samādhi is tranquility (*kṣema*). The root of tranquility is seclusion (*viveka*). The root of seclusion is the mind of joy (*prīti-citta*).

The root of the mind of joy is non-regret (*avipratisāra*). The root of non-regret is the observance of precepts (*śīla*). The root of the observance of precepts is the rain of Dharma (*dharma-varṣa*). One should know that for the practice of cultivation, hearing the Dharma is the root. Regarding "equal with the marks" (*lakṣaṇa-samatā*):
it means that [the teaching] first uses the wisdom of observation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) to illuminate and know that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is illusory and unreal; only...

Regarding the phrase "and so forth": throughout the Tathāgata’s lifetime of teaching, nothing was revealed that does not fall within impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity (that is, the four foundations of mindfulness:

first, contemplating the mind as impermanent; second, contemplating sensation as suffering; third, contemplating phenomena as non-self; fourth, contemplating the body as impure). These four are precisely the opposites of the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Furthermore, there are two aspects to the impermanence of the mind:

first, the moment-to-moment cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); second, the destruction of the continuity of phenomena. These four are also the four characteristics of suffering observed within the sixteen modes of contemplation (*ṣoḍaśākāra*). The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*) contains four verses on the four types of impermanence.

In the past, Prince Pāda-paṅkaja (Spot-footed), desiring to ascend the throne, received the teachings of a non-Buddhist teacher who instructed him that he must take the heads of a thousand kings to sacrifice to his family deity. Having obtained the heads of nine hundred and ninety-nine kings since ascending the throne, and being short of one king’s head, he traveled ten thousand *li* to the north.

There he encountered a king named Śubhaprabha (Good Brilliance), to whom he said: "I wish to be granted permission for one day to feed śramaṇas and pay homage to the Triple Gem. Pāda-paṅkaja granted this request. At that time, Śubhaprabha followed the example of the Seven Buddhas of the Past and invited a hundred Dharma masters.

A hundred high seats were arranged, and twice daily, the *Prajñāpāramitā* in eighty thousand stanzas was preached. The foremost Dharma Master expounded four stanzas for the King; the first was the stanza on the principle of impermanence: "When the kalpa-ending fire concludes, heaven and earth are consumed by a pervasive blaze."

Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans are all reduced to flying ash; when the merit of devas and nāgas is exhausted, they wither and perish therein. If even the two polarities of heaven and earth fall, how can a kingdom possess permanence? (2) The Verse on the Principle of Suffering: Birth, old age, sickness, and death revolve without end.

When affairs contradict one’s wishes, sorrow and grief become afflictions. Desire is deep and calamity is heavy; there is no external wound or ailment greater than this. The three realms are entirely suffering; what reliance can there be in a kingdom? (3) The Verse on the Principle of Emptiness: Existence is fundamentally non-existent; all things are formed through causes and conditions. That which flourishes must inevitably decline.

That which is real is necessarily empty. Sentient beings are restless and agitated, all dwelling like illusions. Both sound and echo are void; so too are the lands. [The fourth line] speaks of the verse on non-self: consciousness has no form and merely rides upon the four snakes. Ignorance nurtures and protects it as if it were a joyful chariot.

The body has no permanent master, and consciousness has no permanent home. Since body and consciousness are already separated, how could there be a land? The above is the general heading; the following is the specific explanation.

First, the explanation of impermanence (the four lines beginning with "The Tathāgata," etc., from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, spoken by Mañjuśrī to Cunda). The first two lines explain impermanence: wind strikes the water and forms bubbles.

How could it possibly endure for long? (One contemplates that all phenomena are as unreal as bubbles on water. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "This body is like a bubble; it cannot endure for long. Moment by moment it is impermanent, appearing suddenly and vanishing suddenly;

hence it is said to arise and perish with speed. The two lines concerning "coming and going" explain suffering and emptiness: the first part provides the analogy, while the second applies it to the phenomena (*dharma*).
Birth, old age, sickness, and death—these eight sufferings torment one incessantly, never ceasing for even a moment.
This accords with the analogy of the revolving wheel. As for the eight sufferings, the four are birth, old age, sickness, and death; to these are added the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
Separation from the beloved, meeting with the hated, and the intense burning of the five aggregates—these constitute the eight [sufferings].
That these eight kinds are all called "suffering" is because birth is like being flayed alive, and death is like a living turtle shedding its shell; the rest may be understood accordingly.
All of you, together, should simply observe your own bodies from head to foot; within them there are only thirty-six things.
This is the third explanation of the impurity of non-self. It is shared [with others]. I exhort all practitioners to observe their own bodies.
The thirty-six things are presented collectively here; they will be listed individually below. First, as for how one observes one's own body, the Buddha said: "There are three matters."
Through the coming together [of conditions], one receives this body. First, the father; second, the mother; third, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Since it arises from these three conditions, how could it be a pure or permanent thing? Since it arises from conditions, how could there truly be a self (*ātman*)?

Question: Apart from the human body, are there also [other forms]?

"Is it by means of three conditions? Answer: The Great Sūtra says: "The peacock conceives a body upon hearing the sound of thunder; the blue jay conceives a body by drinking the tears of the male jay; the *jīvajīvaka* bird conceives a body upon seeing the male dance. It should be said:

Skin, flesh, blood, muscle, tendons, veins, bones, marrow, fat, grease, brain, and membranes.

Spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, intestines, stomach, red phlegm, white phlegm, and the two receptacles of the raw and the cooked.

Regarding the fourth [type of] arousal of the bodhicitta:
one arouses the bodhicitta due to shame, fear, weariness, renunciation, and so forth; one should abandon this impure illusory body and joyfully seek the pure dharmakāya.

"Emerging into Bodhi" (referring to the three stages following the preceding) refers to the fifth, supreme Bodhi, which is the fruit of Buddhahood. The character "zhě" (者) reiterates the preceding heading.
As the Sūtra says: "One should delight in the Buddha-body. The Buddha-body is precisely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
In the Sanskrit language it is called *sūtra*; here it is translated as "Sutra" (契經). A "sutra" encompasses both doctrine (*śāsana*) and principle (*artha*).

Because the doctrine accords with the principle, and the principle accords with the capacity of sentient beings (*yathābhavyatā*), it is named "Sutra" (契經). Taking the phrase "one should delight in [seeking] nirvāṇa" from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, I establish this "Chapter on Generating the Resolve" as its foundational basis.
Joy is aspiration; it is seeking. If one desires to seek the Buddha’s true Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), one must give rise to the bodhicitta and cultivate vast practices and vows.
By means of immeasurable wisdom, one cultivates immeasurable Dharma-gates, and only then can birth [in that state] be attained. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:

"The body of the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding body, the indestructible body, the vajra-body, not a body sustained by various foods; it is the Dharma-body, firm and difficult to destroy for immeasurable billions of kalpas. Mañjuśrī asked the Buddha: "The mind has no form or characteristics, nor does it have a place of abiding. When an ordinary practitioner first gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), upon what basis do they rely, and what kind of sign (*nimitta*) do they contemplate?

The Buddha said: "The sign of the *bodhicitta* contemplated by an ordinary person is like a pure and perfect lunar disc. It dwells luminously within the chest. If one wishes to swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression, one should stay in a secluded and silent room, sit with the body upright and right mindfulness, and form the *vajrabandha* mudrā.

With eyes closed, one contemplates the bright moon within the chest and reflects thus: 'This full lunar disc is fifty *yojanas* in extent; it is stainless, brilliant, and pure, transparent both inside and out, and supremely cooling. The moon is the mind, and the mind is the moon. It is untainted by the dust of defilements and free from delusion.'"

Perceptions do not arise; naturally, body and mind are pure. The great bodhicitta is firm and does not regress (as explained in detail in the sutras). The following clarifies the place where the dharmakāya is born.
"Born from immeasurable merit and wisdom.
This phrase is the general statement; what follows below is the specific explanation. In the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, Mañjuśrī says: "Such radiance is called wisdom.
Wisdom is that which is eternally abiding (*nitya*). That which is eternally abiding has no causes or conditions."
It is born from the six *pāramitās*.
These six are: giving (*dāna*), morality (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). *Pāramitā* is translated here as "reaching the other shore.
By practicing these six dharmas, one crosses the river of stinginess, greed, and so forth, and reaches the other shore of *nirvāṇa*. Having reached it, not only is the *dharmakāya* produced.
The Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is also born [of this]. Hereafter, follow this pattern.
It is born from compassion, joy, and equanimity;
that is, the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). All of the above are termed the Right Path.
It arises from the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).

These thirty-seven factors of the path consist of: the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), and the five faculties (indriya).

The five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. As noted in the second fascicle of the *Xianhou* (Commentary on the Present and Future), within the section on "Obstacles to Learning":
"From such various merits and wisdoms as these, the body of the Tathāgata is born."
This concludes the preceding section. The six fourths are the primary [teachings], while the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the auxiliary dharmas.

These various merits correspond to the aforementioned phrases concerning the various unwholesome dharmas, and they accord with the expression "immeasurable merits" above (as stated in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, fascicle 2: "Those in the world know the words but do not know the meaning.

Because [the former] cannot be produced, one is exhorted to give rise to it. Wisdom is of three kinds: internal phenomena and internal names, external phenomena and external names.
One who is able to know and understand these is called "all-knowledge" (i.e., the wisdom of the two vehicles). One who is able to employ all the path-dharmas of the Buddhas [possesses the latter].
That which initiates all the various seeds of goodness in sentient beings and distinguishes them without error is called the Knowledge of the Paths (mārgajñatā)—this is the wisdom of the Bodhisattva.
That which can know all paths and knows all aspects (sarvākāra) is called the Knowledge of All Aspects (sarvākārajñatā)—this is the wisdom of the Buddha-fruit.

Regarding the four virtues of Nirvana—permanence (nitya), bliss (sukha), self (ātman), and purity (śubha): "permanence" refers to the essence of true permanence, which is non-transient and unchanging. Among the ten thousand...

"Primordial permanence" (gu-heng-ru) does not mean "permanent" in contrast to "annihilation. "Bliss" (le) means peace, tranquility, and extinction; it is the departure from the two types of birth-and-death, where suffering and bliss are fused as one.
It is not "bliss" spoken of in contrast to "suffering. "Self" (wo) has the meaning of sovereignty; it possesses the eight masteries.
One attains great peace and bliss; this is precisely my true self, which is neither self nor non-self, and is not the false and deluded self of ordinary people or externalists.
"Pure" means that the three karmas are purified and the three delusions are forever severed, like a great round mirror entirely free of even the slightest blemish;

it does not mean purity in contrast to defilement. (The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says: "People of the world know the letters but do not know the meaning. What is meant by 'meaning'? It is the manifestation of both self and non-self.")

The impermanent refers to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; the permanent refers to the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata. Suffering refers to all non-Buddhists (tīrthikas); bliss refers to Nirvāṇa. The impure refers to conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma); the pure refers to the True Dharma possessed by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. This is called being free from inversion.

Those who are far removed from the four inversions perceive only this permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Furthermore, these four virtues of permanence and so forth constitute the superior threefold cultivation (tri-śikṣā), whereas compared to the previous third chapter on "Aversion," suffering, impermanence, and non-self are inferior.

(Third, regarding cultivation: by means of the three superior [aspects] of nirvāṇa, one disparages the three inferior [aspects], thereby definitively severing the śrāvaka [path]. In the language of Qin, it is called "the characteristic of all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*). It is named *prajñā* based on its cause, and *sarbba* (Sanskrit: *sarvākārajñatā*) based on its fruit. (The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

Purifying the Buddha-lands and bringing sentient beings to maturity, he has no begrudging attachment to his body, life, or wealth.

"Relying. Within the center, the center appears; within the center, the reliance appears; within the reliance, the center appears; within the reliance, both the reliance and the center appear; within the center, both the reliance and the center appear.

Regarding the two phrases concerning the body, they are extracted from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* and cited as a conclusion: "This upward seeking and downward transforming should be carried out through giving."
Deliverance comes first. Internally, one does not cherish or spare one's own body or life; externally, one is not stingy with wealth or treasures.
Fifth, regarding impartiality toward enemies and kin: one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, free from the distinction between "self" and "other."
5. The mind is free from conceptual discrimination. This clarifies the sublime practice mentioned in the preceding chapter. "Enemy" refers to those who can harm one's body and life;
"relative" refers to those who can protect one's body and mind. To view them as a single entity and not give rise to hatred or love—this is called equanimity.

The *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* says: "Regard that enemy as one's own parent. The Patriarch said: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination. Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and you will see clearly and brightly through all things. The *Sutra on Repaying Kindness* says: "Dharmodgata’s evil mind did not cease."

He nourished his fingernails and claws; when he hid poison beneath them and pinched the Buddha’s foot, the medicine was transformed into nectar, and in the end, it did no harm. Again, he pushed down a rock from the mountain to sever the Buddha’s life-force, yet it only wounded the Buddha’s foot.

Because of the Buddha’s compassionate mind, enemies and kin are equal. The Tathāgata never calculates whether sentient beings have been kind to him; for such calculation would destroy equality. By virtue of equality, there is neither "other" nor "self."
Why is this so? If one perceives the enemy as distinct from the relative, that is discrimination (*vikalpa*). Because of discrimination, various attachments to signs (*nimitta*) arise.
With attachment to signs as a causal condition, various afflictions (*kleśa*) are produced. With afflictions as a causal condition, various evil karmas are created.
With evil karma as a causal condition, one consequently obtains bitter fruits (*duḥkha-phala*).
Question: Why must one be free from the marks of "self" and "other"? Answer: If one perceives [them as] inferior, superior, or distinct—these are the two [types of views].
To "discriminate" means to distinguish between those who are kin and those who are not. To be "attached" means to cling to the marks of self and other.

Because they are distinct, there is no unity; therefore, one discriminates. Because of discrimination, one becomes attached to the marks of self and other, or enemy and kin. This is the causal condition.

This is because internal mental discrimination acts as the cause, while external objects—such as people, self, enemies, and kin—act as the conditions, giving rise to the afflictions of hatred and attachment.

Furthermore, with these afflictions acting as the cause and the performance of various evil and rebellious karmic actions acting as the condition, one consequently incurs the fruit of suffering in the three miserable realms.
To give rise to such conceptual discrimination is the very root of birth and death (as the former masters said: "A fleeting thought is the disease; [it must not be allowed to persist]").

This is the medicine: do not fear the arising of thoughts; only fear that awakening is late. Awakening is itself the Buddha. As Mahāmati said: "Buddha means 'awakened. Because he is eternally awakened, he is called the Great Awakened One (Mahābuddha), and he is also called the King of Awakening (Buddharāja).

All of these are accomplished from within the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Since they were already great men, why should I not be so? If you are attached to many forms, you should practice mindfulness of the Buddha. A verse says: 'Mind does not falsely grasp at past dharmas, Nor does it greedily cling to future events.
It does not dwell upon the present; It thoroughly realizes that the three periods of time are entirely empty and still.'"
The sixth is the mindfulness of repaying the Buddha’s kindness. Throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, the Tathāgata sacrificed his head, eyes, marrow, brain, limbs, joints, hands, and feet.

By attaining enlightenment, he repaid this kindness. This refers to the two aspects of the Perfection of Giving (*dānapāramitā*) throughout the Buddha’s vast eons: first, the giving of internal wealth, which is the act of relinquishing [one's own body]. "Sacrifice" (*she*) means to give.
(The postscript to the title: One must first recognize the debt of gratitude and then repay it. To recognize the debt of gratitude is to spontaneously generate the bodhicitta;
to repay the debt of gratitude is to teach all sentient beings to generate that mind. *Marrow* is the fat within the bones. *Brain* is the fat within the head.

(Formerly, King Mahāprabha gave his head to a brāhmaṇa, saying: "Out of compassion for you, I do not oppose your wish and grant you my head, so that in future lives I may obtain a head of wisdom, surpassing those of the Bodhisattva Uttama-śarīra and the Deva Ratna-śikhin.")

Sons of the Buddha, [there were those who] cast off their precious celestial crowns from their heads and even flayed their scalps to give to others; Bodhisattva Priyadarśana, King Candraprabha, and others gave up their eyes; Bodhisattva Kṣemadatta and others gave up their flesh and marrow;

Bodhisattvas such as Dharmeśvara gave up all their limbs, both large and small; Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavīrya gave up his fingers and toes; Bodhisattva Akṣayamati and others gave up their fingernails and toenails; even Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya, King Kāśi, and others split open their chests and extracted their hearts to bestow them upon sentient beings;

Bodhisattva Nityodyukta, King Dṛḍhamati, and others gave up their hands; up to Bodhisattva Aśoka and Devaputra Vijayagāmin, who cut off their ears and noses to give to others—such as these, they are beyond counting.
[Quotation] (The observer should believe and accept this).
Second: Clarifying the giving of external wealth to others.

[In the Mahāyāna Sūtra], Prince Sudarśana of King Śubhavyūha contemplated the True Dharma and attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha; his father, the king, immediately relinquished the throne as if discarding mucus or saliva. He departed...

In their homes they practiced the Way. Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, the Devaputra Śreṣṭhaguṇacandra, and others relinquished the four continents, the great earth, and all manner of adornments to others—let alone a single kingdom or a single city.

The non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, the King Alaṃkāra, and others gave away their wives, children, and so forth to those in poverty. There is nothing more beloved than one’s own body, yet they still gave it away; how much more so their wives and children?
They relinquished even their kingdoms and cities, let alone the seven treasures. They relinquished even the seven treasures, let alone elephants and horses. Such was their practice.
The subtle details need not be mentioned.
For our sake, he practiced various ascetic penances (as stated in the second fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*). "For" means "because.

(For example, King Kapi and others gave their own bodies to impoverished and suffering sentient beings, serving as their attendants and servants; likewise, the Bodhisattvas of Great Compassion and the Devaputra Sunetra and others entered [into such states]).

The hells [are for] saving suffering sentient beings. The reason one cultivates these practices is to sever the notions of self and dharmas and to manifest true centrality. It is only for the sake of sentient beings that the Tathāgata cultivates these various practices.

This kindness and this virtue are truly difficult to repay. (An ancient saying goes: "People see only that their parents gave them physical birth, yet they do not realize they owe the power of the Buddha's grace; for many kalpas they have acted as those who forget kindness and turn their backs on righteousness.")

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Even if one were to carry [the Buddha] on the crown of one's head or bear him upon both shoulders for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges, one could never repay [his kindness].

Because it is difficult to repay as described above, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is cited as proof. "To carry" (*he*) means to take responsibility upon the shoulders; "to bear" (*fu*) means to take responsibility upon the back.
This means that one would immediately attain Buddhahood upon standing on the ground, bearing the burden on one shoulder as the eldest son of the Buddha;

yet even this could not repay even a ten-thousandth part of [the Buddha's] grace (as the former masters said: "If one were to attain Buddhahood this very day, the Lord of the Land of Bliss would already consider it too late"—is this not precisely what is meant?).
If we wish to repay such an kindness as this, we should, in this world, exert ourselves with courageous diligence; endure toil and suffering;
disregard our own bodies and lives; establish the Triple Gem; propagate the Mahāyāna; and extensively transform sentient beings so that they may all together enter into perfect enlightenment.

This demonstrates the method of repaying one's debts of gratitude. Thus, the phrase "repeatedly pointing" refers to the aforementioned acts of kindness (*en*). Regarding the meaning of "kindness" (*en*), it is explained as follows:
both the Buddha and one’s father are called "kindness," while a ruler and a teacher are both called "righteousness" (*gi*).

There are two kinds of kindness: first, the kindness of equal deliverance; second, the kindness that enables one to attain Buddhahood. Desiring to repay these fully in a single lifetime, it is said: "One should, within..."
In this world, one must surely shake off the dust of worldly toil and not allow afflictions to disturb the mind.

With a single mind directed toward the goal, it is called "diligence" (which means being free from all indolence and eliminating negligence). Advancing straight ahead with resolute courage, it is called "valiance. One does not avoid laziness or seek ease.

Therefore, it is said that one must "resist toil" and not seek ease or pleasure; thus, it is said that one must "endure suffering. (Consider, for example, Bodhisattva Miaowang and Great King Suxing, who underwent all manner of suffering;

or Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and King Suvarṇadṛḍha, who sold their bodies and cut out their flesh, breaking their bones to extract the marrow for the sake of seeking the Dharma; or the Bodhisattvas of Diligent Effort, who entered great pits of fire for the sake of seeking the Dharma—all of these serve as examples of those who do not spare their own bodies or lives.

The Buddha always appears in the Southern Continent because he excels in three matters: first, his ability to sever lust; second, his power of mindfulness; and third, his capacity for diligent effort. These three qualities surpass even those of the devas, let alone those of the Northern Continent. If [these three]...

When a treasure is about to collapse, one must forget one's body and life, enduring suffering to establish it. When there are those who wish to suppress and obstruct the sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna and do not practice it, one must be diligent and courageous, braving toil to propagate it. Such ascetic practice as this—

This is not for one’s own sake, but solely to extensively transform all sentient beings so that they may together reach the place of treasure; it is my hope that this may repay even a ten-thousandth part of the Buddha’s kindness. The character "shě" (to give/renounce) constitutes the general purport of this chapter.

Such things as elephants, horses, and the seven treasures are the gift of material sustenance (*āmiṣadāna*); the renunciation of one’s head and eyes, up to the practice of diligence and the endurance of suffering, is the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*);

and the propagation of the Mahāyāna to transform sentient beings so they attain Buddhahood is the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*). As the *Āgama Sūtras* state: "When a Tathāgata appears in the world, he necessarily acts for five purposes."

First, to turn the wheel of Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings; second, to deliver his many parents from past lives in order to repay their kindness; third, to establish those without faith on the ground of faith; fourth, to cause those who have not yet resolved to attain Bodhicitta to do so;
and fifth, to bestow upon them the prediction of future Buddhahood. It is for these five reasons that he appears in the world.
Seventh, regarding the contemplation of the emptiness of the nature of offenses: offenses have no self-nature;
they arise from causes and conditions and exist through inversion.
Seventh, contemplate that the nature of offenses is fundamentally empty. Just as hot water is itself cold ice, so too are karmic burdens themselves liberation.

As the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says: "All dharmas fundamentally have no inherent nature. It is like a person who, with a pen, paper, and ink, combines them to form characters; yet within the paper there are originally no characters. Because they are fundamentally non-existent, they are formed through conditions. If they existed inherently, what need would there be for various conditions?"

It is also like the synthesis of blue and yellow to produce green; one should know that blue and yellow originally lack the nature of green. If it were inherently present, why would they need to be synthesized? It is also like sentient beings obtaining life through food, yet there is truly no life within the food itself.

If life were inherently present, then before eating, the food should already possess life. Thus, the *Cittabhūmi-parivarta* says: "Furthermore, possessing four virtues, one dwells in an araṇya, maintains pure precepts, and adorns oneself: First, observing that one's own self has no inherent nature, one subdues and severs the two attachments, thereby realizing non-self.

The Great Sūtra states: “Nirvāṇa is called an island. Why? third, the realm of asuras (comprised of ghosts, animals, humans, and gods); fourth, the realm of hell-beings (such as the eight cold and eight hot hells); fifth, the realm of hungry ghosts (of nine types and ten categories).

Pleasure and equanimity: due to evil karma as the cause, one experiences the retribution of suffering in the three miserable realms;

due to wholesome karma as the cause, one experiences the retribution of pleasure among humans and devas (in the four continents and the six heavens of the desire realm); due to immovable karma as the cause, one experiences the differentiated retributions of the higher realms (the form and formless realms).

Furthermore, within the three realms, the bodies of suffering and pleasure are the direct retribution (*vipāka*) for individual karma, while the superior or inferior vessel-worlds (*bhājana-loka*) in which they dwell are the circumstantial retribution (*niṣyanda-vipāka*) upon which suffering and pleasure depend. These are interconnected and are also termed "revolving" (*saṃsāra*).

This means that after being born, one dies again; after dying, one is born again. Birth and death do not cease (as when one dies in the heavens and is born among humans, and so forth; this can be understood by analyzing the successive transitions).

That which is born from a shell is called egg-born; that which emerges from being contained and stored is called womb-born; that which is born through reliance on moisture is called moisture-born; and that which suddenly comes into existence where there was none is called transformation-born.

There are three types of karma: first, wholesome; second, unwholesome; and third, immovable. These three karmas have the power to summon the six realms of existence, continuing without end and without cessation.

We, [Name] and others, from time immemorial until this very day, while receiving retribution within the six realms of existence— human or celestial—
have possessed this mind-consciousness that has constantly harbored ignorance and delusion, filling our chests to overflowing.

The mental consciousness and its faculties are preceded by the karma of the mind. The mental consciousness is that which stores; delusion (ignorance, lack of wisdom, lack of faith, and the failure to seek liberation) is that which is stored.
"To harbor" means to contain within. Delusion is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the root of all defiled mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*).
"Abundant" means much. Since it is said that one "constantly harbors" them and they are "abundantly full," only evil arises and no goodness is produced thereafter.
It is immeasurable. It disturbs the chest and the breast; "chest" (*xiōng*) refers to the inner breast or the mind.
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the three roots of poison:
greed, hatred, and delusion. These are three of the six fundamental [afflictions] that are stored within the *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness); thus, all wholesome mental factors...
Because they cause one to lose mindfulness and forgetfulness, they are called "poisons" (*viṣa*). Furthermore, because they can give rise to and grow all manner of evils, they are called "roots.

When the three poisons are transformed, they become the Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*). The roots of the three poisons are the causes of karma; through these causes, one performs actions.
Therefore, it is said that "one commits all sins. The following cases are to be understood by analogy.
Alternatively, one may commit all sins due to the three outflows (*āsrava*).

The three outflows (as set forth in the *Abhidharma-śāstra*) are: first, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*; pertaining to the desire realm); second, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*; all afflictions of the two higher realms, excluding ignorance); third, the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
The "outflows" (*āsrava*)—namely, ignorance within the three realms—cause the mind to flow and disperse incessantly, falling into the three realms; thus they are called outflows.
Alternatively, they are so named because they cause one to commit all manner of transgressions through the three types of suffering.

The three types of suffering (with the three feelings as their cause): first, the feeling of suffering gives rise to the suffering of suffering (the three realms are already suffering; the desire realm is even more so);

second, the feeling of pleasure gives rise to the suffering of change (suffering when pleasure perishes, equal to that in the three miserable destinies); third, the feeling of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure gives rise to the suffering of conditioned formations (this is the intermediate suffering, which extends throughout the formless realm).
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions by relying on the three perversions:

perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), and perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*). Due to these three perversions, one conceives of suffering as pleasure.

To perceive pleasure as suffering, the permanent as impermanent, the impermanent as permanent, the non-self as self, the self as non-self, the impure as pure, and the pure as impure—is this not perversion? (From the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Fascicle 2).
Or, out of craving for the three realms of existence, one commits all manner of transgressions.
The existence of desire, the existence of form, and the existence of formlessness (which are the three realms). To not forget the causes and effects of these three realms is called "existence.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless, causing affliction and confusion to all beings within the six paths and four modes of birth.
Today, with shame and remorse, I repent for them all.

Such offenses as these collectively summarize the sins from the three poisons up to those pertaining to the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) to serve as the conclusion. Hereafter, follow this pattern.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which is immeasurable (*apramāṇa*) is called boundless (*ananta*). Because no limit can be found, it is named immeasurable."

Furthermore, [so-and-so] and others, from beginningless time until this day, have committed all manner of transgressions due to the four stations of consciousness (the term "consciousness" is absent in the Southern Canon).

The station of consciousness in form (*rūpa-vijñānasthiti*), the station of consciousness in feeling (*vedanā-vijñānasthiti*), the station of consciousness in perception (*saṃjñā-vijñānasthiti*), and the station of consciousness in mental formations (*saṃskāra-vijñānasthiti*); these are the four. (From the *Abhidharma-kaṅkaraṇa-śāstra*).
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the four floods (*catur-ogha*).

1. The outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*; the afflictions of the desire realm, excluding views and delusion); 2. The outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*; the afflictions of the two upper realms, excluding views and delusion); 3. The outflow of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*; the views of the three realms); 4. The outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*; the delusions of the three realms).
These are also called the four yokes (*yoga*), together with the four graspings (*upādāna*) mentioned below; all are set forth in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the four graspings (*upādāna*):

grasping at sensual desire (*kāma-upādāna*), grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*), grasping at precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-upādāna*), and grasping at the doctrine of self (*ātma-vāda-upādāna*). These are called "graspings" because they cause the continuity of one's own personal existence to proceed without interruption.
Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to four attachments:
first, the attachment that what is not born is born; second, the attachment that what is not extinguished is extinguished; third, the attachment that what is severed is not severed;

and fourth, the attachment that what is not eternal is eternal. "Attachment" (執) here means grasping. Together with the four conditions mentioned below, these are cited from the *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué shūsòng*).
Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to four conditions:

first, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), which is the conjunction of all dharmas; second, the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which consists of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*); third, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Dharmas have no basis. There are four predominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*), yet dharmas cannot be apprehended.
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions because of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

These four great elements are the deluded body—the internal four great elements consisting of earth, water, fire, and wind, which are formed through provisional combination (the external four great elements being as can be known).
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the four bonds (*bandhana*):
the bond of greed, the bond of hatred, the bond of attachment to precepts and rituals, and the bond of attachment to views.

Because these four do not transcend the triple world and do not lead to liberation, they are collectively termed "bonds" and are also called the "four fetters" (*saṃyojana*). This is from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the four types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*): for emotions, for forms, for food, and for sexual desire.

These constitute the four cravings (having examined various sūtras and śāstras extensively, it appears that only the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* mentions "four loves," which refers to the attachment to the four matters of offerings, such as food and drink).

Master Guifeng’s fourfold analysis of "love" (*ai*) and "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) distinguishes between them: there are cases where it is craving but not love, such as when a person loves busyness—it is not a craving for busyness itself; there are cases where it is love but not craving, such as when a person loves watching people fighting or killing one another—who would ever crave such things? There are also cases where it is both craving and love. That is to say:
Regarding fame, profit, wealth, and sensual beauty—these are neither objects of greed nor of craving (meaning they are circumstances that run contrary to one's true nature).
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*):

the womb-born, the egg-born, the moisture-born, and the transformation-born. These constitute the four births as set forth in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. This concludes the section [wherein] the meaning is made manifest.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; they have tormented and disturbed all sentient beings throughout the six realms.
Today, with shame and remorse, we repent them all.
Furthermore, [Name] and others, from time immemorial until this day, whether due to the five stages of abiding...
Afflictions (*kleśa*) produce all transgressions.

Regarding the five stages of abiding (*pañca-vāsa-bhūmi*): first, the stage of abiding in all views (the views of the three realms, which are the afflictions of conceptual discrimination); second, the stage of abiding in desire-attachment (the nine grades of volition in the desire realm);

third, the stage of abiding in form-attachment (the four levels of the form realm, each with nine grades of volition); fourth, the stage of abiding in formless-attachment (there are four levels, each with [nine grades of volition]).
The nine grades of thought; the five stages of abiding in ignorance (the cognitive hindrance).
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

"Hindrance" (*āvaraṇa*) signifies that which covers the reality. The *Zhiguan* states: Greed (*rāga*) [chasing after the five desires of the past and losing right mindfulness]; Anger (*vyāpāda*) [conceiving of others...]

Affliction (which causes anger to persist), sleep (wherein the mind and spirit are clouded and shrouded in dark gloom), restlessness (performing useless acts with a mind of regret), and doubt (not doubt regarding principles, but doubt that obstructs meditative concentration)—
these constitute the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇāni*).
Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the five types of stinginess (*mātsarya*). These are:

stinginess regarding one’s dwelling (having a house or quarters and not wishing for others to reside there); stinginess regarding one’s family (cherishing one’s own disciples and household, not wishing for others to become acquainted with them, and regarding the gifts of others as if they were the loss of one’s own property—this is also called "stinginess regarding the protection of others' things");

stinginess regarding praise (not extolling the virtues of others, fearing that they might surpass oneself); stinginess regarding wealth; and stinginess regarding the Dharma. This is set forth in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the five views:

first, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which clings to "self" and "mine"; second, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), which calculates based on the body as either annihilation or permanence, thereby falling into two extremes;

third, the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which holds the aforementioned views to be supreme or efficacious, or falsely claims that all tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena are permanent, blissful, self, and pure; fourth, the grasping at precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which regards what is not a cause as a cause; and fifth, wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which denies causality.
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions through five types of mental states:
first, the sudden impulse; second, seeking; third, determination; fourth, defilement or purity; and fifth, the outflowing continuity. These constitute the five mental states.
Such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless, tormenting all sentient beings throughout the six realms.
Today we reveal them and repent for them all in their entirety.
Furthermore, [Name] and the others, from time immemorial until this day, whether due to the six sense organs...
Committing all manner of transgressions: (1) the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*)—the aspect of looking with joy or anger;

(2) the ear faculty (*śrotra-indriya*)—the aspect of listening and continuous examination; (3) the nose faculty (*ghrāṇa-indriya*)—loving fragrances and loathing foul odors; (4) the tongue faculty (*jihvā-indriya*)—tasting flavors such as sweet and bitter;

(5) the body faculty (*kāya-indriya*)—craving smoothness and detesting roughness; (6) the mind faculty (*manas-indriya*)—discernment and deliberation. These six are collectively called the faculties of emotion (*ṣad-indriya*), as they are the roots of emotional consciousness.
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions through the six consciousnesses:

the eye-consciousness (perceiving the false colors of dark and yellow), the ear-consciousness (distinguishing between sounds of suffering and pleasure), the nose-consciousness (observing the swirling light of odors), the tongue-consciousness (discriminating between the heterodox and the orthodox in speech), the body-consciousness (manifesting various postures according to circumstances), and the mental consciousness (conceptualizing and revolving within emptiness).
By transforming these six consciousnesses, one can achieve the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the six types of perception (*saṃjñā*).

The *Xiyuan* (Analysis of the Profound) states: "The six consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, each have their corresponding perceptions (that is, the perception associated with the eye-consciousness, up to the perception associated with the mental consciousness)."
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the six types of sensation (*ṣaḍ-vedanā*).

When the six sense faculties are able to apprehend their respective six objects, this is called "sensation" (as stated in the *Śūnyatā-parivarta*: "The eye perceives forms, and so on, up to the mind perceiving dharmas").
Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the six modes of activity.
The six faculties, such as the eye and so forth, each have their respective domains; thus, each has its respective function. As the *Dharmapada* states:

"In the past, there was a man who practiced the Way by a river for twenty years, yet he thought only of the six sense objects, and his mind found no peace. The Buddha went to deliver him, manifesting himself as a śramaṇa and staying overnight with him beneath a tree. That night, under the bright moonlight, a tortoise emerged from the river. A jackal wished to devour it, but the tortoise withdrew its head and tail."

The tortoise withdrew its four limbs and tucked in its shell; the jackal found no opportunity and departed. The practitioner saw this and said to the śramaṇa, "The tortoise possesses armor to protect its life, so the wild dog finds no opening. The śramaṇa replied, "People of the world are not like this tortoise.

They indulge their six sense-faculties, allowing external demons to find an opening. He then spoke a verse: "Hide the six as a tortoise hides its limbs; guard the mind as one guards a city. With wisdom, wage war against Māra; if victorious, there shall be no affliction. One must know the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); it can slay those thieves."
Alternatively, all transgressions may be created due to the six types of craving.

The Abhidharma states: each of the six sense organs, such as the eye and so forth, has its respective object of contact through which craving arises (craving arising from visual contact, up to craving arising from mental contact).
Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the six doubts.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "Greed, anger, delusion, pride, doubt, and discursive thought—these six are all accompanied by doubt (also known as innate delusion). As asked in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*:"

"From what do stinginess, greed, and envy arise? Answer: "They arise from ignorance (*avidyā*). "Furthermore, from what does ignorance arise? Answer: "It arises from heedlessness (*pramāda*). "Again, from what does heedlessness arise? Answer: "It arises from inversion (*viparyāsa*). "Furthermore, from what do inversions arise?"

Answer: It arises from the mind of doubt. Because of doubt, one gives rise to perversions. Upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, the net of doubt is immediately removed. When doubt is removed, perversions are removed; when perversions are removed, stinginess and the like are all eliminated.
Such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless, vexing and disturbing all sentient beings throughout the six realms.
Today, with shame and remorse, I reveal them all and repent. (At this point, the characters for "shame and remorse" were originally absent.)
Furthermore, [so-and-so] and others, from beginningless time until this very day, have committed all manner of transgressions due to the seven outflows (*āsrava*),
or have committed all manner of transgressions due to the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), or have committed all manner of transgressions due to the eight inversions (*viparyāsa*).

The seven outflows (*āsrava*) are: first, views (the intrinsic nature of the outflow); second, the sense faculties (associated with the outflow); third, forgetfulness (the basis of the outflow); fourth, evil (induced by the outflow); fifth, intimacy (generated by the outflow);
sixth, craving (intermingled with the outflow); seventh, mindfulness (the cognitive obstruction of the outflow). The seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are stated in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*:

the latent tendency of desire, the latent tendency of anger, the latent tendency of craving, the latent tendency of pride, the latent tendency of ignorance, the latent tendency of views, and the latent tendency of doubt. [End of] external [section].

The Path alone possesses eight inversions (1. view of self; 2. sentient beings; 3. life-span; 4. person; 5. permanence; 6. annihilation; 7. existence; 8. non-existence). Ordinary persons and followers of the Lesser Vehicle both possess eight inversions (the four of ordinary persons:

1. reckoning the impermanent as permanent; 2. reckoning the unsatisfactory as satisfactory; 3. reckoning the non-self as self; 4. reckoning the impure as pure. The four of the Two Vehicles: 1. reckoning the permanent as impermanent; 2. reckoning the satisfactory as unsatisfactory;
3. reckoning the self as non-self; 4. reckoning the pure as impure. [Cited from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*]).
Or due to the eight impurities, one commits all manner of transgressions; or due to the eight sufferings, one commits all manner of transgressions.
Such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless, vexing and disturbing all sentient beings within the six realms. Today we disclose them and repent of them all.

The eight impurities (*aṣṭa-mala*) are: affliction through recollection, affliction through non-recollection, affliction through both recollection and non-recollection, affliction regarding "I," affliction regarding "mine," affliction regarding intrinsic nature, affliction regarding differentiation, and affliction regarding grasping (also called the eight false conceptualizations).

Because they defile the intrinsic nature of afflictions, they are called "impurities" (*mala*) (as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*). The eight sufferings (*aṣṭa-duḥkha*) are: birth, aging, illness, death, and enmity with those one hates.
Encountering what one dislikes, separation from what one loves, not obtaining what one seeks, and the intense burning of the five aggregates.
Furthermore, [so-and-so] and others, from time immemorial until this day, have committed all manner of transgressions due to the nine afflictions,
and have committed all manner of transgressions due to the nine fetters.

First, they vex my own body; second, they hate my kin; third, they praise my enemies. These three, occurring across the past, present, and future, constitute nine types of vexation (as stated in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*).
"Tie" (*saṃyojana*) refers to that which binds and does not allow for dispersal (because it can cause suffering to coalesce).
They are: first, the tie of craving; second, the tie of aversion; third, the tie of pride; fourth, the tie of ignorance; fifth, the tie of views; sixth, the tie of grasping.

The fetters: 1) the fetter of views, 2) the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances, 3) the fetter of doubt, 4) the fetter of sensual desire, 5) the fetter of ill will, 6) the fetter of attachment to existence, 7) the fetter of envy, 8) the fetter of avarice. A "fetter" (saṃyojana) is that which is diametrically opposed to liberation.
One may commit all manner of transgressions due to nine conditions, or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the ten afflictions (kleśa).

The nine conditions are: the condition of light, the condition of space, the condition of the sense organ, the condition of the object, the condition of mental attention (*manasikāra*), the condition of the fundamental support, the condition of the support for defilement and purity, the condition of the support for discrimination, and the seed-condition.
The verse says: Visual consciousness arises from nine conditions; Auditory consciousness arises from only eight (excluding the condition of light);

Olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses arise from seven (excluding the condition of light and the condition of space); The latter three [mental consciousnesses] arise from five, four, and three respectively. (The "latter three" refers to the mental consciousnesses associated with the three types of objects.)

The final three consciousnesses are the sixth, the seventh, and the eighth. The five, three, and four [conditions] are assigned to these three consciousnesses respectively. Thus, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises from five conditions, as it does not rely on the four conditions of light, space, the sense organ, and the object. The seventh consciousness (*manas*) has only three conditions, as it does not rely on the other six;

it relies solely on the conditions of the defiled and pure support (*kliṣṭa-śuddha-āśraya*), the condition of discrimination (*vibhāga-āśraya*), and the seed-condition (*bīja-pratyaya*). The eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) arises from only four conditions; compared to the seventh consciousness, it adds the fundamental support-condition (*mūla-āśraya-pratyaya*).

The fundamental support is the *ālaya-vijñāna*. The support for both defilement and purity is the seventh consciousness (*manas*). The support for discrimination is the sixth consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). As for the ten afflictions: first, anger (*krodha*);

second, vexation (*upānaha*); third, resentment (*upanāha*); fourth, concealment (*mrakṣa*); fifth, flattery (*māyā*); sixth, deception (*śāṭhya*); seventh, arrogance (*mada*); eighth, harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*); ninth, envy (*īrṣyā*); and tenth, avarice (*mātsarya*).
These ten constitute half of the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), as detailed in the *Śata-dharma-vidya-mukha-śāstra*.
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the ten fetters (*paryavasthāna*), or due to the eleven pervasive proclivities (*anuśaya*).
As for the ten fetters: first, the fetter of anger (*krodha*; resentment); second, the fetter of concealment (*mrakṣa*; hiding one's own faults); third, the fetter of drowsiness (*styāna*;

the stupor of mental consciousness); fourth, the fetter of torpor (*middha*; the darkening of the five sense-faculties); fifth, the fetter of restlessness (*auddhatya*; frivolous wandering); sixth, the fetter of agitation (*uddhata*; the turbulence of the three karmas); seventh, the fetter of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*; committing offenses in private).

1. Lack of self-shame (*āhrīkya*) [the fetter of not feeling shame within oneself when committing an offense]; 2. Lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) [the fetter of not feeling shame before others when committing an offense while exposed]; 3. Avarice (*mātsarya*) [the fetter of being unable to bestow wealth or the Dharma through generosity]; 4. Envy (*īrṣyā*) [the fetter of the mind becoming distressed by the prosperity of others;

these are "fetters" (*paryavasthāna*), which bind one to birth and death so that liberation cannot be attained]; 5. The pervasive factors (*paryavasthāna*) [so called because they cause one to wander extensively through the evil realms]:

1. lack of faith (*āśraddhya*); 2. laziness (*kausīdya*); 3. lack of self-shame (*āhrīkya*); 4. lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*); 5. excessive greed (*abhidhyā*); 6. excessive anger (*vyāpāda*); 7. excessive [delusion] (*moha*).

1. Delusion; 2. Non-faith; 3. Laziness; 4. Forgetfulness; 5. Distraction; 6. Lack of discernment; 7. Ignorance; 8. Torpor; 9. Heedlessness; 10. Avarice; 11. Harmfulness (the opposites of these are called the eleven virtuous mental factors).
Or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the twelve bases (*āyatana*). Or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the sixteen views.

As for the twelve bases—meaning that they mutually interpenetrate—they consist of the six internal bases and the six external bases. The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind constitute the six internal bases;

they belong to the subject (*grāhaka*) because they are capable of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing. Form, sound, odor, flavor, tangibility, and mental objects constitute the six external bases; they belong to the object (*grāhya*), being the objects of attachment for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing.
[This refers to] the bases (*āyatana*). They are also called the twelve bases. Regarding the sixteen types of views, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: 1.

The view of a self (*ātman*), which gives rise to the notions of "I" and "mine. 2. The view of a being (*jantu*), such as [the notion] that a father has a son. 3. The view of an experiencer (*vedaka*), [referring to] the accomplishment of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

4. The view of a living being (*jīva*), [referring to] the capacity to perform actions. 5. The view of a sentient being (*sattva*), [referring to] birth from the aggregation of the aggregates (*skandha*). 6. The view of a nourisher (*poṣa*), [referring to] the act of nurturing.

(Through causes and conditions, they are long). 7. Those who possess the number [of the seven groups] perceive and see that all phenomena have numbers. 8. Those who are "persons" perceive and see that they falsely conceive of themselves as being persons.
9. Those who are "doers" perceive and see the hands and feet as agent and object. 10. Those who are "instigators of action" perceive and see the power to employ others. 11.

Those who are "arisers" perceive and see the performance of karma for future lives. 12. Those who are "instigators of arising" perceive and see that they also cause others to act. 13. Those who are "experiencers" perceive and see suffering and pleasure.
14. The recipient of the fruit manifests [it]; this is knowledge and vision (the loathing of suffering and pleasure). 15. The knower knows and sees;
the five consciousnesses are called "knowledge. 16. The seer knows and sees; [this refers to] contemplating forms and images. Prajñā is termed the sixteen-fold self.
Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the eighteen *dhātus* (realms). Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the twenty-five *ātman*s (selves).

The six faculties (*indriya*), the six objects (*viṣaya*), and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) constitute the eighteen realms (*dhātu*). [The term *dhātu* has three meanings: first, the sense of analytical discrimination; second, the sense of a genus or lineage; third, the sense of a boundary.

The twenty-five selves (the twenty-five *tattvas*, as set forth in the *Śata-śāstra*) are as follows: 1. *Avyakta* (the Unmanifest), the primordial nature of the world, gives rise to *buddhi* (intellection); 2. from *buddhi* (the intermediate state) arises...

The mind arises. Third, from the mind (the conceit of "I") arise the five sense objects (form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch). From the five sense objects arise the five great elements (earth, water, fire, wind, and space).

From the five great elements arise the five organs of cognition (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body), the hands, feet, and mouth, along with the organ of excretion and the organ of procreation (the five organs of action), and the organ of the mind (the organ of equanimity).
Together these constitute eleven organs; combined with the aforementioned [five sense objects], they total [sixteen].
This constitutes twenty-four [categories]. Adding the self (ātman) as the sovereign truth makes twenty-five selves.
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the sixty-two views.
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness each possess four permutations, such as: "the aggregates are large and the self is small," or "the self is within the aggregates."
"I am large; the aggregates are small," "the aggregates are within me," "I am distinct from the aggregates," and "the aggregates are identical to me. Each aggregate thus possesses four propositions.

With the five aggregates, this constitutes twenty. When distributed across the three periods of time, they become sixty. Adding the two fundamental views of annihilationism and eternalism, they total sixty-two.

Alternatively, due to the [perception of] the truths (*satya*) and reflection, the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) and one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*) burn fiercely day and night. Regarding the perception of the truths:

they comprise thirty-two proclivities of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—namely, ten proclivities under the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), seven each under the truths of origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*) (excluding the view of a self-body [*satkāyadṛṣṭi*], the view of extremes [*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*], and the attachment to precepts and rituals [*śīlavrataparāmarśa*]), and eight proclivities under the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) (excluding the two views of a self-body and extremes).

There are twenty-eight proclivities of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)—namely, nine proclivities under the truth of suffering (excluding anger [*vyāpāda*]), six each under the truths of origin and cessation (excluding anger, the view of a self-body, the view of extremes, and the attachment to precepts and rituals), and [six under the truth of the path].

There are seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*): excluding anger, the [view of] self, and the [view of] extremes. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are twenty-eight underlying tendencies: nine underlying tendencies in the stage of suffering (excluding anger, the view of self, and the view of extremes); six each in the stages of origin and cessation (excluding anger, the view of self, the view of extremes, and the attachment to precepts and rituals);

and seven underlying tendencies in the stage of the path (excluding anger, the view of self, and the view of extremes). Together, these constitute eighty-eight underlying tendencies. Regarding the cultivation of insight (*bhāvanā*), they comprise four underlying tendencies of the desire realm: first, greed; second, anger; third, delusion; and fourth, pride.

These four latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) by one proceeding toward the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, up until the fruit of *anāgāmin*, when nine grades are finally severed. The three latent tendencies of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)—namely, (1) greed, (2) delusion, and (3) pride—are all abandoned through the path of cultivation by one proceeding toward the fruit of *arhat*.

The three latent tendencies of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)—namely, (1) greed, (2) delusion, and (3) pride—are likewise so. Thus, there are ten latent tendencies in total across the three realms;

together with the previously mentioned afflictions of view (*darśana-heya*), they constitute the ninety-eight latent tendencies. (However, these three [formless realm] latent tendencies are abandoned only upon reaching the fruit of *arhat*. The term "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) means that which drives or impels.
This is for the sake of meaning. It is because it causes the mental states of those who practice to circulate through the three realms.

The one hundred and eight afflictions consist of the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), to which the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*)—such as shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*)—are added, thus forming one hundred and eight proclivities.
These one hundred and eight proclivities, throughout the twelve periods of the day, blaze like a raging fire; even the slightest fuel of wholesome merit is entirely reduced to ashes.
Ashes! Why do you not take warning?
You open the gates of all outflows (*āsrava*), commit every kind of transgression, and afflict the worthy and the sages as well as the four modes of birth, pervading the three realms.
It extends across the six realms of existence, leaving no place to take refuge.
These are the gates of all outflows (*āsrava*), the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction (*kleśa*). There are two types of noble ones (*ārya*):

first, those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), for whom the four fruits constitute the sages (*ārya*) and the four paths constitute the worthies (*bhadra*); second, those of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), for whom there are the three worthies and ten sages. In total, these have not yet reached *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
The cities of the world are all like leaky gates through which sentient beings pass in and out. The three realms are the places where one creates transgressions and undergoes suffering;

the four modes of birth and the six destinies are the sentient beings who create transgressions and undergo suffering. "Pervasive" (biàn) means "all-encompassing" (zhōu); "extending" (jiàn) [refers to the continuity of this state].

This is the meaning of "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*). "Mī" is the meaning of "filling. It is precisely because delusions and karma follow one another in succession and retribution and response revolve in cycles that the six realms of existence pervade the three worlds.
Because retribution and response revolve in cycles and delusions and karma follow one another in succession, [suffering] blazes fiercely day and night, opening the gates of all outflows (*āsrava*);
one only enters and does not exit. Thus, the burning house of the three worlds blazes fiercely day and night; for this reason, it is said to be "non-existent" (*an-asti*).

There is a place where one may take refuge. (Question: Why do you say there is no place to take refuge? Answer: One rides upon tainted causes to produce tainted fruits; relying upon tainted fruits, one further creates tainted causes. Thus, cause and fruit mutually support one another.)
It is continuous and uninterrupted; therefore, it is said to be pervasive and all-encompassing, leaving no space to escape it (the following shows the method for seeking refuge).
Today, with utmost prayer, I turn toward the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages; with shame and remorse, I reveal my transgressions and repent them all.

"Supreme prayer" means a most sincere and earnest supplication. "The ten directions" refers to the four cardinal points, the four intermediate corners, together with the zenith and nadir, which constitute ten;
these all contain Buddha-fields and the Three Jewels. "Shame and remorse" is the mind that emerges from the burning house. "Confession" [is the act of revealing one's transgressions].

This is the mouth through which the outflows emerge. When one possesses this mind and these words, all outflows are blocked and one escapes from the burning house. (The disclosure is like uprooting a tree:

first one loosens the soil surrounding it, and once the roots and sprouts are exposed, the tree falls of its own accord. By relying on the power of the Triple Gem and using the sharp spade of shame and remorse, one digs away the concealed heart, confessing the faults of one's own mind;

thus the forest of transgressions collapses and the root of karma is pulled out. The preceding section has extensively enumerated the characteristics of offenses and completed the ritual of purification. The following section concerns the making of vows: whether one has committed an offense or not, one should all practice confession. If one confesses an offense, the offense is extinguished; if one prays when there is no offense, [merit is gained].)

This causes merit to arise. Furthermore, through the addition of utmost sincerity, not only does merit increase, but the power of wisdom and all spiritual qualities are spontaneously accomplished. Next, one should successively make vows to bring these merits to fulfillment. To merely repent of transgressions without making vows is like a pure crystal vase.
One does not store lion’s milk (the following cases are analogous).
May [I and others], by virtue of the merit produced through this repentance of the three poisons and all afflictions,
in birth after birth, have the three types of wisdom become clear, the three forms of penetration become radiant, the three sufferings be extinguished, and the three vows be fulfilled.

Regarding the first of the general characteristics mentioned above—the gravity of the three poisons—all afflictions (*kleśa*) are subsumed within these three categories: outflows (*āsrava*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and perversions (*viparyāsa*).

Below this, it clarifies that from the arising of afflictions, demerit (*pāpa*) is extinguished and merit (*puṇya*) is produced; this applies not only to the present but to future lives as well, for it is thus in all successive births.

The following sections follow this pattern. As for the "three wisdoms" (*tri-prajñā*): first is wisdom through hearing (*śruta-maya-prajñā*, the gate of the ear); second is wisdom through reflection (*cintā-maya-prajñā*, the gate of the mind); and third is wisdom through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya-prajñā*).

(The Gate of the Middle Way Contemplation) To hear without listening, one lacks the cause for receiving nourishment. To listen without reflecting, one lacks the profound purport. To reflect without practicing, one will ultimately never realize the principle.

Therefore, one must clarify the "three penetrations" (*trividya*). "Penetration" means clarity. First is the penetration of the divine eye-knowledge (*divyacakṣus-jñāna*); second is the penetration of the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*);
third is the penetration of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*). These three should be luminous (the meaning is found in the middle fascicle).
The three sufferings (the manifestation of names and meanings). The three vows are: first, the vow that all sentient beings may realize and know the Dharma;
second, the vow to preach the Dharma for sentient beings with an insatiable mind; third, the vow to sacrifice body and life to protect and uphold the True Dharma.

These vows shall be fulfilled (one should know that untainted wholesome dharmas do not stop here, but these are merely mentioned briefly. Why? Because the untainted is inexhaustible; whereas the aforementioned unwholesome dharmas can be repented and eliminated, the tainted has its limit).
I vow that by virtue of the merit produced from this repentance for the four consciousnesses (the original text includes the character "zhu," which is not required here) and all other afflictions,

may I, in birth after birth and life after life, broaden the four immeasurable minds, establish the karma of the four reliances, extinguish the four evil destinies, and attain the four fearlessnesses.

The four immeasurables (the four *apramāṇas*) are: first, loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which is able to bestow happiness; second, compassion (*karuṇā*), which is able to extract suffering; third, sympathetic joy (*muditā*), which rejoices in the happiness of others;

and fourth, equanimity (*upekṣā*), which regards enemies and kin as equal. These four states of mind should be expanded; when expanded, they become immeasurable. That which is immeasurable is necessarily impartial.
"Equality" means there is no partiality. Regarding the four objects of faith: first, faith in the Buddha (rejoicing in constantly praising the Buddha);

second, faith in the Dharma (rejoicing in desiring to hear the Dharma and constantly mindful of its practice); third, faith in the Sangha (capable of practicing the two benefits and rejoicing in making offerings to the assembly); fourth, faith in the precepts (rejoicing in being free from the five desires).
