We, [Name] and others, from beginningless time until this day, have either stolen people’s wives and concubines, abducted the women of others,
violated those of pure integrity, defiled bhikṣuṇīs, destroyed the brahmacarya of others, coerced them unrighteously, looked upon them with turbid minds and evil glances,
or addressed them with mocking and derisive speech.
"Brahmacarya" refers to the practice of pure precepts. "Bi" (逼) has the meaning of the physical body; "po" (迫) means to press or constrain. A mind harboring lustful impurity is called a "turbid mind.
To steal glances with a sidelong eye is called "evil gazing. "Chao-diao" (潮調) refers to flirtatious jesting. (In the Mahāyāna Sūtra, the Bodhisattva himself says: "I maintain pure precepts.")

Even if one does not engage in union with women, if upon seeing a woman one engages in banter, joking, or laughter; or if outside a wall or partition one hears the sound of a woman’s bracelets, bangles, and so forth, and a mind of attachment arises, even to the point of pursuing her—none of these can be called being fully endowed with pure precepts.
Furthermore, some may have brought shame upon their families by defiling the reputation of the virtuous and good; others may have committed impure acts with five types of men.
Such offenses are immeasurable and boundless. Today, with utmost sincerity, I repent of them all.

There are five kinds of this intense suffering: jealousy and transformation. (In the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, when the Buddha describes Ānanda as being endowed with eight kinds of inconceivable qualities, the fourth states:

"For more than twenty years, following me in my coming and going, even upon seeing women among kings, kṣatriyas, or noble families of great lineage, as well as women of the devas and nāgas, he did not give rise to a mind of desire; how much less would he feel shame for the households of others? Having finished the repentance.
Next, one makes a vow to accomplish virtue:

"By virtue of the merit produced from this repentance for the transgressions of lust and so forth, may I, in birth after birth and life after life, be spontaneously transformed and born without depending on a womb;
may I be pure and radiant, endowed with the marks and signs of excellence and luminous splendor."

The *pao* (胞) is the fetal membrane. When a mother is pregnant for three months, it is called the *tai* (胎). (As the *Shijing*, "Jiao-bian" commentary states: "Does one not dwell alone within the mother’s *tai-pao*?").

If one is born in the Western Land or the pure lands of the ten directions, one always attains transformation by lotus birth, which differs from receiving birth via the *tai-pao* in the five turbidities and evil worlds.
Because there is no filth, it is pure; reversing the aforementioned turbid mind, because there are no obstructions, it is brilliant and clean.
Regarding the marks and signs and the radiance [of the Buddha], as explained in the Verses Praising the Buddha by Śakra:
the six sense faculties become clear and bright; one becomes sharp, intelligent, and penetrating, realizing that affection and attachment are like shackles, and observing those six sensory objects.
Like an illusion and like a magical transformation, one becomes definitively weary of and detached from the objects of the five desires; even in dreams, no perverse thoughts arise.
Neither internal nor external causes and conditions can ever move such a person. Having performed repentance and made vows, one takes refuge in and pays homage to the Triple Gem.

Being fully endowed with the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are opened; not being deluded by the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), the six sense faculties are clarified.

May the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*) become the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Because one constantly practices the six sublime conducts, the ears are acute, and the nose, tongue, and body are keen.

The eyes become clear and the mind becomes penetrating; thus the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) are bright and the three types of penetration (*vidyā*) are lucid (the term "lucid" [kāi-lǎng] translates the previous phrase regarding escaping the prison and emerging from the river).

What is on the hands is called shackles (*zhì*); what is on the feet is called fetters (*gù*). (Regarding those who contemplate sensory objects as illusions and so forth: it is like the five hundred princes who once gathered together to sit by the edge of a lotus pond, each seeing their own forms reflected in the water.

They suddenly awakened to the fact that all phenomena are like illusions, like transformations, like things seen in a dream; that these physical forms in the water have no reality. They left the household life to practice the Way, and all attained the fruits of the Path. What was previously called the causal conditions of the five desires is here abandoned. No.
Wrong thoughts (the opposite of the aforementioned wrong views).
Having already finished repenting for the three karmas of the body, we shall now proceed in order to repent for the four evil karmas of the mouth:

first, harsh speech; second, false speech; third, frivolous speech; and fourth, [double-tongued] speech. First, one binds the three [karmas] of the body as before; now, one should descend and initiate the subsequent four [karmas] of the mouth. Harsh speech, false speech, frivolous speech, and double-tongued speech.

The tongue (the *Bao'en jing* says: "Now, the mouth and tongue are the axes that carve the body and the calamities that destroy it. One should know that all manner of misfortunes issue from the mouth").
There are three grades of observing the precepts of the mouth: superior is not speaking what is unlawful; middling and inferior are not committing the four karmas of the mouth.

If one commits these toward the Triple Gem, the transgression is even more grave (*Bao'en jing* says: "Parents are the most supreme field of merit within the triple world; the Sangha is the field of merit for transcending the triple world. As in the case of the former *vina* who fell ill...")

A monk requested some clarified butter and oil. [The other] then reviled him, saying, "Why do you not eat excrement and urine? Because of this, he fell into the state of a worm in a cesspool for ninety billion kalpas. The rest is as explained in the Brahmajāla Sūtra.
The Sūtra states: "The transgressions of verbal karma can cause sentient beings to fall into the hells or suffer as hungry ghosts.
If they are reborn among animals, they take the form of an owl or an owlet; those who hear their cries cannot help but feel loathing."
The *xiūliú* is a mother-eating monster bird, known as the *xiāo*. In Jiangdong, it is called the *gùè*. It cries twice at once;
its evil sound is associated with excessive lust, and thus all who hear it find it loathsome.
If one is born among humans, the breath shall always be foul; whatever one says, people will not believe or accept;

one’s kin and retinue will be discordant, and one will constantly delight in strife and contention. Since such evil fruits result from the karma of speech, we today take refuge in the Triple Gem with utmost sincerity and repent for all [transgressions].
When praising the Buddha’s Dharma with one's mouth, it constantly emits the fragrance of blue lotuses; now, by defiling others with harsh speech, the breath of the mouth is perpetually foul.

Because of such evil speech and a lack of faith in cause and effect, one causes others to harbor disturbing thoughts, thereby inviting retribution. Even if one is later reborn among humans, [the consequences remain].
People do not believe his words either. Not only distant acquaintances, but even close friends and kinsmen are at odds with him.
He constantly delights in composing verses that explain the meaning of discord. This first clarifies the evil fruits of verbal karma; next, the fourfold repentance will be explained in sequence.
First, the confession of harsh speech. This is first presented in general terms:
[Name] and others, from beginningless time until this day, have committed various transgressions through the karma of harsh speech within the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence.
Our utterances have been coarse and vulgar, and our speech has been violent and overbearing.
Harsh speech refers to words of grievance, poisonous insults, and curses—speech that is unbearable to hear.

Just as one says a dog is "wild" (*kang*) when it should not be approached, this serves as a metaphor for ugly, coarse, and violent language (as in the *Han Shu Xu*: "The wild and unruly Qin destroyed our sacred culture"; Yan Shiguo [commented]: "An appearance of coarseness and wickedness").
This is further divided into two parts; the first concerns human society.

Regardless of whether others are honorable or humble, close or distant, noble or lowly, if even the slightest thing does not meet their expectations, they immediately harbor anger and resentment. They resort to verbal abuse, insults, and humiliation;

their conduct becomes so vulgar, indecent, and foul that nothing is left unsaid. This causes those wronged to harbor grievances that they do not forget for the rest of their lives, leading to a succession of calamities and the formation of enmity that knows no end.

Following from the preceding two lines: the clergy and the laity are of one essence. If one does not inquire into the distinctions of honor and lowliness, one will indulge in coarse speech and lack of propriety at will.

Whether near or distant, all people possess this [human nature]; if one does not inquire into the distinctions of kinship and distance, one lacks benevolence (*ren*). As for the noble and the humble...
To fix distinctions based on high or low status, regardless of whether one is noble or base, is unrighteous. To harbor anger and resentment at even a slight failure to meet one's wishes is unwise.
Because of harboring anger in the heart, one curses others with the mouth; thus, it is evident that there is no truthful speech in such a mouth.

Due to this single transgression of the mouth, the five constant virtues are all lost. How can one not be cautious? "Věi" (猥) means miscellaneous or impure. "Xiè" (褻) means frivolous or disrespectful intimacy.
"Filth" (*hē*) means defilement; it is difficult to describe fully, hence it is said that "there is nowhere it does not reach. It is for this reason that it provokes the anger of others.

Generally, to have something held in the mouth is called *xián* (to衔). [Sentient beings harbor resentment and thereby harm their own bodies, just as a mule conceives and thereby destroys its own frame, or like the plantain tree, which withers once fruit has grown.]
It forms a continuous chain of enmity. This principle encompasses both the horizontal and the vertical dimensions. Horizontally, it binds one in resentment across the four quarters;
vertically, it links one through kalpas as vast as space. Thus, it is inexhaustible and without end.

Furthermore, there may have been instances where we have brought resentment upon Heaven and Earth, reviled the spirits and deities, disparaged the sages and worthies, or slandered and defiled the virtuous and good.
The karmic offenses arising from such evil speech are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, we repent of them all.

Second, "defiling" (*yīnwán*) means impurity or filth. It refers to such acts as cursing heaven and reviling earth, or incanting rain and rebuking the wind. "Denigrating" (*biǎn*) means to censure; "reproaching" (*chì*) means to scold.
To fabricate evil and concoct ugliness to defile another's pure reputation is called "false accusation and defilement" (*wúwū*). "Thus below" [refers to] the double conclusion.

Harsh speech invites a retribution of many heads (according to the *Baoen jing*, the bhikṣu Junti fell into the form of a white dog because he had slandered and reviled sages and worthies in the past; upon hearing Śāriputra preach the Dharma, he...).

If one can repent and make a vow, and encounter a virtuous friend, their transgressions will be exhausted, and they will be reborn among humans; there, meeting a Buddha, they will attain the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Therefore, one should keep in mind the kindness of virtuous friends and the Buddha.

Furthermore, when Lady Mṛgī was a young girl, she insulted her mother with a single evil word, saying, "She is like a beast. Due to the causal conditions of this harsh speech, she was born from the wombs of deer for five hundred lifetimes. The Buddha told Ānanda: "When people are born into this world, calamity arises from the mouth. One must guard the mouth more carefully than a fierce fire.

A fierce fire burns but a single lifetime, whereas the blazing fire of evil speech burns for countless lifetimes. While ordinary fire consumes worldly wealth, evil speech consumes the seven noble riches (*saptadhanāni*)."
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this very day, through the karma of false speech, we have committed various transgressions;
seeking fame and material gain within our minds, we concealed our true feelings, practiced deceit, and remained oblivious to our own nature with shameless faces.

2. The karma of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*): It has no influence whatsoever; it consists of fabricating and creating false words. *Xi* (希) means desire (*icchā*). (The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "There are three desires for those who have left the household life:

first, evil desire, which is the wish to be the leader of all the great assemblies, to preach the Dharma so that it is accepted with faith, and to receive great offerings and the like; second, the desire to cause the fourfold assembly to know that one has attained the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) up to the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), for the sake of gain and support;

third, the desire for desire, such as a bhikṣu desiring to be born in the Brahma heaven or even in a Kṣatriya family to obtain sovereignty. *Ni-qing* (匿情) means concealing the reality; it is to hide one's true feelings.

"Deceitfully contriving falsehoods" means practicing deception and artifice; "transforming into falsehood" means shifting one's state to become deceitful. "Obscuring the mind" means clouding the natural principles of Heaven; it refers to a person who deceives their own heart.
"Thick-skinned" means having a face as hard and thick as armor, showing no sign of shame on one's countenance. These two phrases refer to the concealment of one's true feelings.
The general purport of the first chapter. Below follows the explanation of the text in five parts. First, the general explanation:
pointing to existence while speaking of emptiness, and pointing to emptiness while speaking of existence.
As the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "It is like a person who, seeing the horns of an ox through a fence from afar, says he sees an ox; or seeing clouds, he says [he sees rain]."
Seeing rain, and seeing the actions of body and speech, one then says one sees the mind. Although one does not truly see the ox, the rain, and the mind, none of them are false.
If one were to falsely construct such a statement despite there being no connection whatsoever, the sin would be beyond description. Be careful with your precepts! Be careful with your precepts!
Second, an explanation regarding how the six sense organs of a single body assist in the formation [of perception].
To say one has not seen when one has seen; to say one has seen when one has not seen. To say one has not heard when one has heard; to say one has heard when one has not heard.

The first two lines are from the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, concerning the fourth of the ten grave precepts of the Bodhisattva precepts: false speech. This refers to the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) contributing to the commission of false speech.
Likewise, never having heard a sound with the ear, or never having smelled an odor with the nose, yet falsely claiming to have done so—[these are all instances of such deception].
To hear and yet falsely claim not to have heard—this is the ear-faculty and nose-faculty assisting in the commission of false speech.
To know and say one does not know; to not know and say one knows; to have done and say one did not do; to not have done and say one did.
The tongue can perceive tastes; the mind can perceive dharmas. These two faculties, the tongue and the mind, assist in delusion.
The body faculty can perform both good and evil deeds; this body faculty assists in false speech.
Deceiving the sages and saints, and deluding the people of the world.
[The character for] "knot" (jie) follows. As above, the six sense organs assist in delusion; above, they deceive the sages and saints, and below, they delude the ordinary and ignorant.

(The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The habit of deception involves mutual cheating, arising from mutual entrapment. When this false entrapment does not cease, the wandering mind creates villainy. Thus there are dust, excrement, urine, filth, and impurity, like dust following the wind, such that each has nothing to see.")

Because these two habits combine, there occur such matters as drowning and being submerged, leaping and tossing about, flying and falling, drifting and sinking. For this reason, the Buddhas designate deception with the same name as "killing" (*ghātana*). When a Bodhisattva sees deception, they view it as treading upon a venomous snake.
As for matters concerning father and son, ruler and minister, relatives, or old friends, there was never a time when their conversations were honest and sincere;

this caused others to mistakenly lend them credence, leading to the ruin of families and the downfall of states—all of which originated from this. (The phrase "咸此由之" is rendered as "咸此由之"; in the Southern Canon it appears as "之由.")
Third: Clarifying how [false speech] can destroy family and state. Nothing is closer than father and son;

yet because of false speech, they are separated by a barrier in between, their mutual trust is shaken, and each inflicts harm upon the other, leading to the ruin of the family. Nothing is more righteous than the relationship between ruler and subject;
yet because of unrestrained wickedness and incitement to delusion, they inflict mutual harm, leading to the calamity of the state's downfall. As for others of the same clan...
Relatives by blood, distant kin, friends bound by shared resolve, and long-standing companions—none of them fail to be incited by false speech, thereby brewing resentment and grievance.
(The two phrases beginning with "There is something" refer precisely to false speech: there is something spoken, yet it is not truthful; this is falsehood.

"Erroneous" means mistaken (as in the *Xunzi* passage: "mistaken in chaotic doctrines"). "To listen and believe" means to hear their words and accept them as reality. False speech is like... [text ends]

Like a reed pipe, people do not discern its nature; they incline their hearts to believe it, even to the point that—whether on a large scale as states (where the domain of the Son of Heaven and feudal lords is broad, termed "states") or on a medium scale as households (where the domain of ministers, high officials, and those below them is narrow, termed "households"), or on a small scale among friends and acquaintances—they all take false speech as their starting point and thereby ruin themselves.
The original intent behind creating false speech is the desire for fame and profit; at the very least, it is for personal gain.
A single person, though no more than one stout family, can cause the whole world to follow them in error, thereby bringing about a great calamity.
How could their guilt not be accordingly grave?
Some resort to deceptive illusions, constantly praising themselves and claiming to have attained the four dhyānas, the four formless absorptions, ānāpāna, and prāṇa.
Regarding the sixteen aspects of contemplation:
there are four types of deluded ones who falsely claim to have attained worldly fruits.

These sorcerers employ the deceptive and illusory arts of non-Buddhist heterodox paths to delude people (they constantly praise themselves, leading directly to the phrase "all have reached my domain"; the two characters for "attained" lead directly to "non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas"). They claim to have attained the four dhyānas.

This refers to attaining the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the heavens of the four *dhyānas* (the eighteen heavens of the realm of form consist of three heavens each from the first to the third *dhyāna*, and nine heavens for the fourth *dhyāna*.

The *Zongjing lu* states: 1. Practicing with heterodox views, rejoicing in higher realms and loathing lower ones—this is the meditation of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). 2. Believing in correct cause and effect, yet practicing through joy and aversion—this is the meditation of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). 3. Realizing the principle of the emptiness of persons and attaining the partial truth—this is the meditation of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).

4. Penetrating the two types of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—and practicing—this is the meditation of the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*). The four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*) refer to the meditative absorptions attained in the four heavens of the formless realm.

[Also: (1) the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space; (2) the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness; (3) the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness; (4) the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These four belong to the formless heavens of the empty realm; hence they are called the "four formless absorptions. *Ānāpāna* [is explained as seen previously].

Regarding the "contemplation of the sixteen aspects" (*ṣoḍaśākāra-vipaśyanā*), the *Śāstra* states: "The first stage of the roots is called the 'Dharma of Heat' (*uṣmagata*). This is a specific form of the mindfulness-establishment (*smṛtyupasthāna*) that takes the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena as its object.

When practiced in this way, it can burn the fuel of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and serves as the precursor to the fire of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), like the stage of drilling for fire where the initial heat is produced. It is able to fully observe the objects of the Four Noble Truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*). By virtue of this, one fully cultivates the sixteen aspects and is able to proceed toward the [Four Noble Truths]."

Because it is the actual principle, it is called "practice" (*saṃskāra*). Alternatively, it is named after the principle itself; these are the sixteen aspects of the truths (*satya*). First, regarding the four aspects observed under the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*): 1. Impermanence (*anitya*): because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arise and perish anew through causes and conditions. 2. Suffering (*duḥkha*): because one observes that the five aggregates are oppressed by impermanence. 3. Emptiness (*śūnya*):

because within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), neither a single characteristic nor distinct characteristics exist. 4. Non-self (*anātman*): because within the five aggregates of clinging, a self (*ātman*) or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*) cannot be found. Second, regarding the four aspects observed under the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*): 1. [The first aspect...]

1. Accumulation (*samudaya*): The defilements (*kleśa*) and outflows (*āsrava*) that are capable of summoning the fruit of suffering. 2. Cause (*hetu*): Contemplating the six causes as they produce the fruit of suffering is called the practice of cause (*hetu-carita*). 3. Condition (*pratyaya*): Contemplating the four conditions as they produce the fruit of suffering is called the practice of condition (*pratyaya-carita*). 4. Arising (*jāti*): Because one again receives the body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) in a future existence.

3. Contemplating the four aspects (*ākāra*) under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*): 1. Exhaustion (*kṣaya*): Contemplating the exhaustion of all varieties of suffering in *nirvāṇa*. 2. Cessation (*nirodha*): Contemplating the extinction of the fire of the defilements in *nirvāṇa*. 3. Sublimity (*praṇīta*): Because *nirvāṇa* is the foremost among all phenomena.

4. *Nissaraṇa* (Renunciation): Because *nirvāṇa* is the departure from the worldly phenomena of birth and death. 4. Regarding the four aspects (*ākāra*) of the Path Truth (*mārgasatya*): 1. *Mārga* (Path): That is, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), which can lead to *nirvāṇa*. 2. *Nyāya* (Rightness): The thirty-seven factors are not inverted (*aviparīta*) phenomena.

3. *Pratipad* (Practice/Track): The thirty-seven factors are the destination reached by all noble ones (*ārya*). 4. *Nairyāṇika* (Leading out/Conveyance): Because the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) can transport the practitioner to the three doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*). In summary, one contemplates the Four Noble Truths by cultivating these four aspects.

Four times four makes sixteen aspects of contemplation (*ṣoḍaśākāra*). Having cultivated this stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), the practitioner next gives rise to the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*). This is like a mountain peak where a person does not remain long; if no obstacles arise, one will surely pass over this mountain and reach that mountain beyond. If obstacles are encountered, one immediately regresses. If no obstacles arise, one will certainly reach the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*). Once one has entered the stage of Patience, because one is extremely capable of enduring the objects of the Four Noble Truths, one next gives rise to the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), as it is preeminent within the mundane world. Thus, one contemplates the objects of the Four Noble Truths by practicing the sixteen aspects of contemplation in their entirety, gradually approaching the roots of goodness for the vision of the truths. Immediately thereafter, taking the objects of the Noble Truths of the desire realm as its focus, one gives rise to the "Dharma-patience of the outflow-free state" (*anāsravadharmakṣānti*). This patience is called "Dharma-knowledge" (*dharmajñāna*). [End of] Part One. Part Two. Lower Section. First. Chapter on the Path of Seeing. First. 2. A soft and supple voice; 3. A harmonious and agreeable voice; 4. A voice of venerable wisdom; 5. A voice not effeminate; 6. An unerring voice; 7.

knowing the meanings of all phenomena and penetrating them with complete clarity. 2. Eloquence of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*): distinguishing the names and designations of all phenomena without obstruction. 3. Eloquence of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*): explaining and speaking without hindrance, enabling each person to attain understanding. 4. Eloquence of joyful exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*): [the ability to explain] the twelve divisions of the scriptures.

Sūtra (teaching according to the faculties and natures of beings). Talent refers to skillfully responding to the capacities of sentient beings. Second, harmonious speech (the opposite of the former, double-tongued speech). This results from having previously created verbal karma.
Due to a lack of wisdom and eloquence, he now speaks only words of reconciliation and mutual benefit;

Apart from the sentient-being mind, there is no separate Buddha; therefore, there is only speaking and no listening. 3. Both speaking and listening coexist, because the mind and the Buddha do not obstruct the manifestation of sentient beings. 4. Both speaking and listening are quiescent, for the sentient being and the Buddha are mutually identical, mutually negating and mutually vanishing.

Furthermore: 1. Sentient beings are entirely within the Buddha-mind; thus, the Dharma is encompassed through the gate of fruition (phala) without exception. 2. Sentient beings and the Buddha are mutually expansive, as cause and effect penetrate one another. 4. Sentient beings and the Buddha are mutually negating, as the two positions are equally fused. The ritual: three invocations and three prostrations. That we do not do so now is because we have not yet mastered the meaning of the words.

First, the preceding section is concluded; now, the subsequent section begins. The text is divided into six parts, the first of which concerns the eye organ (*cakṣurindriya*).

Regarding the forms encountered by the eye, there are two types: first, insentient forms; second, sentient beings. Precious playthings and jeweled ornaments are "respected forms.

Or the ear may crave pleasant sounds—the notes of the pentatonic scale, stringed instruments, pipes, and flutes, or the singing and music of performers;

By the merit of this repentance of the faculty of the tongue, I pray that this tongue may always partake of the food of the joy of Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna.
4. Not craving the flavor of the blood and flesh of sentient beings. 5. The merit of the faculty of the tongue:
among the five kinds of food, the two foods of Dharma-joy (*dharma-prīti*) and the bliss of meditation (*dhyāna-prīti*) are supreme (the *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "There are five supramundane foods:

the food of the bliss of meditation, the food of aspiration, the food of mindfulness, the food of liberation, and the food of Dharma-joy"; the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Although one consumes food, one takes the bliss of meditation as one's sustenance"). One does not crave the blood of sentient beings.
When the flesh is removed, the foul odor vanishes and the nectar is attained.
By the merit of repenting for the faculty of the body, I vow that this body shall don the robe of the Tathāgata and wear the armor of patience.
Reclining on the bed of fearlessness, sitting upon the seat of the dharma-emptiness.
Five: the merit of the faculty of the body. Cultivating the Tathāgata’s dharma of quiescent extinction possesses the sense of being "worn" (adorned), and is therefore like clothing.
Patience has the sense of being "firm," and is therefore like armor—armor being golden mail. To dwell among the multitude without fear is peace and bliss.

The meaning is as follows. Thus, as stated in the "Dharma Master" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "One should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat;

only then should one extensively expound this sūtra for the fourfold assembly. The Tathāgata’s chamber is the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings. The Tathāgata’s robe is the mind of gentleness and forbearance. The Tathāgata’s seat is the emptiness of all phenomena. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that when a great bodhisattva bestows a bed:
May all sentient beings obtain the bed upon which the God among Gods lies; may they attain great wisdom and sit in the station of the four *dhyānas*;

may they lie upon the bed where Bodhisattvas lie, obtaining the bed of peace and stability, the bed apart from birth and death, the bed of great *nirvāṇa*, the lion’s reclining bed, the unsurpassed bed, the bed of patience, the bed of fearlessness, the bed of purity, the bed of wholesome dharmas, and the bed of reclining on the right side.

The four *ārūpya-dhyānas* are the concentration of stillness; therefore, they are like a seat. (The *Cittabhūmi-parivarta* says: "Bodhisattvas of superior capacity always sit long in the open air without lying down; Bodhisattvas of middling capacity always sit without lying down among branches and leaves; Bodhisattvas of inferior capacity... )
Within the stone chamber, he constantly sat and did not lie down. Thus, these three types of root-ordained bodhisattvas sit upon three kinds of seats (the rest as explained in the sutra).
By the merit of this repentance of the mental faculty, may this mind achieve the ten powers and penetrate the five sciences.
6. Deeply contemplate the two truths and the principle of the equality of emptiness. The merit of the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*):
the faculty of mind perceives with subtle clarity, like seeing within a dark chamber. The Ten Powers (detailed below in the section on the Ten Powers and Fearlessnesses).

May one wish for the accomplishment of the faculty of mind. Regarding the five sciences (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*), the *Mahā-śāstra* states: First, the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*; explaining glossaries, defining characters, and classifying terminology).

2. Śilpakarmasthānavidyā (the science of arts and crafts, including mechanics, astrology, and calendrical calculations); 3. Cikitsāvidyā (the science of medicine, including incantations, exorcism, pharmacology, and acupuncture); 4. Hetuvidyā (the science of logic).

(V. Examining the heterodox and the orthodox; investigating the true and the false. Five: Inner Science (*adhyātma-vidyā*) (thoroughly elucidating the five vehicles and the subtle principles of cause and effect).

Regarding these five sciences, one wishes for the fundamental faculties to penetrate and fully comprehend them (the Bodhisattva of the fifth stage awakens to the five inner sciences; as for the five outer sciences, the first four are the same, while the fifth is called the science of seals and signs). Regarding the two truths: First, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Within the gate of Buddha-activity, not a single dharma is abandoned—such as exhorting ministers to loyalty, sons to filial piety, states to order, and families to harmony; promoting goodness by demonstrating the bliss of heaven, and rectifying evil by revealing the [retributions of] hell.

The sufferings of the hells are all conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Second is ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which reveals the principle of primordial quiescence. In this single nature, all is harmoniously integrated; on the ground of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a single speck of dust can be received.

It points out that the myriad existents are themselves True Suchness (*tathatā*) and brings the three vehicles back to the ground of reality. All these rely upon ultimate truth. One should aspire to contemplate deeply both these two truths and the principle of the equality of emptiness.

(The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The two truths are in reality one; they are spoken of as two as a skillful means (*upāya*). It is like a person who is intoxicated and has not yet sobered up, who sees the sun and moon revolving and thus speaks of a 'revolving sun' and a 'non-revolving sun. A sober person sees only the non-revolution, not the revolution. The duality of revolution is coarse; non-revolution is subtle.

Regarding the principle of the equality of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samatā-tattva*): In the analytical contemplation (*vibhanga-vipaśyanā*) of the Hīnayāna, this is a conceptual construction (*manasikāra*). One first destroys the attachment to a personal self (*pudgala-grāha*), next destroys the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), and only thereafter enters into the principle of the equality of emptiness.

In the contemplation of essence (*svabhāva-vipaśyanā*) of the Mahāyāna, there is no distinction between person and phenomena, and emptiness is not sequential; therefore, it is called "equality. Nevertheless, it is through the emptiness of equality that one realizes the principle of equality. When both person and phenomena are empty, it is called "universal emptiness" (*ubhaya-śūnya*). Universal emptiness...

It is also emptiness (i.e., the emptiness of equality). Through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), one transforms the path, bringing emptiness into the provisional (*saṃvṛti*). When the contemplations of the Path flow together as two currents, this is "the dual flow," which is precisely equality. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"If bodhisattvas cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, and equanimity and attain the stage of the 'only child,' when they cultivate the mind of equanimity, what stage do they further attain? Answer: When cultivating the mind of equanimity, they dwell in the stage of the equality of emptiness.

Just as Subhūti dwells in the stage of the equality of emptiness, he does not perceive the existence of six types of relatives, acquaintances, or those who are hateful and disliked; nor does he perceive the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense bases (*āyatana*), sentient beings, or the life-span. This is because, like empty space, there are no six types of relatives and so forth. Thus, all things are [empty].

All dharmas are likewise; their mind is equanimous, like that empty space. Why is this? Because they have skillfully cultivated the emptiness of all dharmas. From this one emptiness, there arise eleven kinds of emptiness and so forth. When a bodhisattva attains these eleven emptinesses, they abide in the stage of the equality of emptiness. As the *Huayan shu* says:
"The myriad practices are cultivated in unison through the transcendence of both extinction and illumination; the sudden and the gradual are entered simultaneously without obstruction."

From the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*), one enters the stream of the Dharma, increasing in clarity from moment to moment and manifesting the Tathāgata’s great patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

[The circulating edition adds the four characters: "arising of the ten wondrous practices. "Skillful means" refers to the provisional (*upāya*); "entering the Dharma" refers to the real (*bhūta*). (Because one is endowed with the ten powers, the five sciences, the two truths, and so forth, this constitutes the wisdom of skillful means rather than dry wisdom.

Regarding the ten wondrous practices: first, the non-duality of form and mind is the wondrous practice of the object; second, the non-duality of internal and external is the wondrous practice of wisdom; third, the non-duality of cultivation and nature is the wondrous practice of conduct; fourth...)

1. The non-duality of cause and effect is the sublime practice of position (*sthāna*). 2. The non-duality of the fivefold defilement and purity is the sublime practice of the Dharma (*dharma*). 3. The non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) is the sublime practice of resonance and response (*prabhāva*). 4. The non-duality of self and other is the sublime practice of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). 5. The non-duality of the three karmas (*trikarma*) and 6.

the non-duality of the provisional and the real—these two are both the sublime practice of preaching the Dharma (*deśanā*). 7. The non-duality of receiving nourishment is the sublime practice of benefiting others (*anuśaṃsā*), which includes the sublime practice of [benefiting] one's retinue.

Because they are non-dual, they are called "sublime" (*praṇīta*). Because of sublime wisdom (*prajñā*)—which is profound and signless (*animitta*)—one is able to give rise to sublime practices. Furthermore, wisdom belongs to the mind, while skillful means (*upāya*)...

This is liberation. Regarding persons, there are four permutations for analysis: 1. Those liberated by wisdom but not liberated in mind are the followers of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas).
2. Those not liberated by wisdom but liberated in mind are Bodhisattvas. 3. Those liberated in both ways are Buddhas. 4. Those liberated in neither way are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Regarding those who have entered the stream of the Dharma-water, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The craving for desire is parched and dried up; the faculties and their objects do not meet; it is purely wisdom."

Wisdom. When one’s wisdom is dry, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*). The habit-energies of desire are initially dried up, yet one has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma-flow. At this point, by means of this very mind, one flows into the perfect and wondrous; delusive thoughts are extinguished, and the Middle Way becomes purely true—this is called the Abiding in Faith (*śraddhā-vihāra*).

One is then able to give rise to the ten wondrous practices and connect with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma-flow; this is what is meant by "flowing into the perfect and wondrous. As for "Great Forbearance regarding Non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*): "Non-arising" refers to the dharma that is neither born nor extinguished.
As for calling it "forbearance," it is because this dharma is on the verge of being realized but has not yet been realized, much like enduring a matter [before its resolution].
Because it is neither retained nor emitted, this patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) is the unsurpassed Dharma of the Tathāgata; therefore, it is called "Great.
Through the progressive illumination of every thought-moment, the Great Patience regarding Non-arising is manifested from this.
Having made the vow, one takes refuge by paying homage to the Triple Gem.
Concluding the preceding section on the nature [of the practice], once the recitation of the repentance text is finished, one should immediately conclude with the Three Refuges.
Record of What Was Heard Regarding the Middle Volume of the *Compassionate Water Repentance Method* (Cibei Shuichanfa).
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Zhuzhong Zhizheng of Qingluo Hermitage in Gulu.
Record of What Was Heard Regarding the Lower Volume of the *Compassionate Water Repentance Method*. Recorded by the Śramaṇa Zhuzhong Zhizheng of Qingluo Hermitage in Gulu.
All Buddhas, out of compassion for sentient beings, have expounded the general dharmas of the Water Repentance Ritual. Now, we take refuge in all Buddhas.
Homage to Vairocana Buddha! Homage to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha!
Homage to Amitābha Buddha. Homage to Maitreya Buddha.
Homage to Dragon-Seed Supreme Honored King Buddha. Homage to Dragon Sovereign King Buddha.
Homage to Jewel-Victorious Buddha. Homage to Awakened Flower Samādhi Sovereign King Buddha.
Homage to the Buddha Kāṣāyadhvaja. Homage to the Buddha Siṃhanāda.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. Homage to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Homage to the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha; homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Vairocana means "Pervading All Places"; it is the Dharmakāya. It is also translated as "Universal Radiance," referring to the Saṃbhogakāya.
Śākyamuni means "Able Sage" or "Silent One"; it is the Nirmāṇakāya. As for the Dharmakāya...
The essence of the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) is the Response Body itself; it is the function of the Original Dharmakāya.
Since essence and function are one and the same, this is followed by Amitābha. Because he possesses the essence of immeasurable life, he is able to manifest the function of immeasurable light.
Through the function of immeasurable light, the essence of immeasurable life is revealed. This essence and this function penetrate both the past and the future; therefore—

This is followed by the Honored One who is to succeed as the Regent (Upapadya). Since the three bodies are now fully manifested and the three periods of time are mutually interpenetrating, this could not be achieved by any other than a courageous and noble one who has attained great mastery;

therefore, it is followed by the Most Honored King of the Dragon Seed (Nāgottama-rāja). This Dragon Seed is most supreme, manifesting transformations everywhere while maintaining complete sovereignty; therefore, it is followed by the Dragon...
O Sovereign King, possessing this wondrous essence and wondrous function, he is most honored and most noble, naturally transcending all other sages.

Therefore, he is followed by the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava. Such supreme and victorious essence and function both arise from wondrous samādhi and wondrous wisdom, from wondrous cause and wondrous fruit.
Cause and effect penetrate one another; beginning and origin are harmonized as one; principle and wisdom are identical as one.
Therefore, he is followed by the Buddha Awakening Flower Samādhi Sovereign King.
Only such persons of immense capacity can exhaust the defilements of worldly toil, erect the great banner of the Dharma, and cast out the heterodox to return to the orthodox;
thus, he is followed by the Buddha Kāṣāya Banner. Only those capable of establishing the Dharma banner may occupy the lion throne to preach the Great [Dharma].
The Dharma delivers the great masses; therefore, it is followed by Siṃhanāda Tathāgata.
One who wishes to deliver the world with the lion’s roar must be a person of great wisdom who pervades both heaven and earth and penetrates from antiquity to the present;
thus, it is followed by Mañjuśrī. Even if one possesses wisdom, if it is not adorned by great practice, it is like having eyes but no feet.
What can they accomplish? Therefore, this is followed by the Great Practice of Samantabhadra;

thus, eyes and feet assist one another, and oil and light depend upon each other, naturally becoming fully endowed with vast virtue and function. With every step raised and taken, the dens of Māra are shattered.
Therefore, this is followed by Mahāsthāmaprāpta. All of this arises from their firm and profound vows and their encompassing wisdom and virtue. Thus it is said:
This is followed by Kṣitigarbha (Dizang). As described above, his great wisdom, great practice, great function, and great vows are not something possessed separately outside of his nature;
they are entirely the wondrous essence of the vastness of self-nature, giving rise to the boundless wondrous function that responds to all things.
Thus, he adorns the ocean of nature and perfects the three bodies (trikāya); for this reason, he is followed by Mahāvyūha (Dazhuangyan). Nevertheless, although he possesses these...
The great compassion that is unconditional and the great pity that is of one essence with all beings: within this, not even the slightest dharma can be found.
Though one were to spend eons as vast as the sands of the Ganges, traverse countless lands, and deliver immeasurable beings, one would never have moved or touched so much as a single hair’s breadth.
Therefore, it is followed by Avalokiteśvara. Thus Yongjia said: "Not seeing a single dharma is the Tathāgata; only then does one receive the name."
Regarding the Avalokiteśvara-ear: A monk asked Zen Master Zhaoxian, "The bodies of all the sages are identical;
why are their names each different? He replied: "Returning to the source from the locus of the eye-faculty is called Mañjuśrī. Returning to the source from the ear-faculty is named Avalokiteśvara.
Returning to the source from the mind is named Samantabhadra. Mañjuśrī is the Buddha’s wondrous wisdom of observation; Samantabhadra is the Buddha’s..."

The wondrous conduct of non-action; Avalokiteśvara is the Buddha’s unconditioned great compassion. These three sages are the Buddha’s wondrous function, and the Buddha is the true essence of these three sages.
As for their function, there are sands-of-the-Ganges-like provisional names; as for their essence, they are collectively named the One Buddha. Question:
What kind of vows must a practitioner make, and what kind of Buddha must they become? Answer: To become a Buddha where no Buddha exists.
The Buddhas who have already attained realization are as described above; these are the ten Buddhas. The nature and vows that all Buddhas must inevitably fulfill are as described above;
these are the six Bodhisattvas. Question: Regarding the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the two lands, East and West, what is their relationship as principal and retinue?
Answer: In the Eastern Land, Śākyamuni is the principal, while Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra serve as his retinue and his vows.
"I pray that you will save the land of Eastern Zhendan. In the West, Amitābha is taken as the principal; Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta serve as his attendants and objects of aspiration.

These attendants of the Western Sage are intended to save the eastern lands. Although there is thus a distinction between the principal and attendants of the East and West, all take the arousal of the bodhicitta as their fundamental principle.
This mind takes wisdom, compassion, and the vow as its essence—just like Mañjuśrī.
Avalokiteśvara is wisdom; Guanyin is compassion; Samantabhadra and Kṣitigarbha are the Kings of Vows. The rest is as explained previously. Question:
The Three Jewels are the hearts of sentient beings, surpassing the hearts of parents for their children.
Why is it that some today fail to revere the Triple Gem and instead give rise to contempt and envy? Answer: It is because they do not believe in cause and effect. [This was] once seen by King Aśoka.
The *Avadāna-sūtra* states: Once, a traveler saw a corpse by the roadside, upon which a celestial deity was scattering flowers and stroking it with his hand.
The traveler asked for the reason, and the deity replied: "This was my former body.

In a previous life, I revered the Triple Gem, was filial toward my parents, loyal to my sovereign, and trustworthy toward my friends; I cherished the teachings of my father and teachers, which has caused me [to attain this state]."
He was reborn in heaven; therefore, he has come to repay his debt of gratitude. As he proceeded further, he saw another corpse being whipped by an evil spirit.

He also asked the reason for this. The spirit said, "This was my former body. In life, I slighted and deceived the Triple Gem, and I was unfilial and disloyal, committing various kinds of wrongful acts.
This caused me to undergo this evil retribution, and so I have come to whip it. Since this is the case, why does each [retribution] not reach its respective perpetrator?"
Cease your worldly activities. Diligently exert yourself and pay respectful homage to the Triple Gem; will you not thereby preemptively eliminate all future regrets?
Having paid homage to the Buddhas, next perform the repentance of the three actions of body and four actions of speech.
Having completed the repentance for these, next perform the repentance for all obstacles that arise between [oneself and] the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
"Having already repented" (*yǐ chàn*) below concludes the preceding six sense organs and subsumes them within the characters for body and speech. Next, "furthermore" (*cì fù*) below has two meanings:
first, it takes up the remaining "obstacles" (*zhàng*) from the preceding section to initiate what follows; second, it enumerates the various obstacles interspersed among the Three Jewels.
In the sutras, the Buddha said: "A human body is difficult to obtain; the Buddha-dharma is difficult to hear; the Sangha is difficult to encounter; faith is difficult to generate;
the six sense faculties are difficult to possess in their entirety; and virtuous friends are difficult to find."
Citing the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* to indicate the root of the cessation of hindrances, the *Vaipulya Sūtra* states:

While the Buddha was resting with Ānanda, he took some soil from the ground with his fingernail and asked, "Is the soil on my nail more, or is the soil of the great earth more? Ānanda replied, "The soil on the nail is extremely small;
the soil of the earth is infinite. The Buddha said, "Those who obtain a human body are like the soil on the nail; those who lose their human body [are like the soil of the earth]."
It is like the soil of the great earth. When the Buddha went to a melon garden, he took a pinch of soil from under his fingernail as an analogy;

it is just like this. Consider that human birth is difficult to obtain—this statement is most worthy of sober reflection. Be careful not to let it slip by. The Buddha-dharma is difficult to hear, and even more so is the meeting with a Buddha in the world.

The True Dharma is difficult to hear (referring to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*). The Eastern Heavenly King says that for one hundred and eighty *kalpas* there has been no Buddha; the Southern King says it has been over one hundred and thirty *kalpas*; the Upper King says that in the past, throughout immeasurable *kalpas*, time passed in vain without a Buddha;

and it is further said that even across immeasurable lands, the name of this sutra could not be heard. Now that we have finally heard it, how fortunate we are! The Sangha is difficult to encounter—specifically those who uphold the precepts and propagate the Dharma.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "If the five precepts are not observed, the path to the human and celestial realms is cut off."
The five precepts are firmly maintained; thus humans and devas intersect. Having already obtained a human body and encountered the Triple Gem, it is truly lamentable not to practice at this time.
Faith is difficult to engender; one should therefore engender the mind of faith, the mind of observing the precepts, and so forth.
The six sense faculties are difficult to possess in their entirety; now, fortunately, they are complete. Possessing them yet failing to practice—when else shall we wait?

A virtuous friend; a spiritual benefactor (as the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "In all that one does, one seeks not personal pleasure, but always acts for the sake of sentient beings; one does not merely practice the ten wholesome paths oneself, but also leads others to practice goodness").
Now, we have together planted roots of goodness in past lives, obtained these human bodies with all six sense faculties intact, and furthermore encountered virtuous friends to hear the True Dharma.
Yet, in the midst of this, each of us has failed to exert ourselves with a wholehearted diligence;
we fear that in the future we shall sink long into myriad sufferings with no time of escape. For this reason, today we seek compassion and repent with utmost sincerity.
The preceding statement spoke generally of what is difficult to obtain; this passage clarifies that all of these have been obtained. One should prepare for the Path while there is still time.

Because of having planted roots of goodness in the past, one has now obtained a human body with its six sense faculties complete. That which was difficult to obtain has been obtained; that which was difficult to possess has been possessed.
Furthermore, one encounters virtuous friends and hears the True Dharma; thus, that which is difficult to encounter has been encountered, and that which is difficult to hear has been heard.

Yet, if one cannot exhaust one’s mental and physical strength to apply diligent effort with the five limbs [of prostration], I fear that in the future one will long remain submerged in manifold sufferings, and the time of liberation will be difficult to determine.

(The phrase "cannot exhaust one's mind" contrasts with the aforementioned "having planted roots of goodness in past lives," and connects through to the following six sections. Therefore, the following section concludes the preceding brief explanation.

The cause for the arising of obstacles. Below, the matters concerning the arising of obstacles are extensively set forth in three parts. First, the specific repentance for karmic obstacles incurred between encounters with the Buddhas:
(Name), from beginningless time until this day, my mind has been constantly shrouded by ignorance and my will obstructed by afflictions;
thus, upon seeing the physical forms and images of the Buddhas, I have been unable to offer complete reverence and respect.
Seeing images of the Triple Gem and failing to prostrate or make offerings; immediately prostrating [only] to the second [of the three]; being irreverent in these two types of action;
showing contempt for the Sangha; harming virtuous friends; destroying stupas and monasteries; burning scriptures and images; and shedding the blood of a Buddha.

The text is divided into five parts. First, "slighting the Sangha. "Mie" means to treat with contempt or to look down upon (as in the *Yangzi*: "By observing the sun and moon, one knows that the myriad stars are insignificant"). Now, as for the Sangha:
They are the disciples of past Buddhas and the causes for future Buddhas; how can they be treated with contempt? Second, regarding arrogance toward the Way:
it is difficult to find virtuous friends, yet one instead harms them. "Harms" (can) means to plunder; as the *Mencius* says, "one who robs righteousness is called a plunderer.

Third, destroying stūpas and monasteries. Fourth, burning scriptures and images. Scriptures are the Dharma-body of all Buddhas; images are the physical manifestations of all Buddhas. Now, having seen the Way...
When the ritual is completed, it is customary to consign [the remains] to fire; however, this is truly inappropriate. Therefore, Yunqi prohibited it.
Fifth is shedding the blood of the Buddha, such as when Devadatta pushed a mountain to crush the Buddha, or instances such as scraping gold from the Buddha’s face.

Or they may dwell themselves in a magnificent hall, yet place the honored image in a lowly and filthy spot, subjecting it to smoke and sun, wind and rain, dust and filth, and damage from sparrows and rats;
living and sleeping together with it, they never show it even a single act of reverence.
Lowly: dwelling in a damp and low-lying place; whereas one’s own residence is a lofty tower or magnificent pavilion.

Vulgar: dwelling in a crowded and impure place; whereas one’s own residence is a splendid hall or beautiful mansion. Or, being near a hearth, one is smoked by fumes; lacking repairs, one is scorched by the sun or buffeted by the wind.
Or, lacking shelter, one is drenched by rain and dew; or being near a workshop, one is defiled by dust and dirt. Or...
The palace gates remained closed for many days. Consequently, during the day flying birds would damage [the offerings], and at night running rats would ruin them.
Sometimes images were kept within the rooms, and sometimes mats were spread before the images; thus, those who lived and slept together never showed any reverence, leaving the items exposed.

It is also written as 曬. That which is light and scattered in the earth is called *chen* (dust). That which is heavy, thick, and accumulated is called *tu* (earth). Both are capable of staining, defiling, covering, and obscuring.
*Dùn* (pronounced *pén* with a departing tone) refers to the scattering of dust. To dwell together [with others] without performing acts of reverence means that one’s etiquette is deficient.

(The *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisūtra* states, in the verse of the Great Brahmā King worshipping the Buddha’s shadow: "The Tathāgata dwells in the sun-cave; leaping his body into the heart of stone, he is like the sun, unobstructed.")
Endowed with the marks of golden light, I now prostrate my head in worship to the Muni, the World-Honored Savior. If even the Buddha’s shadow is to be revered, how much more so his image!
Or having left images exposed before them without initial adornment, shielding the lamps and candles, locking the temple gates,
and obstructing the Buddha’s radiance— such transgressions as these, today with utmost sincerity, I repent of them all.
Standing before the image, one remains naked and bare-bodied, never adorned with ornaments or finery; this is because they have been unable to exert themselves with total sincerity and diligence.

The term "yu" (宇) refers to the eaves extending from all four sides of a building. The first chapter concludes. Below is the second section: the distinct method of repentance for intervening offenses and hindrances.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day, whether amidst the Dharma, one has grasped sutra scrolls with impure hands,
or while facing scriptures and books, engaged in improper or worldly speech.
The Dharma refers to all the Buddha-dharmas of the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Regarding those with "unclean hands":
whether they have not yet washed their hair or body, or have just finished the small or large excretions, or have handled any defiled objects, they must all wash them until they are pure.
