Therefore, today with utmost sincerity, I take refuge in the Buddha and perform repentance according to the Dharma.
The preceding citations from the sutras serve as scriptural proof; this concludes the section on the intention of the Confession Master.
Below follows a detailed explanation of how various karmas flow forth from shamelessness and lack of remorse, consisting of seven parts.

We, [Name] and others, from time immemorial until this very day, have either believed in heterodox and inverted views, killing sentient beings or offering sacrifices to *chimei*, *wangliang*, ghosts, and spirits in the hope of prolonging our lives, yet we never attained such results;
or we have falsely claimed to see ghosts and feigned the words of deities. We now repent of all such transgressions.
I. Chapter on Erroneous and Perverted Views. *Jie* (pronounced as in *jie*) means to understand; it is superior to hearing (*wen*). *Zou* means to advance; it is superior to [mere] understanding.
*Chimei* refers to powerful ghosts—the essence of aged things and the anomalies of mountains and marshes. *Wangliang* refers to those who do not clearly perceive the True Suchness of the One Mind.
Because they do not clearly perceive the self-nature of True Suchness, they are called *wang*; because they do not realize that there is only this One Mind, they are called *liang*. They long for...

This is mere hope. To speak falsely of seeing ghosts and spirits—such as those who summon the dead to capture ghosts, or children and female shamans who allow spirits to possess them and utter chaotic words—is to borrow such means in the hope of attaining longevity.
Not only will one fail to obtain the wish for increased years, but one will moreover find it difficult to escape the sufferings of hell.
Furthermore, from beginningless time until this very day, we have perhaps acted with arrogance and conceit, being haughty and self-important;

or, relying on our lineage, we have treated all others with contempt, looking down upon the lowly because of our own nobility, and bullying the weak because of our strength; or we have indulged in drinking and incited strife.
I do not avoid intimacy or estrangement; I remain muddled and intoxicated all day long, failing to recognize the honorable from the lowly.

For such transgressions as these, I now repent them all. Second: Arrogance and Falsehood. His arrogance and false boasting were not merely held in his heart, but were manifested through his four limbs;
thus it is said they were "in his conduct. With an empty stomach and haughty eyes, his mind looked down upon the four seas. Those who rely on their lineage... relying on—
It is due to the pride of one's noble lineage that the honorable slight the lowly and the strong deceive the weak;

that the many oppress the few—all these arise from arrogance and a lack of reverence, from boastfulness and a lack of humility. Regarding those who drink alcohol, the Sūtras state: "The transgressions are immeasurable;
yet merely passing a vessel of wine to another brings the retribution of being born without hands for five hundred lifetimes, let alone drinking it oneself or inciting others to do so."
Do people drink [alcohol]? There are thirty-six faults, as clarified in the preceding fascicle; they are now briefly set forth here. As it is said:

it is the root of strife and contention, the source of illness. It causes one to beat servants without cause, to kill living beings wantonly, to commit adultery with the wives of others, to steal another's property, to be unfilial toward one's parents, to distance oneself from virtuous people, and to harbor constant anger day after day.
They are filled with anxiety at night. They do not revere the Triple Gem and treat their teachers and elders with contempt; these may be understood by correlating them in order.
Alternatively, they indulge in food and drink without moderation, or eat raw fish and minced meat, or consume the five pungent herbs, thereby defiling and polluting the scriptures and images.
I have treated the pure assembly with contempt, acting according to my own whims and desires without knowing any limits; I have distanced myself from virtuous people and befriended evil companions.
All such transgressions, I now fully repent.
III. Chapter on Moderation in Food and Drink. *Kuài*: finely sliced meat. The Five Pungent Roots (*pañca-gandha*):
as stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*: 1. Garlic; 2. *Gècōng* (i.e., leeks and scallions); 3. *Cícōng* (i.e., common onions); 4. *Láncōng* (i.e., garlic); 5. *Xīngqú* (i.e., coriander).
There are five faults in consuming pungent roots (from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*): 1. Excessive Faults: eating them cooked arouses lust; eating them raw increases anger.
2. The gods are distant; even if they were able to preach the Dharma, the various devas would remain far removed. 3. The ghosts are near;
the ghosts lick their lips and mouths, and they constantly dwell with ghosts. 4. Merit is exhausted; one's blessings and virtues diminish daily, resulting in no long-term benefit. 5. Māras gather;

Māras come to preach the Dharma, reviling the prohibitions and precepts, and attacking the pure assembly. The foul odor of the five pungent vegetables, having already permeated and defiled the Buddha...
The Dharma, as well as pure karma and virtuous friends, are disregarded by the two lines concerning the unrestrained mind; these express the lack of any expectation for deliverance.
The two lines concerning remoteness express the reason for indulging in food and drink.
Whether through arrogance and hypocrisy, obstinacy and self-will, or through lawlessness and insolence, failing to recognize human feelings,
regarding oneself as right and others as wrong, or harboring hopes for mere luck— now I repent of all such transgressions.

4. To covet through inferiority; to boast of one's own talent while being arrogant toward others is called *gònggāo* (haughty pride). To use force and indulge in hypocrisy to deceive others is called *jiǎojiè* (pretension).
*Yǎnjiǎn* refers to arrogance; the *Zuǒzhuan* states it means "arrogance and haughtiness. It describes an appearance of self-elevation and self-importance.
*Báhù* (跋扈) means to be stubborn and defiant. Those who dwell by the water, before the water has risen, construct bamboo fences to wait for the fish.
When the water recedes, the small fish remain alone, while the large fish leap over the *bá* and *hù* of the fence and escape.

This clarifies relying on one's own strength to assert oneself. *Dǐchù* (抵觸) means to strike against or resist. *Tù* (揬) is synonymous with *tóngtù* (傏揬); both signify being contrary to principle or reason. It denotes harboring expectations.
"Zhe" (者) means to hope for and look toward the grace of virtue. "Jiao" (僥) means to seek. "Xing" (倖) refers to obtaining what one ought not to obtain.
This refers to those who, when facing wealth, do not yield; who lack integrity and feel no shame in slaughtering livestock, selling liquor, and deceiving others for their own livelihood.

5. Chapter on Lack of Integrity and Shame. "No yielding when facing wealth" means that in speech one strives to be the first to take. When one sees gain and thinks only of profit, it deviates from righteousness;
it can be known that this harms integrity and cleanliness. What heart of shame could such a person possess? They are already close to the precept against stealing. Next.

Alcohol and meat form a pair. Slaughtered meat violates the precept against killing; selling alcohol violates the precept against drinking (as detailed in the Brahmajāla Sūtra and in the preceding commentary).
Next, as for the union of mind and speech: deception arises from the mind, while falsehood is uttered by the mouth.

Relying on these two evils to seek one’s own livelihood, one may engage in lending and interest, calculating profits by the hour and selling off the days. One accumulates wealth through stinginess and parsimony, greedily seeking more without satiety, and accepts offerings from others.

Nurturing [the mind] while being neither ashamed nor abashed forms a pair with the preceding section on "moderation regarding wealth. Regarding the lending of loans and the calculation of principal and interest: this is termed "income and expenditure" (chur-ru-pi-li).
Because the original capital can produce profit, it is called "interest" (hsi), just as parents can give birth to children; thus, the lending of loans is so named.

To take profit means that the monthly [earnings] do not exceed five [units], etc.; this is calculating by the hour and selling by the day, which serves only to nourish a greedy mind; hence it is said, "to accumulate by subtraction.
"One who greedily seeks without satiety" means one whose scheming never ceases (as in the *Zuozhuan*:

"Lord Yu possessed jade, and Lord Gong asked for it. He offered it. Lord Gong asked for his precious sword again. Lord Yu said, 'This is to be insatiable'"). The Great Sūtra says: "To provide for the Sangha is to provide for the Triple Gem"; people follow [this principle].
The Buddha said: "One makes offerings to the Buddha for the sake of liberation; one makes offerings to the Dharma; and when the Sangha receives them, one makes offerings to the Sangha.
Yet there are those who lack the virtue of precepts and yet vainly accept the offerings of the faithful. All such transgressions, I now fully repent."

They possess no virtue of pure precepts whatsoever. They receive the offerings of the faithful in vain. Having committed the aforementioned acts of sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, lying, and drinking intoxicants, they live by means of deception; all of this is devoid of virtue.
Or they beat their slaves (the reading "dǐng" is used for "nú-dì"), and drive their servants (the Southern Canon reads "lì"); they inquire neither of hunger nor thirst, nor of cold nor heat.
Or they may destroy bridges and cut off roads. All such transgressions as these, I now repent. Six: *jiāxiāngduì* (家鄉對).
"Duì" means to strike or to encounter directly. According to the *Zhou Lǐ*, at fifteen one becomes a *tóng*; this is a general term for male and female servants.
There is hunger and thirst by day; there is cold and heat by the year. Is it right to employ laborers without inquiring into their circumstances or considering their strength?
Now, slaves are the children of others. Those who are masters should cherish them with the heart of nurturing a child;
those who are servants should also serve their masters with the heart of serving a father. In this way, each finds their proper place. As for now...
It is not that they wish to repay their debt of gratitude; rather, it is that the host has been excessively generous. Alas! To turn back and demand what was left over—what can one do about this?
Within the lanes and alleys, some cut down the great bridges to block the masses, while others remove the small beams to intercept the passage.
"Du" means to block. To block a thoroughfare is to cut off the path of travel.

Whether it be roads in cities or the countryside, whether the ground is covered with bricks and tiles or the path is overgrown with weeds, one must ensure that people of all ages find it inconvenient to walk or ride.

That which causes clothes to be soaked, socks to be wet, or shoes to be torn and boots destroyed—none of these are appropriate. In all matters that affect the human heart, such actions must never be undertaken.
Or they may be negligent and self-indulgent; indeterminate and distracted; playing dice and go; gathering in crowds and assemblies; consuming food, drink, wine, and meat;
mutually disturbing one another with farewells and partings; engaging in aimless chatter; and discussing the affairs of the world.
7. The Internal and External Correspondence: The Retribution of Heedlessness. A Great Sūtra states that there are thirteen retributions for heedlessness:
first, delighting in performing worldly activities; second, delighting in speaking useless words; third, constantly delighting in sleep;
fourth, delighting in discussing worldly affairs; fifth, constantly delighting in associating with evil friends; sixth, constantly delighting in indolence and laziness; seventh, constantly...
8. Being despised by others; 9. Forgetting what one has heard immediately after hearing it; 10. Delighting in dwelling in remote borderlands;
11. Being unable to subdue the sense faculties; 12. Causing a lack of contentment; 13. Not delighting in emptiness and stillness; 14.
Having incorrect views, being outwardly dissolute and inwardly self-indulgent; 15. The state of neutral indifference (*avyākṛta*), when one is dazed and muddled.
"Scattered and distracted" refers to times that are neither good nor evil. "Chuppu" (ch’u-p’u)—that is, *shuanglu* (double-sixes)—was invented by Laozi for use in divination;
nowadays people cast them as a game. "Weiqi" (wei-qi)—the Great Board Game—was created by Yao to instruct his son Danzhu, and Shun likewise used it to instruct his son Shangjun.
Its principles encompass squareness and roundness, motion and stillness; none but the wise can master it.

Confucius said: "Are there not those who engage in board games and dice? To do so is still better than idling away one's time. [The commentary] says: "This implies that there is a way of harm, deception, strife, and falsehood. There are three grades of prohibitions against drinking.
Superior: not passing wine vessels to others. Middling: not teaching others to drink. Inferior: not drinking oneself. There are ten faults in eating meat.
As the *Lan* (Overview) states: First, sentient beings are originally one’s own kin. Second, when sentient beings see those who eat meat, they are immediately struck with fear.
Third, it destroys the faith of others. Fourth, it diminishes the heart of compassion. Fifth, it increases the power of evil *rākṣasas*.

1. The habit-energy of the *kṣetra* (field). 2. Six [factors] that cause one to fail in the practice of incantations. 3. Regarding the bodies and lives of sentient beings as no different from one's own. 4.
Being abandoned by the devas and worthy sages, while being terrified by malevolent spirits. 5. That which issues from impurity. 6. Death and falling into the evil realms.

"Disturbing the guest and disturbing the host" (*rǎo kè rǎo zhǔ*): the host provides a send-off for the departing guest (*jiàn zhǔ*). (The term *jiàn* is used extensively; it refers to providing wine and food for travelers.)
From year to year, all was in vain; I have lost my days. Throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night, I did not cultivate meditation or recitation.
Indolent and lazy, I lay like a corpse all day long.
The first, middle, and last parts of the day constitute the three divisions of the day; the first, middle, and last parts of the night constitute the three divisions of the night.

This refers to what is called "when the day is insufficient, it is continued by the night. As the *Śāsanānuśāsana Sūtra* states: "During the day, one should diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas with a focused mind."
Do not let the time pass in vain; during both the first and last watches of the night, do not allow your practice to falter. During the middle watch, recite the sūtras to regulate yourself.
Do not, for the sake of sleep, allow this one life to pass empty-handed and without attainment.

*Dhyāna*—fully called *dhyāna*, here translated as "quiescence"—means to still the thoughts and forget external conditions, directly investigating one's own mind to achieve sudden awakening to non-arising.
"Recitation" refers to such practices as the recitation of mantras, the reading of sutras, and the mindfulness of the Buddha.
Because one does not cultivate these, one falls into the two maladies of torpor and distraction; is this not to waste one's days in vain and to pass the months and years in emptiness?
To lie like a corpse means to lie stiff like a dead body during the clear daylight; has one not heard of Confucius rebuking Zai Yu for this?

Regarding the six objects of mindfulness, his mind does not apply itself to them; upon seeing the superior achievements of others, he immediately gives rise to envy, harbors malice and cruelty in his heart, and fully arouses the afflictions.

The Six Recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). [Recollection is defined as focusing the mind with single-minded intent; this is from the *Mahāsūtra*. 1. Recollection of the Buddha: He is the compassionate Teacher (furthermore, he possesses the marks and signs of excellence, meritorious virtues, and the vow to manifest the Buddha-body). 2. Recollection of the Dharma:

It is the Mother of the Buddhas of the three periods of time (it is the rule for practice, capable of eliminating the fetters and afflictions, and it involves the vow to turn the wheel of the Dharma). 3. Recollection of the Saṅgha:

They are the field of merit for humans and devas (they possess various kinds of merit and act on behalf of the Buddha to transform and enlighten sentient beings). 4. Recollection of the Deva Realm: It is eternal life and peace (possessing all manner of wholesome karma, it results in [rebirth in] that realm).

One should mindfully recollect the Victorious Body and the All-Knowing One among the Gods of Full Heaven; this purifies body and mind, can extinguish all evils, accomplishes the factors of enlightenment, and fulfills all vows.
Contemplate giving: it universally relieves poverty (it can shatter stinginess and greed, grow the fruits of merit, and abandon all afflictions). As for "the mind not managing":
the mind does not attend to these six matters; instead of attending to and managing them, one simply yields to indolence, lacking any sense of alertness regarding superior matters.

This refers to such practices as investigating Chan, listening to the teachings, observing the precepts, and reciting the Buddha's name. To fail to practice these supportive activities and instead harbor jealousy is to forget one's fundamental nature;
it gives rise to all manner of afflictions, leading one to commit every kind of evil.
This causes fierce winds of evil to blow upon the firewood of transgressions, keeping it constantly ablaze without respite.

All subtle virtues of the three karmas are utterly consumed by this flame. Once all wholesome dharmas are exhausted, one becomes an icchantika and falls into the great hells, with no prospect of escape.
Therefore, today we offer our most earnest prayers and prostrate ourselves before the Triple Gem of the ten directions, repenting for all our faults.

"All evils" refers to the karma produced by the afflictions (*kleśa*), which does not go beyond the ten non-virtuous actions and so forth. The "mad winds of the afflictions" blow upon the fuel and fire of sinful evil.
"Slight goodness" does not go beyond the five precepts and the ten virtuous actions. When evil arises, goodness perishes; therefore, it is said that "both are burned.
*Icchantika*—this is translated as "lacking faith" (also called "one who has fallen away from the virtuous mind"). Thus, the following section concludes [the argument].
All the various transgressions committed throughout the past—whether light or heavy, coarse or subtle;
whether committed by oneself, incited in others, or rejoiced in;
whether forced through the use of power or even through praising those who practice unwholesome dharmas—I now, with sincere resolve, repent of them all.
To summarize the preceding text: "light" refers to minor good or evil deeds and the like; "heavy" refers to such things as the icchantikas falling into the great hells.
The rest is easily understood. This concludes the general presentation of repentance. Below follows the formulation of vows to accomplish virtue.
I pray that by virtue of the merit arising from all these evil deeds through this repentance, in birth after birth and life after life, I may be compassionate, harmonious, loyal, and filial;
humble and patient; possessing integrity and a sense of shame; and greeting others with words of inquiry before they have even spoken.

*Ci* (Compassion) translates the opposites of the preceding [Section 1] (killing sentient beings, etc.), Section 3 (eating raw meat and minced fish, etc.), Section 6 (beating and driving servants, etc.), and Section 7 (eating meat, disturbing others, and envying superior matters, etc.).

*He* (Harmony) translates the opposites of the preceding [Section 2] (arrogance, disdain, and inciting strife, etc.), Section 4 (recklessness and defiance), and Section 7 (inflicting cruelty and giving rise to all manner of afflictions, etc.).

*Loyalty* (*zhong*) translates the opposites of the preceding [Section 1] (false speech and claiming to see ghosts, etc.), Section 5 (deceiving others for one's own livelihood, etc.), and Section 6 (pulling down bridges and blocking roads, etc.). *Filial Piety* (*xiao*) [shares the same meaning as] the above *compassion*.
The same applies to humility. The Way arises from modesty and withdrawal; virtue arises from tranquility and harmony. As the Sūtra says: "Be humble toward all bhikṣus.
This stands in contrast to the former [sections]: Section Two, on arrogance, self-exaltation, and contempt for others; and Section Three, on intruding upon and disparaging the pure assembly.

Patience. This is the opposite of the preceding [Section 2: Quarreling and not avoiding kin or strangers]. Knowing integrity. This is the opposite of the preceding [Section 1: Soliciting favors; Section 4: Hoping for luck; Section 5:

Failing to yield when facing wealth and lacking integrity]. Greeting with a preemptive inquiry. In the "Detachment from the World" chapter (*Lokottara-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, among the ten kinds of hands possessed by Bodhisattvas, the third is the "Hand of Preemptive Inquiry.
It is so called because one extends the right palm to welcome and guide others.
This is the meaning of humility.

One should follow what is good, be upright and prudent, maintain purity, practice righteousness and yielding, distance oneself from evil companions, constantly encounter virtuous conditions, and restrain the six sensory faculties.
Guarding the three karmas, enduring toil and suffering with a mind that does not retreat or sink, one establishes the vow for Bodhi and does not fail sentient beings.

"Xun" (循) means to follow; "shun" (順) means to accord with; "liang" (良) means goodness; "zheng" (正) means uprightness; and "jin" (謹) means prudence and purity, which implies freedom from greed and defilement.

In practicing righteousness and yielding, one does not seek gain unscrupulously when facing wealth. To distance oneself from evil friends reverses the previous section on "Associating with Evil Friends.

To constantly encounter virtuous conditions reverses the previous description of how various evil winds blow upon the firewood of transgressions, causing the flames to blaze so that even subtle virtues are consumed.

To restrain the six *indriyas*—where *indriya* refers to the faculties, namely the six consciousnesses such as the eye-consciousness—is to prevent them from grasping at the six sense objects (*viṣaya*), thereby reversing the previous state.

The six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) are not merely words passing through the mind. One guards the three karmas (*trikarma*), does not indulge in the ten non-virtues (*daśākuśala*), and turns away from negligence and self-indulgence.
To withstand toil and endure suffering—*han* meaning "courageous" and referring to *vīrya* (diligence)—is to turn back the aforementioned laziness and indolence.

Establishing the vow for Bodhi is precisely the generation of the Bodhicitta. Since generating this mind necessarily entails delivering sentient beings, one does not fail [one's responsibility]. (Fangben)
To take up this burden.
Having made these vows, I take refuge and pay homage to all Buddhas (concluding the preceding and introducing what follows):
Namo Vairocana Buddha; Namo our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha. Homage to Maitreya Buddha.
Homage to Dragon-Seed Supreme Honored King Buddha. Homage to Dragon Sovereign King Buddha.
Homage to Jewel Victorious Buddha. Homage to Awakened Flower Samādhi Sovereign King Buddha.
Homage to the Buddha Kāṣāyadhvaja. Homage to the Buddha Siṃhanāda.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. Homage to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Homage to the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha; homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, I shall next perform repentance (concluding the preceding and initiating what follows).

Hitherto, I have already repented the affliction-obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the karma-obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*). As for the remaining retribution-obstructions (*vipākāvaraṇa*), I shall now proceed to disclose and repent them in their proper order.
First, I shall summarize both types of obstructions: those remaining in the subsequent fruits of rebirth, from the hells up to the asuras.

The evil realms, as well as the immeasurable remaining retributions among humans and devas, are all to be repented of in succession. (The Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "There are three kinds of remaining retribution: first, the remaining retribution of afflictions.

If a person habitually indulges in desire and the retribution ripens, they fall into hell. Upon emerging from hell, they receive the bodies of animals—pigeons, sparrows, mandarin ducks, parrots, blue jays, fish, turtles, monkeys, roe deer, and gazelles; these are such cases.)

If one obtains a human body, one receives two retributions: that of a eunuch or a woman, or being without sexual organs. Even if one succeeds in leaving the household life, one violates the first grave precept. If a person, with a mind of intense gravity, cultivates and draws near to anger, once the retribution ripens, they fall into hell.

Upon emerging from hell, they receive the body of an animal—such as a venomous snake, a lion, a tiger, a wolf, a hawk, or a falcon. If they obtain a human body, they are fully possessed of the sixteen evil modes of conduct. Even if they leave the household life, they violate the second grave precept.

If there is cultivation [of delusion] and the retribution of folly ripens, they fall into hell. Upon emerging from hell, they receive the body of an animal—such as the forms of an elephant, a pig, an ox, a sheep, a flea, a louse, a mosquito, or a gnat. If they obtain a human body, they are deaf, blind, mute, or dumb; they are humpbacked, crippled, or crooked; their faculties are incomplete, and they are unable to receive the Dharma. Even if...

Having left the household life, one’s faculties may be dull and dark, and one may frequently violate the heavy precepts, even down to the offense involving five coins. If one habituates oneself to arrogance, when the retribution ripens, one falls into hell. Upon emerging from hell, one receives the body of an animal—such as a dung-worm, a camel, a donkey, or a large horse.

Even if born among humans, one craves the status of a slave or servant, remaining impoverished and begging for alms. Even if one manages to leave the household life again, one is held in contempt by others and breaks the fourth precept. Such are the residual retributions of afflictions; only by cultivating and accumulating the Great Nirvāṇa can they all be severed and eliminated.

Once these are removed, all remaining karma becomes pure. (The term *pī* means to uncover or reveal; *chén* means to set forth or enumerate; it refers to recollecting one's past transgressions in order to seek repentance.)

The Sūtra says: "When the retribution for karma arrives, there is no place—neither in the void, nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering between the rocks of the mountains—where one may escape and not receive its fruit. Only through the power of repentance can it be eliminated."
This is a verse from the *Brahmaṇa-parivarta-maraṇa-parihāra-sūtra*. The Buddha said that there are two kinds of obstacles:

first, the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*); second, the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). If one possesses these two, one cannot be transformed [by the Dharma]. Formerly, four brothers studied the arts of the immortals and each attained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Knowing their own lifespans were ending, they sought to avoid death through their supernormal powers; one leaped into the air and hid himself.
As for physical forms: one may enter the great ocean, traveling three million six hundred and sixty thousand li, yet not reaching the bottom, remaining therein;
or one may split a mountain and hide one's form among the rocks, thinking that impermanence will come from nowhere to find them;
or one may conceal oneself within the earth—yet none of these can escape death. Those who enter the void fall to the ground like ripe fruit falling from a tree. Entering...
Those who go to sea die to be devoured by fish, like bait fallen into a river. Those who hide in the mountains die to be swallowed by beasts, like birds fed to hawks.
Those who enter the earth die like a *kṣa* or *gavaya* being overturned. Having observed and known this, the Buddha spoke of these four types of people.

Though one wishes to abandon past karmic retributions, the three poisons have not yet been eliminated; how can one avoid this affliction? (In both editions of the Canon, the character is "stone" [石]; there are those who have changed it to "market" [市], which I fear is an error.

The character for "retribution" [報] is "retribution"; in the original sutra, it is the character for "karma" [業]). "Direction" refers to the direction toward which one is heading. An ancient worthy said: "The Way has no fixed location; its illumination depends on the person.
The Dharma is beyond seeing and hearing; its realization depends on wisdom. Indeed, karma and retribution are the opposite of the Way; thus, one should also...

It is said: "Karmic retribution has no fixed location; liberation from it depends on the person. The Dharma is free from bondage and liberation; illuminating it depends on wisdom. How do we know this to be so?
Śakra Devānām-Indra manifested the five signs of decline; his heart was filled with intense fear, and he took refuge with sincerity in the Triple Gem.

By means of these five signs, one may extinguish [the karmic obstacles] and extend one's heavenly lifespan. Instances such as these, as clarified in the scriptural teachings, are not limited to a single case. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The five signs of decline for the devas are: the flowers upon their heads wither; sweat breaks out from under their armpits; their lower garments become stained with filth; their bodies emit foul odors; and they take no pleasure in their original seats. These are the great five signs of decline, the omens of certain death. Furthermore, it continues: ...and so forth. If one can contemplate these five signs of decline, one will immediately realize that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. By contemplating them in this way, one will give rise to the mind of renunciation, cultivate the path of liberation, and attain the fruit of Arhatship. This is called the "contemplation of the five signs of decline" (*pañca-vyasanāni*). It is said that even if one has committed the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), by contemplating these five signs of decline, one will be able to eradicate those grave offenses and attain the stage of non-retrogression. Therefore, one should constantly contemplate these five signs of decline. If one can practice this contemplation, one will surely attain liberation. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "If there are sentient beings who hear of these five signs of decline, they will immediately develop a heart of revulsion toward the world and seek the path of liberation. One should know that this is the supreme method for attaining liberation. Therefore, one must diligently cultivate this contemplation. A *yojana*—here translated as "limited measure" (corresponding to a postal station in this region)—is eighty *li* for the large, sixty *li* for the medium, and forty *li* for the small;

one *yojana* consists of these [units]. The fixed number of eighty-four thousand is because, by opposing the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates and entering the gates of worldly affliction (*rajas*), one incurs this retribution. This occurs through the five faculties encountering the five objects.
At that time, there are five hundred internal and external afflictions each, totaling one thousand. With seven branches for each, they become seven thousand.

When these are applied to the three periods of time, they amount to twenty-one thousand. Furthermore, when categorized by greed, hatred, delusion, and their equal distribution, they become eighty-four thousand.
Below the section on the three types of sinners, the physical dimensions of the Avīci Hell are explained; specifically, even a single person fills it to its full extent.
The people are also full; therefore it is called "pervasive" (*prabhūta*) and also "full" (*pūrṇa*).

Due to the causes and conditions of their karmic offenses, they do not obstruct one another. The fire from above penetrates below, and the fire from below penetrates above, extending to the east, west, south, and north.
They pass through and overlap one another like fish on a griddle; their fat and grease are entirely consumed. The suffering of sin within this place is likewise so.
Fourth, resolving objections: The Great Sutra says, "The wise contemplate the sufferings of hell—from a single hell up to one hundred and thirty-six hells.
Each individual hell has various kinds of suffering, all of which arise from the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma."
5. Next, one contemplates the sufferings of ghosts and animals, up to all the various sufferings of humans and devas;

these all arise from the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma. (This concludes five [points]. The phrase "fire above, fire below" further clarifies the meaning of immeasurable fierce fires [in total six lines;

cited from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, fascicle 19]. "Below" [is read as] "bottom. 6. "Like fish... and so forth. This cites a simile to clarify the manner of experiencing suffering: fierce [fires] are present in all six directions.
Fire. When the sinner enters it, he is like a fish entering a griddle; his physical form is scorched and withered, like the fat of a fish that has been consumed.
This corresponds to the lower grade [of suffering].
At the four gates of this city dwell four great copper dogs, their bodies measuring four thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, with fangs and claws as sharp as blades.
They are tall, with eyes like flashes of lightning. Furthermore, there are immeasurable birds with iron beaks that soar through the air with outspread wings, devouring the flesh of the sinners.
The ox-headed hell-wardens have forms like rākṣasas and possess nine tails; their tails are like iron forks.
They also have nine heads, each topped with eighteen horns, and upon each horn are sixty-four eyes. From every single eye, flames burst forth.
Various glowing iron balls burn the flesh of the sinners. Furthermore, when they roar with a single outburst of hatred and anger, their sound is like a thunderclap.

(7) Within the hells, there are three kinds of extraordinary things: first, great copper dogs, whose appearance is terrifying; they flash like lightning. As for the word "dogs," [it refers to] both...
1. The light of the eyes shines and flashes from east to west like a bolt of lightning. 2. Many birds inflict harm;

it signifies the exertion of valor, the momentum of rising up in indignation. 3. The forms and voices of the hell-wardens are terrifying; "bèng" (pronounced *bēng* with a departing tone) means to gush forth or surge up.
Roaring: a sound of fierce indignation, like the growl of a tiger or the thunderous roar of a lion;
at times, it suddenly emits a sound of wrath like a bolt of lightning from a cloudless sky.
Furthermore, immeasurable and boundless wheels of blades descend from the air, entering through the crowns of the sinners' heads and exiting through their feet.
Thereupon, the sinners suffer pain that penetrates to the very marrow of their bones and agony that cuts into their livers and hearts.
Thus they pass through countless years, unable to seek life and unable to seek death. Today, for all such retributions, [they] all bow their heads in prostration.
8. Repenting with a sense of shame and remorse. 9.

"Clearly manifesting the instruments of suffering without interval" explains the uninterrupted nature of time. 10. "Thus, below... explains the uninterrupted nature of time. 11. The two phrases beginning with "seeking birth" [explain the uninterrupted nature of intention].
"Clearly manifesting life without interval. Thus [the text] concludes below. The preceding section has finished the repentance for the retribution of the Avīci Hell;

the following section repents for the remaining various hells. This is largely identical to the "Ten Causes and Six Retributions" in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*; as the text is extensive, it is not cited here.
Next, I further repent for the retribution of having one’s body and head severed upon the mountain of knives and the forest of swords in hell;

I repent for the retribution of being burned and boiled in the cauldron of boiling water and the furnace of burning coals in hell; I repent for the retribution of being scorched and consumed upon the iron bed and the copper pillar in hell.
This is the third chapter, comprising twenty-one minor sections. Among the ten habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), this is that which is summoned and experienced by the habit of anger.

1. The Sword-Tree Forest (*asipattravana*): This is one of the sixteen *yūthavardhana* (increasing realms). 2. The Cauldron of Boiling Water (*kumbhīpāka*): This refers to various types of large copper cauldrons and the like.

It is that which is experienced as the vision of fire within the sixfold mutual retribution (*ṣaḍvidha-pratipratyaya*). 3. Burning (*tāpana*): This means to scorch; it is the state of being scorched to the utmost.
In the Blackened (Kṛṣṇa) Hell, one is not yet scorched, nor has one finished [suffering].

One repents for the retribution of the blade-wheel and the chariot-fire hells, and the sin of being split by gravel. One repents for the retribution of the tongue-pulling and plowing hell, and its agonizing pain.
One repents for the hell where the sea swallows iron balls and molten copper is poured into the mouth, whereby the five internal organs are consumed.
4. The retribution for the sin of being scorched to a pulp. Confession of the retribution for the Iron Grinding Hell, where one's flesh and bones are ground into dust.
5. The meaning of being split open by gravel—gravel being small stones—to be crushed to pieces; the agony of suffering, the utmost extremity of pain.
Sixth: The five internal organs—the heart, liver, spleen, kidneys, and lungs—are the five viscera. Initially they become red and putrid;
finally, they wither and dissolve away due to having swallowed glowing iron balls and molten copper. Seventh: The bones are ground into powder by the habit of anger. Thus it is.

I repent for the karmic retribution of having one’s limbs and joints severed in the Black Rope Hell. I repent for the karmic retribution of distress and suffocation in the Ash River and Boiling Excrement Hell.
I repent for the karmic retribution of having the skin split open and being nakedly frozen in the Salt Water and Cold Ice Hell.
I repent for the karmic retribution of mutual slaughter and injury in the Great Hell of Jackals, Wolves, and Hawks.
8. Black Rope (Kālasūtra): Like the dismemberment of corpses in the world, it involves tearing and scattering [the body].
This is one of the eight hot hells. 9. Boiling Excrement (Kukūla): Excrement that boils and seethes; its vapor is hot and foul-smelling.

One suffers from distress and confusion because, throughout one's life, one used public authority, power, wealth, and status to oppress others. Having incurred a foul reputation, one now suffers from both the stench and the suffocating air.
Response: Ten. Throughout his life, he frequently relied upon or disparaged others, including those who were indifferent or even those who slaughtered cattle and sheep for profit.
Furthermore, it is caused by such acts as stripping others of their clothing and so forth—this is the eleventh. Or, it is like a jackal harming a dog, or a dog harming a jackal;
thus it is said they "harm one another. This results from the habituation of anger, which leads them to inflict mutual injury upon one another.

Repent of the *Khaḍga-nakha* (Sword-Claw) Hell, where beings strike and seize one another, and suffer the retribution of being hacked and pierced. Repent of the *Agni-kunda* (Fire-Pit) Hell, and the retribution of being roasted and grilled.
Repent of the *Dvau-śilā-saṃghaṭṭana* (Two-Stone-Crushing) Hell, and the retribution of having one’s physical frame shattered and broken.
Repent of the *Saṃghāta-Karṇa-kṛṣṇa* (Mass-Conjunction and Black-Ear) Hell, and the retribution of being dismembered and flayed.
12. Generally, the sharp edge of a blade turned downward is called a *kṣura* (spur). It refers to striking with the hand like the claws of a rooster or an eagle, or plucking and seizing.
One may strike with a blade or pierce with a weapon, such as the "sharp-edged blades" mentioned in the *Li-ti* (歷聽).
13. This should be understood. 14. *Kē* (pronounced *kě*) is the sound of stones striking one another. 15.

Regarding Saṃghāta (The Crushing Hell): many instruments of suffering arrive together, and beings are crushed by joining forces against one another. It is one of the eight hot hells. Regarding Kālasūtra (The Black-Eared Hell):
because of the crushing [in Saṃghāta], there is not even a hair’s breadth of empty space; thus, both ears and eyes are pitch black. This is the explanation.
I repent for the dark and gloomy Flesh Mountain Hell of being sawn apart, gouged out, or pierced by arrows;
I repent for the retribution for sins of being executed and mangled in the Hell of Being Sawn Apart and Nailed to the Body.

Repent for the retribution of being severed and cut; repent for the retribution of the Iron Club Hell where one is suspended upside down; repent for the retribution of being butchered and dismembered;
repent for the retribution of the Burning Heat and Screaming Hells; and repent for the grievous suffering between the Great and Small Iron Ring Mountains during the long, dark night of ignorance.
Unaware of the retribution for sins against the Three Luminaries, I repent before the Āpāpa Hell,
the Āpāvāpa Hell, the Aṭaṭa Hell, and the Alala Hell.
16. *Cuo* (挫): to break or injure. 17. *Dìng* (去呼; pinyin: qù hū): to nail down. *Duàn* (斷; pinyin: duàn): to sever. 18. Confucian texts still explain the "hanging by the feet" (*dàoxuán*).
The *Mùlián Zhōngyuánjié Yúlánpén* was composed for this purpose. 19. *Jiāorè* (燋熱): the Hell of Intense Heat (*Tāpana*). *Jiàokuàn* (叫喚):
the Hell of Wailing (*Raurava*) and the Hell of Great Wailing (*Mahāraurava*). These are three of the eight hot hells (*bā rèdìyù*) and are characterized by great affliction.
It is also a matter of grievance and injustice (as stated in the *Bao-en jing*). Twenty: Between the two Iron Ring Mountains, Great and Small, there is darkness because the three lights are absent.
From the uppermost to the lowest, the various hells involve different sufferings, and in all of them there are ox-headed jailers.
The horse-faced yakṣas and others, each with great strength, pursue and press upon them from all sides. This is summoned by the power of one's own karma;
it is not bestowed by heaven nor granted by men. One should know this in advance and not delude oneself.
(21) *Papa-babba*, *ṭaṭa-rara*: these are the sounds of endurance of the cold within the *Hima* (Cold) hells.
Thus, within all these eight cold and eight hot hells, there are further eighty-four thousand subsidiary *kalābu* hells as their retinue. To summarize:
the eight cold hells are: first, Arbuda; second, Nirarbuda (these two are named after the way the body is forced by the cold to form blisters that then split).
3. Arbuda; 4. Huhuva; 5. Hahava (these three are named after the sounds produced by those suffering from the cold); 6. Utpala; 7. Padma; 8.
Mahāpadma (these three are named after the way their bodies split open like three kinds of lotuses: first, the blue lotus; second, the red lotus; third, the great red lotus).
These are the eight cold hells (as opposed to the *utsada* or supplementary hells). The eight hot hells have been explained previously. Each of these eight hells has—

There are four gates, and each gate has four subsidiary hells, namely: the Pit of Hot Ashes (Kukūla), the Swamp of Rotting Corpses (Kunapa), the Forest of Sharp Blades (Asipattravana), and the River of Boiling Water (Nadī Vaitaraṇī).

These are the *utsadas* (supplementary hells). There are sixteen such *utsadas*, and when calculated across the eight main hells, there are one hundred and twenty-eight in total; all are called the "Wandering *Utsadas*" (because beings wander through them). [There are those who wander there purely.]
Because their suffering increases further, they are called "Increasing Wanderings" (*Utsada*). Together with the eight great hells, these constitute one hundred and thirty-six seats.

Committing the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) oneself brings about the suffering of the eight great hells; teaching others to commit evil and rebellious acts brings about the sixteen subsidiary *utsada* hells.
As for the eighty-four thousand [hells], they are caused by the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*). "Subsidiary" (*parivāra*) means the same as...

Regarding the term "affiliates" (jùshǔ): this refers to the eight cold and eight hot great hells, which together comprise one hundred twenty-eight *yòuzēng* (accessory) hells. Within these, there are further eighty-four thousand *gélǐ* (sub-segmented) hells that correspond to and are mutually affiliated with the great hells;

by combining these various sufferings, they constitute the great hells. Thus, they are called "affiliates. The great and small hells combine to form a whole, just as a person has a circle of large and small relatives. How tragic!

Five hundred years in the human realm constitutes a single day and night in hell, where the lifespan is one thousand years. Since beginningless time, how many of our parents from past lives who have fallen into such heavy retribution we shall never know! If even the minor hells are like this...

How much more so for the King of the Avīci Hell! There, sixty small kalpas of the human realm constitute a single day and night, and the lifespan is twenty thousand years. What end can there be to such suffering? Furthermore, one must pass through inconceivable periods of time—how painful it is to contemplate this!

Within this, there are the sufferings of sin: the agony of roasting and boiling, the flaying of skin and scraping of flesh, the carving of bones and beating of marrow, the extraction of entrails and the pulling out of lungs—immeasurable sufferings that cannot be heard and cannot be described. *Namo Buddha*.
This refers to the intense suffering within the hells, which is unbearable even to hear described. First, one should join the palms in homage to the Buddha. "Shua" (pronounced *she*) means to scrape.
The Sūtra states: "A single recitation of the Buddha’s name extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.

The Master of Repentance invokes "Namo Buddha," feeling profound compassion for the sentient beings in the hells who, due to the causal conditions of their beginningless evil karma, have incurred such bitter retribution.

We have witnessed this; we ought to reflect deeply within ourselves. Therefore, the following text offers a general supplication, confessing and purifying before the Buddha so that we may be freed from suffering and attain happiness.
Those who are here within these realms today may have been our parents throughout countless lifetimes since beginningless time, or our various kinsmen and associates.
After we and they pass away, we might well fall again into such hells as these.

Today, with cleansed hearts and earnest prayers, we prostrate ourselves, bowing our heads to the ground before the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Bodhisattvas of the great earth, seeking their compassion and repenting our transgressions.
May all these retributions for their sins be utterly extinguished.
This is for the purpose of collectively extinguishing the sins of those within this hell, together with their fellow practitioners and virtuous friends.

They cleanse their minds, prostrate themselves, and repent with sorrow; their three karmas are thus filled with sincerity. (Question: What Dharma should be preached to the assembly in hell? Answer: One should preach that the nature of sin is fundamentally empty.)
Neither existing within, nor without, nor in between, may they cause a single thought-moment to transcend the ten stages at once.

Having completed the repentance for the retributions of the hells and so forth, I vow that by the merit produced from this repentance for the retributions of the hells and so forth, the iron city of Avīci shall be immediately destroyed and entirely transformed into a Pure Land.
May the names of the evil paths and all other hells, as well as all instruments of suffering, be turned away and [transformed].

The conditions of suffering—the mountains of knives and trees of swords—transformed into jeweled groves; the boiling cauldrons and glowing coals became lotus flowers from which beings were born through transformation;
and the ox-headed hell-wardens abandoned their cruelty, giving rise to compassion and harboring no evil thoughts.
Thus, the sentient beings in the hells were freed from the fruits of suffering and ceased to create further causes.
This is the aspiration to be free from suffering and to attain happiness. "The other hells" refers to the sixteen hells, extending even to the subsidiary hells (*upapatti-naraka*).

"Instruments of suffering" refers to the implements used for inflicting additional torment. "Transformed into" means they become or turn into [such things]. The four lines concerning the mountain of blades (*śastra-parvata*) are as follows:
That which is suffering is itself bliss. Below the "ox-head" [hell], that which is the thought of cruelty is itself the mind of compassion.

Once the sentient beings in hell have departed from suffering, they will no longer create the causes for further imprisonment. The above clarifies the departure from suffering; below, it clarifies the attainment of bliss.

They experience equal peace and bliss as in the third dhyāna. Having simultaneously and together aroused the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment and performed repentance, they single-mindedly believe in and pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem.

"Equally experiencing" means receiving [it] with complete equanimity. The "sublime joy apart from rapture" constitutes the Third Dhyāna (1. Parittaśubha Heaven; 2. Apramāṇaśubha Heaven; 3. Śubhakṛtsna Heaven).

This is the supreme bliss among humans, to which nothing can equal it. Being free from the sexual desires of men and women, those who take the joy of dhyāna as their sustenance give rise to the mind set on the Unsurpassed Way—that is, they give rise to the mind of Unsurpassed, Perfect, and Complete Enlightenment—at that very moment.

The phrase "those in prison and those at the altar speak forth simultaneously" means they all utter [the names] together at once (at the end of the section on repentance, this concludes the preceding and introduces what follows).
Namo Vairocana Buddha. Namo our Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha.
Namo Amitābha Buddha. Namo Maitreya Buddha.
Homage to the Buddha Dragon-Species Supreme Honored King. Homage to the Buddha Dragon Sovereign King.
Homage to the Buddha Jewel Victorious. Homage to the Buddha Awakened Flower Samādhi Sovereign King.
Homage to the Buddha Kāṣāya Banner. Homage to the Buddha Lion’s Roar.
Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. Homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva. Homage to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
Homage to Mahāvyūha Bodhisattva. Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, one next performs repentance. Having already completed the repentance for retribution in the hells, one shall now, in turn, perform repentance for the retribution of the three evil realms.

Within the text, two layers of phrasing conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one. This concerns the repentance for removing the retribution of the three evil realms (the animal realm, the hungry ghost realm, and... within the category of karmic results.

Including the asuras and the aforementioned hells, there are four [realms]. "Retribution" refers to recompensing one for their past causes. The following citation from the sutra provides a general explanation, divided into five sections.
In the sutra, the Buddha says: "Because those with many desires seek much profit, their suffering and affliction are also many. As for those who know contentment..."
Even though one lies upon the ground, one still considers it pleasant; yet one who lacks contentment, even if dwelling in heaven, finds it unsatisfactory.
First, this is a contrast between contentment and lack of contentment regarding one's dwelling. "Cheng" (稱) means to fulfill; "yu" (欲) refers to the five desires.
To find them unsatisfactory means that the more one seeks and the more one obtains, the more one remains lacking. The *Cittabhūmi-parivarta* states: "If one has few desires..."
One who is able to be content should dwell in an araṇya (forest hermitage). A great sūtra states: "The practice of contentment is praised by all Buddhas;
one should joyfully practice it throughout one's life. Siṃhanāda asked the Buddha:

"What is the difference between having few desires and being content? The Buddha replied: "Having few desires means not seeking and not taking; being content means, upon receiving little," [remaining satisfied].
To regret [past misdeeds] and not seek after desired things in the future is having few desires (*alpeccha*). To obtain [possessions] and not be attached to them is contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*).

Not seeking honor and respect is having few desires; obtaining [such honors] and not accumulating them is contentment. (There are further four phrases for detailed analysis, as explained at length in the sūtra.)
Furthermore, to remain far removed from all worldly affairs is called "having few desires. Once having left the household life, not giving rise to a mind of regret is called "contentment.
Having attained contentment, to dwell near a secluded place is called "tranquility. One who lacks contentment does not delight in seclusion;
however, one who possesses contentment always delights in empty stillness. Sitting upright and not lying down, or beneath a tree...
Below [the tree], or in a cemetery, or in an open space—whichever grassy spot is available—he sits upon it. He eats by means of alms-food, satisfied with whatever he obtains;
he either eats in a single sitting or does not exceed one meal a day. He keeps only three robes, robes made of rags from refuse, or woolen garments.
This is called having few desires (*alpeccha*). Having practiced these matters, his mind feels no regret; this is called being content (*saṃtuṣṭa*). Thus it is.
"Practitioner," Kāśyapa, such a person is indeed one who,
when suddenly faced with an urgent calamity in this world, is able to relinquish wealth regardless of its quantity;
yet they do not realize that this body stands upon the edge of the deep pit of the three miserable realms, and that with but a single breath not returned, it shall surely fall.
2. Explained in contrast to birth and death, it reveals the bitter retribution of stinginess: the three paths of fire, blood, and blades (the path of fire refers to hell, so named from its heat;

the path of blood refers to the animal realm, so named from their mutual devouring; the path of blades refers to the hungry ghost realm, so named from being driven by swords and staves). The pit (in ancient texts written as *keng*).

"Also 'to fall into' (which, compared to the deep pits and perilous realms within the afflictive hindrances, or being brought before the official gate for one's crimes and seeking rescue by every possible means—cannot even be illustrated as being a hundred thousand million times more painful than the sufferings of hell; this is the response)."
Suddenly, a spiritual friend exhorted him to cultivate meritorious deeds, urging him to prepare the provisions for wholesome dharmas in the future;
yet, clinging to this stingy mind, he refused to act upon the principle. One who acts in such a manner is utterly foolish and deluded.
3. Not receiving the good teachings, he busies himself with the refined sounds of the Central Plains; his reading fills [his ears] with the "yíng" (映) rhyme of the *Hóngwǔ yùn*. This is "zào" (造).

A virtuous friend, pitying him for his suffering, exhorts him to cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom, and to perform various meritorious deeds—all of which are provisions for future transcendence.
"Zào" (造) means to create. "Lǐ" (理) means to cultivate (corresponding to the character "xiū" [修] above). The Holy Teachings...
Because it is not based [on the truth], it is refuted by saying:
"This is utterly foolish and deluded. Why is this so? In the sutras, the Buddha said: "At birth, one does not bring a single coin; at death, one likewise does not take a single coin away.
To toil the body and amass wealth for these things leads only to anxiety and distress; it benefits oneself not at all, but is merely in vain."
He has nothing; he has no goodness upon which to rely and no virtue to depend on. Consequently, when his life ends, he will fall into the various evil realms.
For this reason, today I take refuge in the Triple Gem and sincerely repent.
Investigating the cause of ignorance and delusion (4). Quoting the scriptures to provide proof: "To carry" means to possess.
One exerts one's body and accumulates wealth, yet the mind is constantly filled with anxiety and distress. At death, nothing is taken along; it serves only as a resource for others.
What benefit is there for oneself? Because one is stingy and does not cultivate merit, one possesses neither goodness nor virtue. Goodness (*śubha*) is the root that eradicates evil;
virtue (*guṇa*) is the essence of the myriad virtues. Therefore, the following section concludes the preceding general confession of the retribution of stinginess and greed.

Below, the three paths are separately opened and repented in sequence. First, one repents of the path of animals (*tiryagyoni*). As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The fundamental cause of sentient beings is the sin of craving for things; when this sin is exhausted, they encounter objects and take form, being called 'strange ghosts' (*piśāca*).

The rest is as explained in the sutra. Furthermore, among the three miserable realms, there are fixed karmas. For example, the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*) are fixed in the three miserable realms, while the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) are fixed in the human and heavenly realms.

Among the ten unwholesome dharmas, there are superior, middling, and inferior grades. Due to superior causes and conditions, one receives the body of a hell-being; due to middling causes and conditions, one receives the body of an animal; and due to inferior causes and conditions, one receives the body of a hungry ghost (*preta*). This section below is divided into six parts.
Next, one further repents for the realm of animals. Within this realm, there is no conscious awareness of the retribution for one's sins. One repents for the retribution of the animal realm:
bearing heavy burdens and pulling plows to repay the debts incurred by others in past lives.
First, as for animals: because they lack wisdom during the causal stage, even if they encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they are unwilling to accept his instruction;
thus, they incur the retribution of ignorance and lack of discernment. Second, the explanation of the text and its meaning is as previously stated.
I repent for [the karmic retribution] within the realm of animals, where one lacks autonomy and is hacked and stabbed by others;
I repent for the karmic retribution of being footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed within the realm of animals.
Third: Within the human realm, one’s mind is enslaved and never at rest; therefore, in the state of fruition, one lacks sovereignty.

One may be beheaded by another, or have one’s neck pierced, or have one’s limbs butchered, or have the flesh of one’s body carved away—sliced and hacked by thousands of knives and ten thousands of blades.
What manner of suffering is this? The previous chapter spoke of repaying debts with labor while alive; this clarifies what follows after death.

Fourth, they repay their debts with their own flesh, blood, and marrow, disregarding the pain. Those without feet include those on land, such as earthworms and the like, and those in water, such as eels and the like.
Those with two feet include those in the air, such as crows, sparrows, doves, and pigeons, as well as those that travel on land.
Such as chickens, geese, ducks, and the like; four-legged animals such as large donkeys, mules, camels, oxen, horses, and the like; small animals such as dogs, sheep, cats, mice, and the like;
aquatic creatures such as turtles, tortoises, and the like; and many-legged creatures such as centipedes, millipedes, and the like.
I repent for the karmic retribution of being devoured by various small insects within the feathers and fur,
or the scales and shells, of my body while in the realm of animals.

5. *Shà* (唼): The appearance of gathering food (as in the *Hànshū*, where it says "sucking blood"). Among beasts, the lion and elephant are the longest in fur; among birds, the phoenix is the longest in plumage;
among creatures with scales and shells, the dragon and *jiāo* are the longest. The rest may be inferred. Furthermore, among winged creatures, for example, the rooster possesses the five virtues;

the crow knows of impending misfortune; the magpie knows of good fortune; and the swallow and wild goose know the seasons. Among four-footed animals, for example, the dog and horse possess righteousness; the dog, in particular, [is loyal] to the end.
One does not turn one's back on one's master. A horse is capable of repaying kindness; those who today turn their backs on gratitude are worse than even dogs and horses.
Thus, within the realm of animals, there are immeasurable retributions for such offenses. Today, with utmost sincerity, I repent them all.
Six. Summary of Receiving Retribution. Next, the repentance for the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"The karmic deeds of the perilous and evil hungry ghosts arise from a mind of greed and stinginess that accumulates wealth, desiring long-lasting prosperity.
They extensively accumulate various evils and do not practice giving. When śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or those who are ill or impoverished come to beg..."
In their hearts they give rise to stinginess and envy; they are unwilling to give, they do not perform meritorious deeds, and they do not uphold the precepts.
Due to these causes and conditions, they fall among the hungry ghosts, divided into five sections.

Next, one further repents for the retribution of the hungry ghost realm, where one suffers from hunger and thirst for hundreds of thousands of myriads of years, never having heard the names of even water or broth;
one repents for the retribution of consuming pus, blood, excrement, and filth as a hungry ghost.
First: The Mahāyāna Sūtra states that when sentient beings are born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), their lifespan lasts for immeasurable hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of years.
They do not even hear of water or grain; how much less could they see it? Even if they manage to perceive water and reach it, it immediately transforms into fierce flames, pus, and blood.
Furthermore, even if they do not transform, many people will hold spears and lances to shield and seize them, preventing them from moving forward.
Even if it rains, the rain turns into fire upon their bodies. Such is the retribution of suffering for hungry ghosts.
For the sake of transforming sentient beings, the Bodhisattva makes a vow to manifest such a body. Second, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "Those born among hungry ghosts may eat vomit."
[They consume] broth, fat, flesh, pus, blood, excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva. Their lifespans are immeasurable.
When they repent and move their bodies as hungry ghosts, all their limbs and joints are set ablaze by the retribution of their sins.
Third. The Sūtra says: "If one receives an object entrusted by another and refuses to return it, one will be reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
First, they dwell among humans; if a person travels at night, they may be seen. Second, they dwell five hundred *yojana* beneath Jambudvīpa, or they dwell in the ocean or on oceanic islands.
Their evil-minded retinues are immeasurable in number; briefly stated, they are as follows."

There are thirty-six kinds; here I shall cite eight of them: 1. *Juhkhu* (Flame-mouth): [They] emit fierce fire from their mouths, while smoke issues from their limbs and joints. 2. *Sūcīmukha* (Needle-throat): Their bellies are as large as drums, while their necks are like needles;

their physical form is emaciated and withered. 3. *Pūtimukha* (Foul-mouth): Their breath is foul and stinking, such that its odor cannot be endured. 4. *Mahāgalagaṇḍa* (Great Goiter): A goiter grows upon their necks, and they consume the pus and blood [of others].

Fifth, Needle-Haired (whose hair emerges like needles and pierces the body). Sixth, Foul-Haired (whose body hair is so foul and filthy that it is unbearable to smell). Seventh, Obtaining Discarded (eating what others have discarded to satisfy hunger).
Eighth, Obtaining Lost (only eating things after they have been lost and are no longer usable). One day and one night for these beings is equivalent to ten years for humans;
five hundred such years constitute a single lifetime, which is the retribution of having a mouth of flames and a scorched body.
4. Repenting for the retribution of the hungry ghosts whose bellies are vast and throats are narrow.
This is the same as the second type of ghost mentioned previously, who suffer from distended bellies and needle-like throats.
Thus, all the immeasurable sufferings within the realm of hungry ghosts, we today prostrate ourselves in supplication and repent them all.
5. Summary and Question. Regarding animals and hungry ghosts: what Dharma is taught to deliver them? Answer:

It is taught that they must sever fundamental ignorance at its root, thereby causing them to abandon hunger, thirst, and the feverish afflictions of their state, so that they may be reborn among humans or devas; thus, they cross over the path of these two sufferings.
The repentance for the realm of hungry ghosts is concluded. Next is the repentance for the realm of asuras, which constitutes the fourth major section and is divided into four subsections.
Next, one further repents for all the spirits and ghosts within the realm of the asuras, regarding the retributions for their crimes of flattery, sycophancy, arrogance, and deception.

First, the asura: this is translated as "non-deva. Although in their causal stage they wished to obtain a celestial body, because they did not believe in right action and the power of the field of merit, they instead obtained the state of an asura.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that among the sentient beings of the desire realm, there are three...
Planting roots of goodness yields the fruit of rebirth in the higher realms as gods; the middle grade yields the fruit of rebirth as humans; and the lower grade yields the fruit of rebirth as asuras.
Because the fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana*) shroud the minds of asuras, their hearts are largely crooked and perverse, making it extremely difficult for them to attain the Way.

Although the gods are also subject to these fetters, they possess straightforward minds and believe in the Way. Thus, although asuras resemble the gods, because they are close to the Way yet find it so difficult to reach, [they fall into this state].
They dwell beneath humans; they are the enemies of the heavens, known as the Asura Kings. Within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), they can manifest transformations of any size at will.
*Āyu* means flattery; *chān* means sycophancy or artful speech; *jiāo* refers to arrogance; and *zhà* means deception or falsehood. (There are four types of Asuras. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"If among the realm of ghosts (*preta*), by the power of protecting the Dharma, one achieves supernatural penetration and enters the void—this is an Asura born from the egg. This belongs to the ghost realm (*pretagati*)."*)

[They are] included therein. If, among the devas, their merit is exhausted and they fall, the place where they dwell is adjacent to the sun and moon. These asuras are born from a womb and are included within the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*).

There are asura kings who uphold the world, whose power penetrates all and is fearless, and who can contend for power with Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings. These asuras exist through transformation and are included within the deva realm (*deva-gati*). Inferior asuras are born in the midst of the great ocean; by day they roam in the void, and at night they return to the water to dwell.

These asuras exist due to moisture and are included within the animal realm (*tiryagyoni-gati*). The aforementioned asura kings dwell at the bottom of the great ocean, beside Mount Sumeru; the city where they reside is named *Prabhā* (Radiance), eighty *yojanas* in length and breadth, and their lifespan is five thousand [years].
One year [of the hells] is equivalent to five hundred years in the human realm.
Herein lies the repentance for the retribution of sins committed within the realm of ghosts and spirits: carrying sand and bearing stones to fill rivers and block the seas.
2. In the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is said that in Kuśinagara there were three hundred thousand powerful wrestlers. The Buddha dispatched Maudgalyāyana to subdue them.
Although Maudgalyāyana taught and transformed them for five years, he was unable to cause even a single person to receive the Dharma.

At one time, when these wrestlers heard that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, they gathered on a level road. The Buddha then manifested a transformed body in the likeness of a śramaṇa and went to where the wrestlers were.
With his three toes, he dug out a massive rock. Upon seeing it, the Malla conceived a sense of inferiority toward himself.
The man said, "Are you able to move this rock so that it leaves the path? I shall lift this rock with my hand and hurl it as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven;
I shall then catch the rock again, place it in my right palm, and blow upon it with my mouth until it is shattered like fine dust. He then...
He preached the Dharma for the Mallas, and they all gave rise to the bodhicitta. Such an action would have been excellent.

Now, by carrying stones, you will undergo retribution throughout long kalpas—perhaps filling rivers to create dry land or damming seas to form sandbars. This is why the banks of rivers and seas are constantly subject to shifting tides and never remain the same;
it is because they have been blocked in such a manner. Question: What Dharma is taught to deliver those in the asura realm?
Answer: He taught the Dharma of non-self to cause them to abandon arrogance and negligence, and to abide in the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).
As stated in the Vaipulya assembly, the Tathāgata bestowed a prophecy upon the asura kings, saying: "In a future age, these shall encounter Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
in the eon named 'Good Name' (*Suvikhyāta*), they shall attain Buddhahood, and all such Tathāgatas shall be named 'Good Name'."
I repent before the ghosts, spirits, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, and all evil demons who, having committed offenses, receive this hideous retribution for their sins by devouring flesh and blood alive.
Third, the rākṣasa is a ghost that eats humans; it specifically devours the vital essence. Within the human heart, there are seven drops of sweet [essence].
Water. It nourishes and sustains the spirit. If a ghost drinks one drop, it causes a person’s head to ache; three drops cause them to faint; seven drops and they die.
If one recites the mantra with single-minded concentration, one will immediately be delivered from this calamity.
The Kumbhāṇḍas are fearsome ghosts. A Great Sūtra says: "When a Bodhisattva sees sentient beings afflicted by ghosts, he immediately makes this vow: 'May I take on the body of a ghost.'"
A body of great stature, a robust body, and a body with many followers—may they hear of this and see it, so that their illness may be immediately cured.
Asuras are here translated as "those who lack physical beauty"; therefore, they are said to receive a retribution of ugliness.
Thus, for all the immeasurable and boundless retributions for sins within the realm of ghosts and spirits,
today I prostrate toward the Buddhas of the ten directions and the great earth Bodhisattvas, seeking their compassion and repenting so that they may all be completely extinguished.
IV. Conclusion. Having completed the repentance for the three retributions above, the following section sets forth vows to seek the merit of accomplishing the Three Paths.
To extinguish evil and promote good must necessarily rely on the power of the Dharma of repentance; thus, the text is divided into four sections.
I vow that by virtue of this repentance for the retribution of animal births and the merit thereby produced, in birth after birth and life after life, may the defilement of ignorance be extinguished;
may I recognize the conditions of my own karma, with wisdom shining brightly, and may the body of the evil realms be severed.
First: The retributions of animals are not uniform; hence the term "equal" (or "various"). "Folly" refers to having many desires and many cravings, as well as a lack of knowledge and understanding.

Because of this folly and lack of wisdom, one receives the retribution of an animal. Now that the nature of wisdom has been opened and clarified, one will no longer be defiled by the impurities of the animal realm.
"Karmic conditions" refers to the accumulation of physical suffering to repay debts, such as being slaughtered, cut apart, or devoured.
Since the conditions of karma have been thus understood through consciousness, I vow that wisdom shall shine brightly and the suffering bodies of the evil realms be severed;
all this is the power of repentance.
I vow that by the merit produced from repenting for the retributions of hungry ghosts and others, I may forever be free from stinginess and greed in birth after birth and life after life.
Regarding the suffering of hunger and thirst: one constantly partakes of the nectar of immortality and the flavor of liberation.
Second, due to the cause of stinginess and greed, one undergoes the fruit of hunger and thirst. This suffering involves the body’s fires flaring up, a distended belly, and a constricted throat.
"Constantly partaking of the nectar of immortality" means being forever free from thirst; "attaining the flavor of liberation" means being forever free from hunger.
I vow that through the merit produced by this repentance for the retributions of ghosts, spirits, and asuras, may I, in birth after birth and age after age, be upright and sincere without flattery;
may I be free from the causes of wrong livelihood and eliminate the fruits of ugliness, thereby bringing benefit and fortune to humans and devas.

Third, "substance" (*zhì*) means rectitude and reality (according to the *Shìfǎ*: "Loyalty and rectitude without depravity is called substance"). If one manifests extraordinary signs for the sake of profit or sustenance, [this is not substance].

To raise one's voice and display an air of authority in order to inspire fear and reverence in others is a state of mind characterized by much crookedness and deviation; it serves as a cause for wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Now, being upright and free from flattery—standing in direct opposition to former habits of sycophancy, arrogance, and deceit—one abandons wrong livelihood.

By cultivating the causes and conditions of right practice, the naturally repulsive fruits are eliminated, and one attains the retribution of physical excellence. Such merit and benefit shall extend universally to both humans and devas.
From this day forth until I reach the site of enlightenment, may I resolutely never again receive retribution in the four evil realms;
except when, out of great compassion for the sake of sentient beings, I dwell therein through the power of my vow without weariness.
Fourth: Reiterating the general confession and making vows is the cause. Reaching the site of practice (sitting at the Bodhi-maṇḍala to attain Buddhahood) is the fruit.
From cause to fruit, one will certainly not again undergo the retributions of the three miserable paths, the asuras, or any of the four evil destinies during the interval.

"Except for the lower [levels]" excludes the vows; it means that one sets aside the arousal of the great compassionate mind and the four great vows of universal salvation (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*) which involve gathering others through "sameness of purpose" (*samānārthatā*) by remaining together with them in the four evil realms (*catur-apāya*) without any thought of satisfaction, solely for the sake of delivering sentient beings. This refers to the four evil realms.

Having already repented for the retributions of the three miserable realms and so forth, we now once again prostrate with earnest entreaty to repent for the remaining retributions of humans and devas.

First, I conclude the preceding section; now, following this, I shall initiate the text on repenting for karmic fruits and retributions, beginning first with the remaining retributions of humans and devas.
We all receive this lifespan of Jambudvīpa; though it is said to be a hundred years, those who complete it are few indeed.
Within that interval, those who meet with untimely death in their prime are beyond measure.
"Bing" means to receive. "Yao-wang" refers to premature death or dying by unnatural means during one's youth.
There are merely manifold sufferings that oppress both mind and body; grief, anxiety, fear, and dread never depart for even a moment.
All of this is because one’s roots of goodness are feeble while evil karma is abundant, causing everything one does in the present to be contrary to one's wishes.
When the fire of suffering sears the mind, the mind finds no joy; when it oppresses the body, the body finds no peace.
